papers.research_question: What is the effect of the feature projector in knowledge distillation, and can an ensemble of projectors improve feature distillation performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the role of the projector in feature distillation, hypothesizing it prevents overfitting to teacher features, and proposes a simple yet effective method using an ensemble of projectors to improve student network performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the positive effect of a projector in feature distillation and shows that an ensemble of projectors can further improve student network performance on image classification tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Adding a projector improves distillation performance even when student and teacher feature dimensions are identical, by disentangling the tasks of feature extraction for classification and feature matching for distillation.
Training a student without a projector leads to overfitting to the teacher's feature distribution, resulting in less discriminative features for classification.
An ensemble of projectors further improves student performance by providing diverse transformed features and improving generalization.
The proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art feature distillation methods on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet across various teacher-student pairs.
Simply increasing the depth or width of a single projector does not improve performance and can degrade it, whereas a horizontal ensemble of shallow projectors is effective.
papers.limitation: The proposed method is only evaluated on image classification tasks; its application to other downstream tasks (e.g., object detection and semantic segmentation) remains for future work.
future_direction: Applying the proposed method to other downstream tasks such as object detection and semantic segmentation.
Exploring how to effectively and efficiently integrate logits and similarity information into the proposed projector ensemble framework.
papers.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers.title: Reactive Model Correction: Mitigating Harm to Task-Relevant Features via Conditional Bias Suppression
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate the unintended overcorrection of model behavior (collateral damage to task-relevant features) when suppressing spurious correlations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a reactive model correction framework that conditionally suppresses artifacts based on model-derived knowledge and XAI insights, minimizing collateral damage to clean samples while reducing reliance on spurious features.
papers.conclusion: Reactive model correction minimizes collateral damage to task-relevant features and demonstrates superior performance over traditional non-reactive post-hoc correction methods.
papers.key_findings:
Artifact concept representations (CAVs) are entangled with non-artifact concepts in the latent space, leading to unintended suppression of valid features when applying global corrections.
Reactive model correction (R-ClArC) preserves model performance on clean samples significantly better than the non-reactive baseline (P-ClArC) while still effectively reducing artifact relevance.
The reactive approach allows for more targeted suppression, such as correcting only for specific predicted classes or when an artifact is detected, reducing harmful overcorrection.
papers.limitation:
The choice of reactive heuristics is not always straightforward, and condition-generating functions may not always be accurate, resulting in the correction not being activated when required.
The method does not fully address all flaws of the underlying correction method (e.g., P-ClArC), such as the entanglement of artifact directions with valid concepts, which can still lead to altered representations even when applied reactively.
future_direction: Application of the reactive principle to other post-hoc correction methods, such as classifier editing, LEACE, and INLP.
Exploration of more granular reactive conditions, such as those based on prediction strategy or artifact relevance.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks are prone to learning and relying on spurious correlations in the training data, which, for high-risk applications, can have fatal consequences. Various approaches to suppress model reliance on harmful features have been proposed that can be applied post-hoc without additional training. Whereas those methods can be applied with efficiency, they also tend to harm model performance by globally shifting the distribution of latent features. To mitigate unintended overcorrection of model behavior, we propose a reactive approach conditioned on model-derived knowledge and eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) insights. While the reactive approach can be applied to many post-hoc methods, we demonstrate the incorporation of reactivity in particular for P-ClArC (Projective Class Artifact Compensation), introducing a new method called R-ClArC (Reactive Class Artifact Compensation). Through rigorous experiments in controlled settings (FunnyBirds) and with a real-world dataset (ISIC2019), we show that introducing reactivity can minimize the detrimental effect of the applied correction while simultaneously ensuring low reliance on spurious features.

papers.title: On the Encoding of Gender in Transformer-based ASR Representations
papers.research_question: How much gender-related information can we linearly erase from an ASR model and what are the implications of linear erasure?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that gender information can be linearly erased from transformer-based ASR models with minimal impact on performance, and reveals that gender is concentrated in the first and last frames in the final layers.
papers.conclusion: This work sheds light on how ASR models encode gender and paves the way to creating usable but speaker-blind embeddings.
papers.key_findings:
Gender can be linearly erased from all layers of Wav2Vec2 and HuBERT without model training.
Linear erasure has minimal impact on ASR performance, as shown by small changes in Word Error Rate (WER).
Gender information is concentrated in the first and last frames in the final layers of the models.
Fine-tuning affects gender encoding, localizing it to specific frames in the later layers.
The ease of gender removal in later layers is due to its localization in shared subspaces within the first and last frame positions.
papers.limitation: lack of non-binary gender labels in the datasets used
papers.abstract: While existing literature relies on performance differences to uncover gender biases in ASR models, a deeper analysis is essential to understand how gender is encoded and utilized during transcript generation. This work investigates the encoding and utilization of gender in the latent representations of two transformer-based ASR models, Wav2Vec2 and HuBERT. Using linear erasure, we demonstrate the feasibility of removing gender information from each layer of an ASR model and show that such an intervention has minimal impacts on the ASR performance. Additionally, our analysis reveals a concentration of gender information within the first and last frames in the final layers, explaining the ease of erasing gender in these layers. Our findings suggest the prospect of creating gender-neutral embeddings that can be integrated into ASR frameworks without compromising their efficacy.

papers.title: Matching the Neuronal Representations of V1 is Necessary to Improve Robustness in CNNs with V1-like Front-ends
papers.research_question: Does precisely matching the distribution of receptive field (RF) properties found in primate V1 (neuronal representations) improve robustness to image corruptions in CNNs with V1-like front-ends, compared to uniform sampling?
papers.core_contribution: Precisely matching the neuronal representations (RF property distributions) of primate V1 in a CNN front-end is necessary to achieve improved robustness to common image corruptions, compared to a front-end with uniformly sampled RF properties.
papers.conclusion: Precisely mimicking the neuronal representations found in primate V1 is necessary to improve robustness in CNNs with V1-like front-ends, suggesting these biological representations are optimized for processing a wide variety of image distributions.
papers.key_findings:
The VOneResNet18 model with biological sampling of GFB parameters shows higher robustness to image corruptions (average relative improvement of 7.85%) compared to the standard ResNet18, and a relative improvement of 8.72% compared to the uniform sampling variant.
Neuronal sub-populations with similar RF properties across the biological and uniform model variants exhibit similar response properties (mean activation, sparseness) and learn similar downstream weights.
The neuronal sub-populations that have the greatest impact on downstream layers differ between the biological and uniform variants, shifting from neurons with high spatial frequency and small RF size (uniform) to neurons with larger RF size and somewhat smaller spatial frequency (biological).
The improvement in robustness from biological sampling is not due to a simple low-pass filtering effect, as both variants contain similar numbers of high spatial frequency neurons and the biological model performs marginally better on clean images.
The non-uniform sampling of the biological distribution is critical for shifting the impactful neuronal sub-populations, explaining the observed difference in model robustness.
papers.abstract: While some convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved great success in object recognition, they struggle to identify objects in images corrupted with different types of common noise patterns. Recently, it was shown that simulating computations in early visual areas at the front of CNNs leads to improvements in robustness to image corruptions. Here, we further explore this result and show that the neuronal representations that emerge from precisely matching the distribution of RF properties found in primate V1 is key for this improvement in robustness. We built two variants of a model with a front-end modeling the primate primary visual cortex (V1): one sampling RF properties uniformly and the other sampling from empirical biological distributions. The model with the biological sampling has a considerably higher robustness to image corruptions that the uniform variant (relative difference of 8.72%). While similar neuronal sub-populations across the two variants have similar response properties and learn similar downstream weights, the impact on downstream processing is strikingly different. This result sheds light on the origin of the improvements in robustness observed in some biologically-inspired models, pointing to the need of precisely mimicking the neuronal representations found in the primate brain.

papers.title: Disentangling the Causes of Plasticity Loss in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: To what extent do known mechanisms of plasticity loss overlap, and how can mitigation strategies be combined to best maintain the trainability of a network?
papers.core_contribution: Plasticity loss can be decomposed into multiple independent mechanisms, and a combination of layer normalization and weight decay is highly effective at maintaining plasticity in nonstationary learning tasks.
papers.conclusion: By addressing multiple independent mechanisms of plasticity loss, we can develop robust learning algorithms for nonstationary problems.
papers.key_findings:
Plasticity loss is driven by multiple independent mechanisms, including preactivation distribution shift, regression target magnitude, and parameter norm growth.
Intervening on any single mechanism is insufficient to avoid plasticity loss in all cases.
A combination of layer normalization and weight decay is highly effective at maintaining plasticity in synthetic nonstationary tasks and naturally arising nonstationarities like reinforcement learning.
The proposed mitigation strategy reduces the combinatorial complexity of searching over mitigation strategies.
papers.abstract: Underpinning the past decades of work on the design, initialization, and optimization of neural networks is a seemingly innocuous assumption: that the network is trained on a \textit{stationary} data distribution. In settings where this assumption is violated, e.g.\ deep reinforcement learning, learning algorithms become unstable and brittle with respect to hyperparameters and even random seeds. One factor driving this instability is the loss of plasticity, meaning that updating the network's predictions in response to new information becomes more difficult as training progresses. While many recent works provide analyses and partial solutions to this phenomenon, a fundamental question remains unanswered: to what extent do known mechanisms of plasticity loss overlap, and how can mitigation strategies be combined to best maintain the trainability of a network? This paper addresses these questions, showing that loss of plasticity can be decomposed into multiple independent mechanisms and that, while intervening on any single mechanism is insufficient to avoid the loss of plasticity in all cases, intervening on multiple mechanisms in conjunction results in highly robust learning algorithms. We show that a combination of layer normalization and weight decay is highly effective at maintaining plasticity in a variety of synthetic nonstationary learning tasks, and further demonstrate its effectiveness on naturally arising nonstationarities, including reinforcement learning in the Arcade Learning Environment.

papers.title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-Based Localization
papers.research_question: How can we produce visual explanations for decisions from a large class of CNN-based models to make them more transparent and explainable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Grad-CAM, a technique that uses gradients flowing into the final convolutional layer to produce coarse localization maps highlighting important image regions for a prediction, applicable to a wide variety of CNN model families without architectural changes or re-training.
papers.conclusion: Grad-CAM is an effective visualization technique for understanding CNN decisions, providing insights into model behavior, failure modes, and biases, and has been successfully applied to image classification, captioning, and VQA tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Grad-CAM produces class-discriminative localization maps that generalize the earlier CAM approach to a broader range of CNN architectures.
Grad-CAM visualizations help diagnose model failure modes, showing that seemingly unreasonable predictions have reasonable explanations.
Grad-CAM is robust to adversarial perturbations and can identify dataset biases, aiding in model generalization and fairness.
Human studies show that Grad-CAM explanations help users establish appropriate trust in predictions and discern a stronger network from a weaker one.
Grad-CAM can be combined with fine-grained visualizations (Guided Backpropagation) to create Guided Grad-CAM, which is both high-resolution and class-discriminative.
papers.limitation:
Grad-CAM produces coarse, low-resolution heatmaps (e.g., 14x14 for VGG/AlexNet).
The discriminative ability of Grad-CAM reduces when applied to earlier convolutional layers or at downsampling layers in architectures like ResNet.

papers.title: FairSteer: Inference Time Debiasing for LLMs with Dynamic Activation Steering
papers.research_question: Can fairness-related concepts be encoded as separable geometric structures in the hidden activation spaces of LLMs, enabling bias mitigation through activation steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FairSteer, an inference-time debiasing framework that detects bias signatures in activations using a linear classifier and applies debiasing steering vectors to dynamically adjust activations, mitigating bias without retraining.
papers.conclusion: FairSteer effectively mitigates social bias in LLMs across multiple tasks through inference-time activation steering, while largely preserving the models' general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
FairSteer improves accuracy and reduces bias scores across six LLMs in question-answering, counterfactual evaluation, and open-ended text generation tasks.
Bias-related features exhibit high linear separability in intermediate transformer layers, supporting geometric intervention.
The method preserves the model's original language modeling and general knowledge task performance.
The debiasing steering vector (DSV) computed from contrastive prompt pairs effectively steers activations from biased to unbiased subspaces.
The biased activation detection (BAD) component is crucial for balancing debiasing efficacy and accuracy preservation.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on a linear classifier may limit detection of complex, non-linear forms of bias.
Effectiveness depends on the quality and representativeness of the biased-unbiased prompt pairs used for DSV construction.
The approach to derive the DSV may not be optimal; the work is a proof of concept rather than a thorough exploration of extraction techniques.
Generalizability to other models, especially large-scale proprietary systems and future architectures, remains uncertain.
future_direction: Refine and enhance the methodology for deriving debiasing steering vectors.
Explore adaptive scaling of the DSV based on the severity of the bias (e.g., using classifier confidence).

papers.title: Neural Redshift: Random Networks are not Random Functions
papers.research_question: What are the inductive biases of neural network architectures that contribute to generalization, independent of gradient-based training?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks have an inductive bias towards functions of a particular complexity (Neural Redshift), observable in random-weight networks, which explains generalization independent of gradient descent.
papers.conclusion: The Neural Redshift provides a fresh explanation for generalization in neural networks independent of gradient-based training and points to avenues for controlling inductive biases.
papers.key_findings:
Random-weight neural networks implement functions of biased complexity, depending on architecture components like activations.
ReLU activations, residual connections, and layer normalization contribute to a simplicity bias (low complexity).
The simplicity bias is not universal; it can be modulated by architecture choices (e.g., weight magnitude, alternative activations).
Transformers inherit similar inductive biases from their building blocks, exhibiting simplicity bias in sequence generation.
Matching the preferred complexity of an architecture to the target function's complexity improves generalization.
papers.limitation: The complexity measures used (frequency, polynomial order, compressibility) do not fully capture the inductive biases of architectures.
future_direction: Characterizing fine-grained differences in inductive biases beyond complexity measures.
Controlling inductive biases to improve generalization on complex tasks or mitigate shortcut learning.
papers.abstract: Our understanding of the generalization capabilities of neural networks (NNs) is still incomplete. Prevailing explanations are based on implicit biases of gradient descent (GD) but they cannot account for the capabilities of models from gradient-free methods nor the simplicity bias recently observed in untrained networks. This paper seeks other sources of generalization in NNs. Findings. To understand the inductive biases provided by architectures independently from GD, we examine untrained, random-weight networks. Even simple MLPs show strong inductive biases: uniform sampling in weight space yields a very biased distribution of functions in terms of complexity. But unlike common wisdom, NNs do not have an inherent "simplicity bias". This property depends on components such as ReLUs, residual connections, and layer normalizations. Alternative architectures can be built with a bias for any level of complexity. Transformers also inherit all these properties from their building blocks. Implications. We provide a fresh explanation for the success of deep learning independent from gradient-based training. It points at promising avenues for controlling the solutions implemented by trained models.

papers.title: Transformers Use Causal World Models in Maze-Solving Tasks
papers.research_question: Do transformers trained on maze-solving tasks acquire causal world models, and how are these models structured and used?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks develop causal world models, with interventions revealing an asymmetry (activation easier than suppression) and positional encodings affect the world model structure.
papers.conclusion: Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks form causal world models that capture maze connectivity, and these representations are used for solving.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers trained on maze-solving tasks acquire causally relevant world models.
Interventions that activate features are more effective than those that remove them (asymmetry).
Models can reason about mazes with more simultaneously active features than seen during training, but fail when the same mazes are provided via longer input sequences.
Positional encoding schemes influence how world models are structured (e.g., Stan uses a compositional code, Terry uses single features).
SAEs are better than linear probes for isolating world models.
papers.limitation: Stan was unable to generalize to sequences containing more connections than it had seen during training, leading to failure in removal interventions.
future_direction: Future research could explore how to impose constraints on AI systems in terms of the features they acquire as a result of training.
Future work could investigate how these findings generalize to more complex environments and tasks.
papers.abstract: Recent studies in interpretability have explored the inner workings of transformer models trained on tasks across various domains, often discovering that these networks naturally develop highly structured representations. When such representations comprehensively reflect the task domain's structure, they are commonly referred to as "World Models" (WMs). In this work, we identify WMs in transformers trained on maze-solving tasks. By using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and analyzing attention patterns, we examine the construction of WMs and demonstrate consistency between SAE feature-based and circuit-based analyses. By subsequently intervening on isolated features to confirm their causal role, we find that it is easier to activate features than to suppress them. Furthermore, we find that models can reason about mazes involving more simultaneously active features than they encountered during training; however, when these same mazes (with greater numbers of connections) are provided to models via input tokens instead, the models fail. Finally, we demonstrate that positional encoding schemes appear to influence how World Models are structured within the model's residual stream.

papers.title: Unraveling the Enigma of Double Descent: an in-depth Analysis Through the Lens of Learned Feature Space
papers.research_question: What is the mechanism behind the double descent phenomenon in deep learning, and how does the presence of noisy data influence its occurrence?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that the double descent phenomenon arises in imperfect models trained with noisy data, and that over-parameterized models interpolate noisy samples among robust data, acquiring the capability to separate information from noise.
papers.conclusion: Double descent is associated with imperfect models learning from noisy data; over-parameterized models use extra parameters to separate noise from information, leading to improved generalization after the interpolation threshold.
papers.key_findings:
The double descent phenomenon is strongly influenced by the presence of noisy data in the training set.
Over-parameterized models that pass the interpolation threshold interpolate correct training data around noisy samples of the same class, effectively isolating the noise.
The prediction accuracy P of noisy labeled data (based on k-NN in the learned feature space) correlates with test performance, indicating models with better generalization isolate noisy data.
The phenomenon is observed across different neural architectures (FCNN, CNN, ResNet) and datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10).
The double descent peak becomes more pronounced with higher ratios of label noise.
papers.limitation:
A comprehensive theoretical framework for the double descent phenomenon is yet to be developed.
The impact of neural network architecture (e.g., depth vs. width) on the underlying mechanisms of double descent is not fully explored.
The k-NN interpretation method is an estimation technique and may not fully capture the complex feature space representations, especially for more complex datasets like CIFAR-10.
future_direction: Developing a deeper theoretical understanding of the double descent phenomenon.
Investigating how variations in network architecture (depth vs. width) influence the double descent mechanism.
Exploring the role of implicit sparsity in feature representations of over-parameterized networks.
papers.abstract: Double descent presents a counter-intuitive aspect within the machine learning domain, and researchers have observed its manifestation in various models and tasks. While some theoretical explanations have been proposed for this phenomenon in specific contexts, an accepted theory for its occurring mechanism in deep learning remains yet to be established. In this study, we revisit the phenomenon of double descent and demonstrate that the presence of noisy data strongly influences its occurrence. By comprehensively analysing the feature space of learned representations, we unveil that double descent arises in imperfect models trained with noisy data. We argue that while small and intermediate models before the interpolation threshold follow the traditional bias-variance trade-off, over-parameterized models interpolate noisy samples among robust data thus acquiring the capability to separate the information from the noise. The source code is available at https://github.com/Yufei-Gu-451/double_descent_inference.git.

papers.title: Interpreting Arithmetic Mechanism in Large Language Models through Comparative Neuron Analysis
papers.research_question: How is arithmetic ability implemented in large language models, specifically the role of attention heads and FFN neurons, and what is the internal logic chain from input to prediction? Additionally, how does the LoRA fine-tuning method work?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Comparative Neuron Analysis (CNA) method to interpret arithmetic mechanisms in LLMs, identifying an internal logic chain of four stages, and applies it to understand LoRA and for model pruning and bias reduction.
papers.conclusion: The paper identifies important attention heads and FFN neurons for arithmetic, proposes the CNA method to construct the internal logic chain, finds LoRA amplifies important FFN neurons, and applies CNA to model pruning and editing.
papers.key_findings:
Arithmetic ability is localized in a few attention heads (arithmetic heads), each specializing in distinct operations.
The internal logic chain from input to prediction consists of four stages: feature enhancing, feature transferring, feature predicting, and prediction enhancing.
LoRA enhances prediction probabilities by amplifying the coefficient scores of important FFN neurons related to the final prediction.
Model pruning retaining only 5% of deep FFN neurons identified by CNA maintains performance on arithmetic tasks.
Model editing by zeroing 18 FFN neurons identified by CNA reduces gender bias by 35.7%.
papers.limitation:
The case studies rely on projecting vectors in vocabulary space, which is empirically interpretable but lacks complete theoretical foundation.
There is a lack of standardization across various studies regarding attribution methods (e.g., different intervention methods).
A potential risk is that attackers can identify and edit important neurons to change model behavior maliciously.
future_direction: Further investigation of the multiplication heads which do not significantly impact accuracy.
Explorations on different datasets for gender bias reduction.
Distinguishing whether a model has been edited to prevent malicious use.

papers.title: Explaining Grokking in Transformers through the Lens of Inductive Bias
papers.research_question: How do inductive biases in the transformer’s learning process control the rate of grokking?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that architectural and optimization choices (inductive biases) control grokking in transformers, and that grokking is more nuanced than a lazy-to-rich transition, with generalization emerging predictably with feature compressibility.
papers.conclusion: The network learns features richly throughout, and generalization emerges predictably with feature evolution across different modulators of inductive bias.
papers.key_findings:
Layer Normalization position strongly modulates grokking speed by shaping shortcut-learning and attention entropy.
Using readout scale as a control for lazy training can be confounded by learning rate and weight decay in adaptive optimizers.
Features evolve continuously throughout training, suggesting grokking in transformers can be more nuanced than a lazy-to-rich transition.
Generalization emerges predictably with feature compressibility across different modulators of inductive bias.
papers.limitation:
The work is restricted to transformers learning modular addition under adaptive optimizers, so findings may not apply to other settings.
The study is not an exhaustive investigation of all possible layer normalization positions.
The main manuscript focuses on one-layer transformers, though findings also hold for depth 3 transformers.
future_direction: Future work may utilize the compressibility measure for grokking setups at large.
Extending the study to other settings beyond modular addition and adaptive optimizers.
papers.abstract: We investigate grokking in transformers through the lens of inductive bias: dispositions arising from architecture or optimization that let the network prefer one solution over another. We first show that architectural choices such as the position of Layer Normalization (LN) strongly modulates grokking speed. This modulation is explained by isolating how LN on specific pathways shapes shortcut-learning and attention entropy. Subsequently, we study how different optimization settings modulate grokking, inducing distinct interpretations of previously proposed controls such as readout scale. Particularly, we find that using readout scale as a control for lazy training can be confounded by learning rate and weight decay in our setting. Accordingly, we show that features evolve continuously throughout training, suggesting grokking in transformers can be more nuanced than a lazy-to-rich transition of the learning regime. Finally, we show how generalization predictably emerges with feature compressibility in grokking, across different modulators of inductive bias. Our code is released at https://tinyurl.com/y52u3cad.

papers.title: From deep learning to mechanistic understanding in neuroscience: the structure of retinal prediction
papers.research_question: How can we systematically extract computational mechanisms from deep neural network models of biological sensory processing, and do these mechanisms match those in the brain?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a systematic model reduction approach combining dimensionality reduction and attribution methods to extract computational mechanisms from deep CNN models of the retina, revealing how the retina acts as a predictive feature extractor.
papers.conclusion: Deep CNN models combined with model reduction can yield conceptual insights into computational mechanisms in the brain, and in the retina, a single model with multiple nonlinear pathways can explain diverse retinal phenomena.
papers.key_findings:
For omitted stimulus response, a reduced model with three pathways (1 OFF, 2 ON) explains the shift in burst peak with flash frequency.
For latency coding, a dual pathway mechanism of slow ON and fast OFF bipolar cells explains the latency shift.
For motion reversal, two channels with nonlinear interactions explain the burst and fixed latency.
For motion anticipation, direction-sensitive inhibition truncates the lagging edge, shifting the peak forward.
The approach validates deep CNNs as a method for generating veridical scientific hypotheses about neural mechanisms.
future_direction: Systematic exploration of universality and individuality across different model initializations, architectures, and recordings.
Extending the model reduction procedure to obtain multilayer reduced models for deeper CNNs of higher cortical regions.
Using complex models to design new stimuli that elucidate functional reasons for model complexity.
papers.abstract: Recently, deep feedforward neural networks have achieved considerable success in modeling biological sensory processing, in terms of reproducing the input-output map of sensory neurons. However, such models raise profound questions about the very nature of explanation in neuroscience. Are we simply replacing one complex system (a biological circuit) with another (a deep network), without understanding either? Moreover, beyond neural representations, are the deep network's computational mechanisms for generating neural responses the same as those in the brain? Without a systematic approach to extracting and understanding computational mechanisms from deep neural network models, it can be difficult both to assess the degree of utility of deep learning approaches in neuroscience, and to extract experimentally testable hypotheses from deep networks. We develop such a systematic approach by combining dimensionality reduction and modern attribution methods for determining the relative importance of interneurons for specific visual computations. We apply this approach to deep network models of the retina, revealing a conceptual understanding of how the retina acts as a predictive feature extractor that signals deviations from expectations for diverse spatiotemporal stimuli. For each stimulus, our extracted computational mechanisms are consistent with prior scientific literature, and in one case yields a new mechanistic hypothesis. Thus overall, this work not only yields insights into the computational mechanisms underlying the striking predictive capabilities of the retina, but also places the framework of deep networks as neuroscientific models on firmer theoretical foundations, by providing a new roadmap to go beyond comparing neural representations to extracting and understand computational mechanisms.

papers.title: Have Faith in Faithfulness: Going Beyond Circuit Overlap When Finding Model Mechanisms
papers.research_question: How faithful are circuits found by edge attribution patching (EAP), and what is the relationship between overlap and faithfulness? The paper also introduces a new method, EAP-IG, to improve faithfulness.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces EAP-IG, a gradient-based circuit finding method that produces more faithful circuits than EAP, and shows that overlap metrics are insufficient for evaluating circuit faithfulness.
papers.conclusion: When comparing circuits, measuring overlap is no substitute for measuring faithfulness; EAP-IG provides a more faithful alternative to EAP for circuit finding.
papers.key_findings:
EAP-IG circuits are more faithful than EAP circuits on many tasks, though activation patching circuits sometimes outperform both.
Overlap (node or edge) does not always imply faithfulness; moderate overlap does not predict faithfulness well.
EAP-IG scores have higher correlation with activation patching scores for important edges, leading to more faithful circuits.
EAP-IG requires few steps (e.g., m=5) to achieve high faithfulness, making it efficient.
Cross-task faithfulness analysis reveals that circuit mechanisms can be shared across related tasks (e.g., Greater-Than variants) but not always.
papers.limitation:
Testing circuit completeness is challenging, and manually-found 'ground-truth' circuits may be unreliable.
EAP-IG does not always match the performance of activation patching (e.g., on the IOI task).
future_direction: Developing more efficient algorithms for computing faithfulness.
Investigating weighted graph edit distance as a metric that accounts for edge importance.
Exploring methods to ensure circuit completeness in addition to faithfulness.
papers.abstract: Many recent language model (LM) interpretability studies have adopted the circuits framework, which aims to find the minimal computational subgraph, or circuit, that explains LM behavior on a given task. Most studies determine which edges belong in a LM's circuit by performing causal interventions on each edge independently, but this scales poorly with model size. Edge attribution patching (EAP), gradient-based approximation to interventions, has emerged as a scalable but imperfect solution to this problem. In this paper, we introduce a new method - EAP with integrated gradients (EAP-IG) - that aims to better maintain a core property of circuits: faithfulness. A circuit is faithful if all model edges outside the circuit can be ablated without changing the model's performance on the task; faithfulness is what justifies studying circuits, rather than the full model. Our experiments demonstrate that circuits found using EAP are less faithful than those found using EAP-IG, even though both have high node overlap with circuits found previously using causal interventions. We conclude more generally that when using circuits to compare the mechanisms models use to solve tasks, faithfulness, not overlap, is what should be measured.

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: Microscopic and collective signatures of feature learning in neural networks
papers.research_question: What are the collective and microscopic signatures of feature learning in Bayesian shallow neural networks in the proportional regime?
papers.core_contribution: In the proportional regime, feature learning in Bayesian shallow neural networks is characterized by a nonmonotonic distance between class manifolds and finite, data-dependent weight correlations.
papers.conclusion: The squared distance between class manifolds and the finite weight correlations are collective and microscopic signatures of feature learning in Bayesian shallow networks in the proportional regime.
papers.key_findings:
The posterior distance between class manifolds remains unaltered in the infinite-width limit but departs from its prior value at proportional width.
The average squared distance is a nonmonotonic function of temperature, and this nonmonotonicity disappears in the infinite-width limit or when labels are randomized.
The hidden-layer weights become correlated in the proportional regime, undergoing a finite displacement.
The nonmonotonicity of the distance aligns with inversion dynamics observed during gradient descent training, serving as an equilibrium counterpart.
The second-order statistics of the weights depends on input patterns in a way not traceable to the infinite-width limit.
papers.limitation:
The results are limited to standard-scaled neural networks and do not apply to mean-field scaling.
The theory does not characterize feature learning closer to the interpolation threshold.
papers.abstract: Feature extraction - the ability to identify relevant properties of data - is a key factor underlying the success of deep learning. Yet, it has proved difficult to elucidate its nature within existing predictive theories, to the extent that there is no consensus on the very definition of feature learning. A promising hint in this direction comes from previous phenomenological observations of quasi-universal aspects in the training dynamics of neural networks, displayed by simple properties of feature geometry. We address this problem within a statistical-mechanics framework for Bayesian learning in one hidden layer neural networks with standard parameterization. Analytical computations in the proportional limit (when both the network width and the size of the training set are large) can quantify fingerprints of feature learning, both collective ones (related to manifold geometry) and microscopic ones (related to the weights). In particular, (i) the distance between different class manifolds in feature space is a nonmonotonic function of the temperature, which we interpret as the equilibrium counterpart of a phenomenon observed under gradient descent (GD) dynamics, and (ii) the microscopic learnable parameters in the network undergo a finite data-dependent displacement with respect to the infinite-width limit, and develop correlations. These results indicate that nontrivial feature learning is at play in a regime where the posterior predictive distribution is that of Gaussian process regression with a trivially rescaled prior.

papers.title: What do End-to-End Speech Models Learn about Speaker, Language and Channel Information? A Layer-wise and Neuron-level Analysis
papers.research_question: What information (speaker, language, channel) is captured in the representations of pretrained speech models, how is it distributed, and can we identify a minimal subset of neurons encoding these properties?
papers.core_contribution: The study shows that speaker, language, and channel information are distributed and redundantly encoded in pretrained speech models, with complex properties like dialect localized in upper layers of task-specific networks, and that CNNs are competitive with Transformers in encoding these properties.
papers.conclusion: The study provides insights into how pretrained speech models encode speaker, language, and channel information, with implications for interpretability, bias mitigation, and model compression.
papers.key_findings:
Channel and gender information are distributed across the network and redundantly available in neurons.
Complex properties like dialect are encoded only in task-oriented pretrained networks and localized in upper layers.
A minimal subset of neurons can encode a property, and salient neurons are sometimes shared between properties.
The analysis highlights the presence of biases (e.g., gender) in the network.
Pretrained models capture speaker-invariant information, and CNN models are competitive with Transformer models.
papers.limitation: Probing classifiers might memorize the task rather than reflect encoded information, though control tasks were used to mitigate this.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more languages and models
Apply findings for model compression and bias mitigation
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are inherently opaque and challenging to interpret. Unlike hand-crafted feature-based models, we struggle to comprehend the concepts learned and how they interact within these models. This understanding is crucial not only for debugging purposes but also for ensuring fairness in ethical decision-making. In our study, we conduct a post-hoc functional interpretability analysis of pretrained speech models using the probing framework [1]. Specifically, we analyze utterance-level representations of speech models trained for various tasks such as speaker recognition and dialect identification. We conduct layer and neuron-wise analyses, probing for speaker, language, and channel properties. Our study aims to answer the following questions: i) what information is captured within the representations? ii) how is it represented and distributed? and iii) can we identify a minimal subset of the network that possesses this information? Our results reveal several novel findings, including: i) channel and gender information are distributed across the network, ii) the information is redundantly available in neurons with respect to a task, iii) complex properties such as dialectal information are encoded only in the task-oriented pretrained network, iv) and is localised in the upper layers, v) we can extract a minimal subset of neurons encoding the pre-defined property, vi) salient neurons are sometimes shared between properties, vii) our analysis highlights the presence of biases (for example gender) in the network. Our cross-architectural comparison indicates that: i) the pretrained models capture speaker-invariant information, and ii) CNN models are competitive with Transformer models in encoding various understudied properties.

papers.title: Explaining Explanations: Axiomatic Feature Interactions for Deep Networks
papers.research_question: How can we explain pairwise feature interactions in neural networks in a way that satisfies common-sense axioms and is applicable to any architecture?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Integrated Hessians, an extension of Integrated Gradients that explains pairwise feature interactions in neural networks, satisfies proposed axioms, works on any architecture, and outperforms existing methods.
papers.conclusion: Integrated Hessians is a theoretically grounded and empirically effective method for explaining pairwise feature interactions in neural networks, applicable to any differentiable model and providing insights in various domains.
papers.key_findings:
Integrated Hessians satisfies interaction completeness, self-completeness, and other axioms for feature interactions.
The method can be applied to ReLU networks by smoothing with SoftPlus, and requires fewer gradient calls for approximation.
Integrated Hessians outperforms existing methods (Shapley Interaction Index, Contextual Decomposition, etc.) in identifying interactions in synthetic data benchmarks.
The method is computationally efficient for models with many features, scaling better than existing methods.
In NLP, Integrated Hessians reveals intuitive interactions like negation patterns, and in drug response prediction, it identifies biologically plausible drug-drug interactions.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown great promise in explaining neural network behavior. In particular, feature attribution methods explain which features were most important to a model's prediction on a given input. However, for many tasks, simply knowing which features were important to a model's prediction may not provide enough insight to understand model behavior. The interactions between features within the model may better help us understand not only the model, but also why certain features are more important than others. In this work, we present Integrated Hessians, an extension of Integrated Gradients that explains pairwise feature interactions in neural networks. Integrated Hessians overcomes several theoretical limitations of previous methods to explain interactions, and unlike such previous methods is not limited to a specific architecture or class of neural network. Additionally, we find that our method is faster than existing methods when the number of features is large, and outperforms previous methods on existing quantitative benchmarks. Code available at https://github.com/suinleelab/path_explain

papers.title: Meta-Learning the Inductive Biases of Simple Neural Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we map circuit structure to inductive bias? The paper presents a meta-learning tool to extract the inductive bias of learning algorithms.
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a meta-learning tool that extracts the inductive bias of supervised learning algorithms by learning functions that are easy for the circuit to generalise, and demonstrates its utility on synthetic and biological examples.
papers.conclusion: The inductive bias is a promising angle for understanding learning algorithms, and the presented meta-learning tool loosens previous assumptions and can be used to interpret biological circuit design.
papers.key_findings:
The tool recovers the known inductive biases of linear and kernel regression.
It can extract a set of orthogonal functions that characterize the inductive bias of a learner.
It can isolate the impact of specific design choices (e.g., architecture, connectivity) on the inductive bias.
The method works on challenging differentiable learners, such as spiking neural networks trained with surrogate gradient descent.
The tool provides normative explanations for connectomic patterns, such as those in the fly mushroom body, through their effect on inductive bias.
papers.limitation:
Requires access to an input distribution, which is often lacking.
Assumes the circuit performs supervised learning, which may not always hold.
Arbitrary functions are hard to interpret.
future_direction: Extend the framework to unsupervised learning objectives.
Use generative modeling to create input distributions when real data is limited.
Apply black-box optimization techniques to directly extract inductive biases from animals.
papers.abstract: Training data is always finite, making it unclear how to generalise to unseen situations. But, animals do generalise, wielding Occam's razor to select a parsimonious explanation of their observations. How they do this is called their inductive bias, and it is implicitly built into the operation of animals' neural circuits. This relationship between an observed circuit and its inductive bias is a useful explanatory window for neuroscience, allowing design choices to be understood normatively. However, it is generally very difficult to map circuit structure to inductive bias. Here, we present a neural network tool to bridge this gap. The tool meta-learns the inductive bias by learning functions that a neural circuit finds easy to generalise, since easy-to-generalise functions are exactly those the circuit chooses to explain incomplete data. In systems with analytically known inductive bias, i.e. linear and kernel regression, our tool recovers it. Generally, we show it can flexibly extract inductive biases from supervised learners, including spiking neural networks, and show how it could be applied to real animals. Finally, we use our tool to interpret recent connectomic data illustrating its intended use: understanding the role of circuit features through the resulting inductive bias.

papers.title: Latent Neural Representations Analysis and Distillation for Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we effectively distill Transformer models when there is a dimensionality mismatch between teacher and student, and how can analysis of latent neural representations (like outlier dimensions) inform better distillation algorithms?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces two novel distillation methods: Attention Map Alignment Distillation (AMAD) for handling mismatched attention heads between teacher and student models, and Emergent Outlier Focused Distillation (EOFD) which prioritizes critical outlier dimensions in latent representations. It also provides the first systematic analysis of emergent outlier dimensions in Encoder-Decoder T5 and instruction-finetuned Flan-T5 models.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods for analyzing and distilling latent neural representations advance the understanding and acceleration of Transformer inference, with AMAD and EOFD demonstrating state-of-the-art distillation performance and generalization across architectures.
papers.key_findings:
AMAD enables effective distillation between teacher and student Transformers with different numbers of attention heads, outperforming conventional methods on vision-language tasks like VQA and captioning.
Outlier dimensions in T5 and Flan-T5 models, identified by unusually large activation magnitudes, are critical for zero-shot performance and are shared across layers within the encoder or decoder, but differ between encoder and decoder.
EOFD, which focuses distillation loss on these outlier dimensions, achieves state-of-the-art performance on the GLUE benchmark and generalizes across BERT, GPT-2, and T5 architectures.
Distillation with AMAD can compensate for the absence of vision-language pre-training, and in some cases, distilled students outperform pre-trained and fine-tuned teachers.
The growth of outlier magnitude in T5 models is more correlated with increasing layer depth rather than overall model size, contrary to findings in GPT models.
papers.limitation: In some cases, a Teacher attention head may not be similar to any Student head after AMAD distillation, indicating a potential failure mode for knowledge transfer.
papers.abstract: Transformer-backed Large Language Models and Large Vision-Language Models are among the most widely used machine learning models recently. However, due to their enormous size, their behaviors and dynamics become difficult to understand and explain, and their inference speed and cost become slow and forbidding. Therefore, understanding their latent neural patterns and distilling their latent neural representations into smaller, cheaper, and faster models are vital for creating more explainable, accessible, and sustainable machine intelligence. However, knowledge distillation algorithms face an inherent challenge in minimizing the divergence between the neural activation representations of a teacher Transformer and a student Transformer: The latent representation spaces of the smaller Student always have lower dimensionality than those of the larger Teacher. We will address this Transformer distillation dimensionality mismatch or reduction problem by analyzing the neural activation patterns within these latent representation spaces and by proposing corresponding novel algorithms for distilling each group of components of Transformers. Our ultimate goal is to advance the field of understanding and accelerating the inference process of large Transformers by studying their latent neural representations.Specifically, we first develop novel algorithms for aligning the heads within the Multi-Head Attention components of these Transformers for latent neural representation distillation. We propose a new Attention Map Alignment Distillation (AMAD) method for Transformers with multi-head attention, which, unlike previous literature, can work for a Teacher and a Student with mismatched dimensionalities in terms of the numbers of attention heads. Specifically, we soft-align different heads in Teacher and Student attention maps using a cosine similarity weighting. The Teacher head contributes more to the Student heads for which it has a higher similarity weight. Each Teacher head contributes to all the Student heads by minimizing the divergence between the attention latent neural activation distributions for the soft-aligned heads.We then advance the understanding and distillation of the latent neural representations of the Feed Forward Network and Layer Normalization components of these Transformers. Previous literature shows that a small subset of dimensions within the high-dimensional latent neural representation spaces of language Transformers emerge as “outliers”, with weights or latent neuron activations of unusually large magnitudes—several standard deviations from the mean—during pretraining, and seem to encode critical linguistic knowledge in a sparse way. We systematically extend these previous findings on emergent outliers to Encoder-Decoder Transformers and instruction-finetuned models at scale, for the first time. We show that emergent outlier dimensions of the Transformer latent neural representations contribute significantly more to zero-shot performance than non-outlier dimensions. Leveraging our findings, we further propose the Emergent Outlier Focused Distillation (EOFD) method, which prioritizes these critical outlier latent dimensions to address the trade-off among these representation dimensions during distillation. Specifically, we propose a weighted MSE loss to place greater emphasis on the emergent outlier dimensions of the latent neural representations, which are identified by the standard deviations of neuron activation magnitudes.We demonstrate that our AMAD and EOFD distillation algorithms achieve state-of-the-art performance empirically and generalize well to different Transformer architectures. Specifically, for AMAD, we experiment on distilling VL-T5 and BLIP and apply the AMAD loss to their T5, BERT, and ViT sub-modules. We show that, under vision-language settings, AMAD outperforms conventional distillation methods on the VQA-2.0, COCO captioning, and Multi30K translation datasets. We further show that even without VL pre-training, the distilled VL-T5 models outperform corresponding VL pre-trained VL-T5 models that are further fine-tuned by ground-truth signals, and that fine-tuning distillation can also compensate to some degree for the absence of VL pre-training in BLIP models. As for EOFD, we empirically show that it outperforms state-of-the-art distillation methods on the General Language Understanding Evaluation (GLUE) benchmark. We further demonstrate that EOFD generalizes well across Encoder-only BERT, Decoder-only GPT-2, and Encoder-Decoder T5 architectures.

papers.title: Representing Deep Neural Networks Latent Space Geometries with Graphs
papers.research_question: How can we enforce desirable properties on intermediate representations of deep neural networks? The paper proposes to represent latent space geometries with graphs (LGGs) and constrain them to address knowledge distillation, latent embedding design, and robustness.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a methodology to represent latent space geometries with similarity graphs (LGGs) and shows how constraining these graphs can address knowledge distillation, latent embedding design, and robustness in deep neural networks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed formalism of Latent Geometry Graphs (LGGs) is effective for knowledge distillation, latent embeddings, and robustness, and could be applied to other problems such as predicting generalization and understanding decisions in deep learning architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Graph Knowledge Distillation (GKD) using LGGs outperforms relational knowledge distillation (RKD) and baseline in compressing a teacher network to a student network.
Using label variation as an objective function for latent embeddings yields test accuracy comparable to cross-entropy and improves robustness to corruptions.
Using label variation as a regularizer to enforce smooth evolution of geometries across layers improves robustness to adversarial attacks and corruptions.
The proposed graph-based formalism is dimension-agnostic and can compare latent spaces of different dimensions.
The methodology is demonstrated on standard vision benchmarks (CIFAR-10) with ResNet and WideResNet architectures.
papers.limitation: The graph construction method (using cosine similarity or RBF kernel) may be influenced by the curse of dimensionality, and graph normalization is not ideal but helps.
future_direction: Applying the LGG formalism to more problems, such as predicting generalization, improving performance in data-thrifty settings, and understanding how decisions are taken in deep learning architectures.
Improving graph construction methods to better handle the influence of dimension on graph comparison.
Using graph convolutional networks in domains that are not typically supported by graphs.
papers.abstract: Deep Learning (DL) has attracted a lot of attention for its ability to reach state-of-the-art performance in many machine learning tasks. The core principle of DL methods consists of training composite architectures in an end-to-end fashion, where inputs are associated with outputs trained to optimize an objective function. Because of their compositional nature, DL architectures naturally exhibit several intermediate representations of the inputs, which belong to so-called latent spaces. When treated individually, these intermediate representations are most of the time unconstrained during the learning process, as it is unclear which properties should be favored. However, when processing a batch of inputs concurrently, the corresponding set of intermediate representations exhibit relations (what we call a geometry) on which desired properties can be sought. In this work, we show that it is possible to introduce constraints on these latent geometries to address various problems. In more detail, we propose to represent geometries by constructing similarity graphs from the intermediate representations obtained when processing a batch of inputs. By constraining these Latent Geometry Graphs (LGGs), we address the three following problems: (i) reproducing the behavior of a teacher architecture is achieved by mimicking its geometry, (ii) designing efficient embeddings for classification is achieved by targeting specific geometries, and (iii) robustness to deviations on inputs is achieved via enforcing smooth variation of geometry between consecutive latent spaces. Using standard vision benchmarks, we demonstrate the ability of the proposed geometry-based methods in solving the considered problems.

papers.title: Robustified ANNs Reveal Wormholes Between Human Category Percepts
papers.research_question: Q1) have robustified ANN models closed the model-human gap in adversarial sensitivity? And, Q2) can arbitrary human percepts be specifically induced in the low pixel budget regime, where human percepts are believed to be highly robust?
papers.core_contribution: Robustified ANNs can discover low-norm image perturbations ('wormholes') that strongly disrupt or precisely modulate human object category percepts, challenging the assumption that human perception is robust to such perturbations.
papers.conclusion: The prevailing assumption that human categorization is highly robust to low-norm image perturbations is challenged; robustified ANNs reveal nearby 'wormholes' that can strongly and precisely change human percepts, and these models are accurate enough to guide us to those wormholes.
papers.key_findings:
Human object category percepts are massively disrupted by low-norm image perturbations discovered by robustified ANNs, with ~90% error rate at perturbation budget 30.
Robustified ANNs enable precise targeted modulation of human category percepts to specific target categories, achieving ~60% target choice rate at perturbation budget 30.
Robustified ANNs have largely closed the model-human gap in low-norm perturbation sensitivity, though humans require about twice the perturbation strength for matched disruption.
The targeted modulation effect generalizes across different source image distributions (in-distribution, out-of-distribution, arbitrary natural images, uniform noise).
Robustified ANNs can induce composite (hybrid) category percepts by combining features of multiple classes in a single image.
papers.limitation:
It is unknown whether wormholes exist for all start images and all target categories.
Robustified ANN models are imperfect approximations of neurobiology and may not discover all wormholes or may predict non-existent ones.
There is still a residual gap in behavioral alignment between models and humans.
The study focused on ResNet50 architecture and mainly ℓ2-norm perturbations; generalization to other architectures or perturbation constraints is not explored.
The paper does not claim that adversarial training is the mechanism by which robustness in humans emerges.
future_direction: Determine whether wormholes exist for all start images and all target categories.
Explore other architectures and image generation algorithms for discovering wormholes.
Investigate alternative, more biologically plausible mechanisms that may give rise to comparably aligned models.
papers.abstract: The visual object category reports of artificial neural networks (ANNs) are notoriously sensitive to tiny, adversarial image perturbations. Because human category reports (aka human percepts) are thought to be insensitive to those same small-norm perturbations -- and locally stable in general -- this argues that ANNs are incomplete scientific models of human visual perception. Consistent with this, we show that when small-norm image perturbations are generated by standard ANN models, human object category percepts are indeed highly stable. However, in this very same "human-presumed-stable" regime, we find that robustified ANNs reliably discover low-norm image perturbations that strongly disrupt human percepts. These previously undetectable human perceptual disruptions are massive in amplitude, approaching the same level of sensitivity seen in robustified ANNs. Further, we show that robustified ANNs support precise perceptual state interventions: they guide the construction of low-norm image perturbations that strongly alter human category percepts toward specific prescribed percepts. These observations suggest that for arbitrary starting points in image space, there exists a set of nearby "wormholes", each leading the subject from their current category perceptual state into a semantically very different state. Moreover, contemporary ANN models of biological visual processing are now accurate enough to consistently guide us to those portals.

papers.title: The Asymmetric Maximum Margin Bias of Quasi-Homogeneous Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What is the maximum-margin bias of quasi-homogeneous neural networks trained with gradient flow on an exponential loss?
papers.core_contribution: Extends maximum-margin bias theory from homogeneous to quasi-homogeneous neural networks, revealing an asymmetric norm minimization that can degrade robustness and explains neural collapse.
papers.conclusion: The work generalizes maximum-margin bias theory to quasi-homogeneous networks, showing an asymmetric bias that can harm robustness and underlies neural collapse.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient flow on quasi-homogeneous networks minimizes an asymmetric norm (only on highest-rate parameters).
This asymmetric norm minimization can degrade robustness compared to homogeneous networks.
The theory predicts a cascading minimization where unnecessary high-rate parameters are discarded.
Applying the theory to networks with normalization layers reveals a mechanism for neural collapse.
papers.limitation:
Assumption A6 (normalized convergence) is needed for technical reasons but may be weakened.
Assumption A7 (conditional separability) is not always satisfied and limits applicability.
future_direction: Relaxing the assumptions such as conditional separability.
Extending the analysis to other loss functions and optimization algorithms.
Exploring implications for robustness and neural collapse in practical settings.
papers.abstract: In this work, we explore the maximum-margin bias of quasi-homogeneous neural networks trained with gradient flow on an exponential loss and past a point of separability. We introduce the class of quasi-homogeneous models, which is expressive enough to describe nearly all neural networks with homogeneous activations, even those with biases, residual connections, and normalization layers, while structured enough to enable geometric analysis of its gradient dynamics. Using this analysis, we generalize the existing results of maximum-margin bias for homogeneous networks to this richer class of models. We find that gradient flow implicitly favors a subset of the parameters, unlike in the case of a homogeneous model where all parameters are treated equally. We demonstrate through simple examples how this strong favoritism toward minimizing an asymmetric norm can degrade the robustness of quasi-homogeneous models. On the other hand, we conjecture that this norm-minimization discards, when possible, unnecessary higher-order parameters, reducing the model to a sparser parameterization. Lastly, by applying our theorem to sufficiently expressive neural networks with normalization layers, we reveal a universal mechanism behind the empirical phenomenon of Neural Collapse.

papers.title: Feature-Learning Networks Are Consistent Across Widths At Realistic Scales
papers.research_question: Can realistic-width neural networks be accurately described by their infinite-width feature-learning limits?
papers.core_contribution: Feature-learning neural networks in maximal update parameterization (µP) exhibit consistent behavior across widths for loss curves, pointwise predictions, internal representations, and dynamical phenomena at realistic widths, motivating the infinite-width feature-learning limit as a good model for deep learning.
papers.conclusion: Infinite-width feature-learning models effectively capture the behavior of realistic-scale networks, with finite-width deviations accumulating over time, especially in offline settings.
papers.key_findings:
For simple tasks like CIFAR-5m, networks of realistic widths (e.g., 128) show consistent loss and predictions throughout training.
For harder tasks like ImageNet and language modeling, consistency holds early in training but deviations grow systematically with training time.
Finite-width effects include initialization-dependent variance (scaling as 1/N) and a bias that cannot be removed by ensembling narrow networks.
In offline training with data repetition, overfitting can break width consistency and even reverse the 'wider is better' trend for ensembled networks.
A spectral perspective shows that finite-width bias arises from differences in eigenfunction-task alignment of the neural tangent kernel.
papers.limitation: The study only exhibits consistency of the infinite-width limit with training time held fixed, not when training time varies jointly with width.
future_direction: Study limits that vary training time jointly with width to infinity, perhaps along a compute frontier.
papers.abstract: We study the effect of width on the dynamics of feature-learning neural networks across a variety of architectures and datasets. Early in training, wide neural networks trained on online data have not only identical loss curves but also agree in their point-wise test predictions throughout training. For simple tasks such as CIFAR-5m this holds throughout training for networks of realistic widths. We also show that structural properties of the models, including internal representations, preactivation distributions, edge of stability phenomena, and large learning rate effects are consistent across large widths. This motivates the hypothesis that phenomena seen in realistic models can be captured by infinite-width, feature-learning limits. For harder tasks (such as ImageNet and language modeling), and later training times, finite-width deviations grow systematically. Two distinct effects cause these deviations across widths. First, the network output has initialization-dependent variance scaling inversely with width, which can be removed by ensembling networks. We observe, however, that ensembles of narrower networks perform worse than a single wide network. We call this the bias of narrower width. We conclude with a spectral perspective on the origin of this finite-width bias.

papers.title: Its Alive: AI Independence Without Human Prompting
papers.research_question: How can representation engineering (RepE) improve transparency and control of AI systems, particularly for safety-relevant concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces representation engineering (RepE) as a top-down approach to AI transparency, providing baselines like Linear Artificial Tomography (LAT) and demonstrating its applicability to reading and controlling safety-relevant concepts in large language models.
papers.conclusion: RepE is a promising top-down approach for enhancing AI transparency and control, with broad applicability to safety-relevant problems, and can accelerate progress in AI safety.
papers.key_findings:
RepE methods can extract representations of high-level concepts like honesty, utility, emotion, and harmfulness.
LAT achieves state-of-the-art on TruthfulQA, improving zero-shot accuracy by 18.1 percentage points.
Representation control can increase model honesty and reduce compliance with harmful instructions, even under jailbreak attempts.
Emotions are represented in LLMs and can be manipulated to affect model compliance and behavior.
RepE provides traction on inner alignment problems like deceptive alignment by enabling monitoring and control of honesty.
future_direction: Further exploration of RepE for transparency and safety of AI systems.
Investigation of emotion representations and their impact on model behavior and concept of self.
Improving robustness and generalization of RepE methods.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we identify and characterize the emerging area of representation engineering (RepE), an approach to enhancing the transparency of AI systems that draws on insights from cognitive neuroscience. RepE places population-level representations, rather than neurons or circuits, at the center of analysis, equipping us with novel methods for monitoring and manipulating high-level cognitive phenomena in deep neural networks (DNNs). We provide baselines and an initial analysis of RepE techniques, showing that they offer simple yet effective solutions for improving our understanding and control of large language models. We showcase how these methods can provide traction on a wide range of safety-relevant problems, including honesty, harmlessness, power-seeking, and more, demonstrating the promise of top-down transparency research. We hope that this work catalyzes further exploration of RepE and fosters advancements in the transparency and safety of AI systems.

papers.title: Building Reliable Explanations of Unreliable Neural Networks: Locally Smoothing Perspective of Model Interpretation
papers.research_question: How can we build reliable explanations for neural network predictions that are robust to adversarial perturbations and consistent in local neighborhoods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RelEx, a method for generating reliable saliency maps by enforcing local smoothness in the explanation landscape, which improves robustness to adversarial perturbations.
papers.conclusion: RelEx provides reliable explanations by ensuring local smoothness, leading to robust saliency maps that identify relevant features even under adversarial attacks.
papers.key_findings:
