RelEx generates saliency maps that are robust to adversarial perturbations and can retrieve the original class from adversarial examples.
The method outperforms previous explanation methods in terms of robustness and feature relevance.
Theoretical analysis shows a trade-off between explanation complexity (L1 norm) and robustness.
Using a batch of noisy copies and L1 regularization helps in learning robust saliency maps.
RelEx identifies input features relevant to the model output for both the input and its neighboring data points.
papers.abstract: We present a novel method for reliably explaining the predictions of neural networks. We consider an explanation reliable if it identifies input features relevant to the model output by considering the input and the neighboring data points. Our method is built on top of the assumption of smooth landscape in a loss function of the model prediction: locally consistent loss and gradient profile. A theoretical analysis established in this study suggests that those locally smooth model explanations are learned using a batch of noisy copies of the input with the L1 regularization for a saliency map. Extensive experiments support the analysis results, revealing that the proposed saliency maps retrieve the original classes of adversarial examples crafted against both naturally and adversarially trained models, significantly outperforming previous methods. We further demonstrated that such good performance results from the learning capability of this method to identify input features that are truly relevant to the model output of the input and the neighboring data points, fulfilling the requirements of a reliable explanation.

papers.title: Fortified Networks: Improving the Robustness of Deep Networks by Modeling the Manifold of Hidden Representations
papers.research_question: How can we improve the robustness of deep networks to adversarial examples by modeling the manifold of hidden representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes Fortified Networks, a method that inserts denoising autoencoders into the hidden layers of a network to map off-manifold hidden states back to the data manifold, improving robustness to adversarial attacks.
papers.conclusion: Fortified Networks provide a practical and effective method for improving the robustness of deep networks against adversarial examples, with the added benefit of providing a signal for distribution shift via reconstruction error.
papers.key_findings:
Fortified Networks improve robustness against standard adversarial attacks (FGSM, PGD) in both black-box and white-box threat models.
The improvements are not primarily due to gradient masking, as evidenced by similar performance against black-box and white-box attacks and successful unbounded attacks.
Fortification in hidden layers is more effective than in the input space because off-manifold points are easier to detect in the abstract hidden space.
The reconstruction error of the denoising autoencoders serves as a reliable signal for detecting off-manifold examples, indicating distribution shift or adversarial attacks.
The method works with different architectures (convolutional networks, LSTMs) and datasets (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR10, Text8).
papers.limitation: The cost of the proposed method is the extended training time due to the search for adversarial examples and training the autoencoders.
papers.abstract: Deep networks have achieved impressive results across a variety of important tasks. However a known weakness is a failure to perform well when evaluated on data which differ from the training distribution, even if these differences are very small, as is the case with adversarial examples. We propose Fortified Networks, a simple transformation of existing networks, which fortifies the hidden layers in a deep network by identifying when the hidden states are off of the data manifold, and maps these hidden states back to parts of the data manifold where the network performs well. Our principal contribution is to show that fortifying these hidden states improves the robustness of deep networks and our experiments (i) demonstrate improved robustness to standard adversarial attacks in both black-box and white-box threat models; (ii) suggest that our improvements are not primarily due to the gradient masking problem and (iii) show the advantage of doing this fortification in the hidden layers instead of the input space.

papers.title: Removing Spurious Correlation from Neural Network Interpretations
papers.research_question: How do confounders like conversation topic affect the identification of neurons responsible for toxic behavior in LLMs, and how can we adjust for them to remove spurious correlations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a causal mediation approach that controls for confounders (e.g., conversation topic) to remove spurious correlations when identifying neurons responsible for toxic behavior in LLMs, showing that toxicity becomes less localized after adjustment.
papers.conclusion: Adjusting for confounders like conversation topic significantly changes the attribution of toxic behavior to MLP units, and the proposed causal mediation approach can be generalized to other spurious correlations.
papers.key_findings:
Adjusting for conversation topic makes toxicity less localized across MLPs in both Bloomz and Phi-3-mini.
The proposed entropy balancing approach can handle high-dimensional textual data by using PCA and sentence embeddings.
The method requires only one forward pass and avoids out-of-distribution examples.
The DAG in Figure 1 is general and can be applied to other confounders like gender bias and hallucination.
Clustering queries into topics reveals different toxicity rates across topics.
papers.limitation: The positivity assumption required for valid inference might be violated due to deterministic relationship between node activations and questions, though dimensionality reduction alleviates this.
future_direction: Mask the identified nodes to show that toxicity decreases.
Use approaches other than clustering for defining conversation topics.
Apply the method to other confounders like gender bias, hallucination, and factuality.
papers.abstract: The existing algorithms for identification of neurons responsible for undesired and harmful behaviors do not consider the effects of confounders such as topic of the conversation. In this work, we show that confounders can create spurious correlations and propose a new causal mediation approach that controls the impact of the topic. In experiments with two large language models, we study the localization hypothesis and show that adjusting for the effect of conversation topic, toxicity becomes less localized.

papers.title: What Is One Grain of Sand in the Desert? Analyzing Individual Neurons in Deep NLP Models
papers.research_question: How can we identify and analyze individual neurons in deep NLP models? The paper also investigates how localized or distributed linguistic properties are, whether neurons are exclusive to certain properties, and how information distribution differs between NMT and NLM.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes two methods for identifying and analyzing individual neurons in deep NLP models: a supervised Linguistic Correlation Analysis and an unsupervised Cross-model Correlation Analysis, and demonstrates their effectiveness through ablation studies.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes two methods for extracting salient neurons and demonstrates their accuracy through ablation experiments, with potential applications in model distillation and neural architecture search.
papers.key_findings:
Open class categories (e.g., verb, location) are more distributed across neurons than closed class categories (e.g., coordinating conjunction, determiner).
The model recognizes a hierarchy of linguistic properties and distributes neurons accordingly.
Important neurons extracted from Cross-model Correlation overlap with those from Linguistic Correlation (e.g., position neurons).
Ablating top neurons identified by Cross-model Correlation causes significant performance drop, validating the method.
Using only top neurons, classifiers can regain much of the performance, suggesting potential for model distillation.
future_direction: Applying the methods to model distillation and neural architecture search
Exploring recent architectures like Transformer and QRNN
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable evolution of deep neural networks in natural language processing (NLP), their interpretability remains a challenge. Previous work largely focused on what these models learn at the representation level. We break this analysis down further and study individual dimensions (neurons) in the vector representation learned by end-to-end neural models in NLP tasks. We propose two methods: Linguistic Correlation Analysis, based on a supervised method to extract the most relevant neurons with respect to an extrinsic task, and Cross-model Correlation Analysis, an unsupervised method to extract salient neurons w.r.t. the model itself. We evaluate the effectiveness of our techniques by ablating the identified neurons and reevaluating the network’s performance for two tasks: neural machine translation (NMT) and neural language modeling (NLM). We further present a comprehensive analysis of neurons with the aim to address the following questions: i) how localized or distributed are different linguistic properties in the models? ii) are certain neurons exclusive to some properties and not others? iii) is the information more or less distributed in NMT vs. NLM? and iv) how important are the neurons identified through the linguistic correlation method to the overall task? Our code is publicly available as part of the NeuroX toolkit (Dalvi et al. 2019a). This paper is a non-archived version of the paper published at AAAI (Dalvi et al. 2019b).

papers.title: Do We Always Need the Simplicity Bias? Looking for Optimal Inductive Biases in the Wild
papers.research_question: Are there practical applications of machine learning where the simplicity bias is detrimental? In these cases, what do the optimal inductive biases look like?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the simplicity bias of ReLU networks is not universally useful and can be suboptimal for certain tasks. It introduces a method to learn dataset-specific activation functions that can improve generalization by inducing a prior of higher complexity.
papers.conclusion: The simplicity bias is not always beneficial, and tailored inductive biases via learned activation functions can improve performance on tasks where ReLUs are suboptimal, such as regression, tabular data, shortcut learning, and grokking.
papers.key_findings:
For image classification, ReLUs are near-optimal and learned activations resemble smooth variants like GeLUs.
For regression tasks, learned activations improve performance by helping networks represent more complex functions.
For tabular data, learned activations (especially input activation functions) improve accuracy by mimicking decision trees' inductive biases with sharp axis-aligned decision boundaries.
In shortcut learning, learned activations can steer the model towards different features, controlling which spurious feature is learned.
For grokking tasks, learned activations can eliminate grokking by better matching the data complexity, supporting the explanation of mismatch between data and architecture.
papers.limitation:
The optimization of activation functions is difficult and may converge to local optima.
The complexity measure (total variation) captures only one aspect of inductive biases.
future_direction: Designing tailored architectures for specific domains.
Characterizing inductive biases beyond complexity.
papers.abstract: Neural architectures tend to fit their data with relatively simple functions. This "simplicity bias" is widely regarded as key to their success. This paper explores the limits of this principle. Building on recent findings that the simplicity bias stems from ReLU activations [96], we introduce a method to meta-learn new activation functions and inductive biases better suited to specific tasks. Findings: We identify multiple tasks where the simplicity bias is inadequate and ReLUs suboptimal. In these cases, we learn new activation functions that perform better by inducing a prior of higher complexity. Interestingly, these cases correspond to domains where neural networks have historically struggled: tabular data, regression tasks, cases of shortcut learning, and algorithmic grokking tasks. In comparison, the simplicity bias induced by ReLUs proves adequate on image tasks where the best learned activations are nearly identical to ReLUs and GeLUs. Implications: Contrary to popular belief, the simplicity bias of ReLU networks is not universally useful. It is near-optimal for image classification, but other inductive biases are sometimes preferable. We showed that activation functions can control these inductive biases, but future tailored architectures might provide further benefits. Advances are still needed to characterize a model's inductive biases beyond "complexity", and their adequacy with the data.

papers.title: Wormhole Dynamics in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Why do deep neural networks (DNNs) generalize well and converge to global minima despite non-convex loss landscapes and overparameterization, focusing on the phenomenon of 'fooling examples'?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an analytical framework for maximum likelihood estimation in deep linear networks, revealing feature collapse and a 'wormhole' solution that bypasses degeneracy, providing insights into generalization and shortcut learning.
papers.conclusion: This study demonstrates that DNNs can generalize from unstructured inputs via maximum likelihood estimation, revealing feature collapse and a wormhole solution that offers a novel perspective on mapping noisy inputs to coherent outputs and shortcut learning.
papers.key_findings:
An analytical solution for maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) exists within a feedforward linear neural network architecture, achievable by maximizing input norms without labeled data or gradient-based optimization.
Overparameterized networks exhibit a collapse in the output feature space (Neural Collapse), improving clustering and generalization by driving pairwise feature angles to zero.
Feature collapse can lead to a state of degeneracy where distinct inputs map to the same output, resulting in zero loss.
A 'wormhole' solution exists that bypasses this degeneracy, enabling the reconciliation of an arbitrary random label with a meaningful human-recognizable label.
The wormhole solution provides a theoretical basis for understanding shortcut learning and how DNNs generalize from fooling examples (seemingly random inputs).
papers.limitation: The analysis is limited to feedforward linear networks, and extending these findings to more complex architectures like convolutional networks or transformers poses challenges that require further investigation.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex architectures like CNNs or transformers by integrating additional mechanisms (e.g., graph-based methods, Fourier transformations, attention modules).
Further research on learning dynamics in unsupervised settings to bridge the gap between theory and practice.
papers.abstract: This work investigates the generalization behavior of deep neural networks (DNNs), focusing on the phenomenon of "fooling examples," where DNNs confidently classify inputs that appear random or unstructured to humans. To explore this phenomenon, we introduce an analytical framework based on maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), without adhering to conventional numerical approaches that rely on gradient-based optimization and explicit labels. Our analysis reveals that DNNs operating in an overparameterized regime exhibit a collapse in the output feature space. While this collapse improves network generalization, adding more layers eventually leads to a state of degeneracy, where the model learns trivial solutions by mapping distinct inputs to the same output, resulting in zero loss. Further investigation demonstrates that this degeneracy can be bypassed using our newly derived "wormhole" solution. The wormhole solution, when applied to arbitrary fooling examples, reconciles meaningful labels with random ones and provides a novel perspective on shortcut learning. These findings offer deeper insights into DNN generalization and highlight directions for future research on learning dynamics in unsupervised settings to bridge the gap between theory and practice.

papers.title: Learning from Emergence: A Study on Proactively Inhibiting the Monosemantic Neurons of Artificial Neural Networks
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether reducing monosemantic neurons in neural networks can improve performance, and proposes a method to proactively inhibit them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper hypothesizes that reducing monosemantic neurons improves model performance and introduces a metric (Monosemantic Scale) and a method (Reverse Deactivation) to inhibit monosemantic neurons during training.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that proactively inhibiting monosemantic neurons via the proposed MEmeL method can improve model performance across various tasks and architectures.
papers.key_findings:
MEmeL improves performance on language (GLUE), image (ImageNet), and precipitation forecasting (HKO-7) tasks.
Monosemanticity decreases with model scale, and inhibiting it can lead to better performance.
Naive deactivation methods can intensify monosemanticity, while the proposed Reverse Deactivation method effectively reduces it.
The proposed Monosemantic Scale metric enables efficient online detection of monosemantic neurons.
Pretraining with MEmeL shows greater improvement than finetuning with it, supporting the hypothesis that reducing monosemanticity enhances general ability.
papers.limitation: Extending the research to very large models (e.g., large language models) is appealing yet impossible for research departments due to limited computational resources.
future_direction: Extending the method to extremely large models trained on large datasets.
Studying the dynamics of MEmeL in more depth.
papers.abstract: Recently, emergence has received widespread attention from the research community along with the success of large-scale models. Different from the literature, we hypothesize a key factor that promotes the performance during the increase of scale: the reduction of monosemantic neurons that can only form one-to-one correlations with specific features. Monosemantic neurons tend to be sparser and have negative impacts on the performance in large models. Inspired by this insight, we propose an intuitive idea to identify monosemantic neurons and inhibit them. However, achieving this goal is a non-trivial task as there is no unified quantitative evaluation metric and simply banning monosemantic neurons does not promote polysemanticity in neural networks. Therefore, we first propose a new metric to measure the monosemanticity of neurons with the guarantee of efficiency for online computation, then introduce a theoretically supported method to suppress monosemantic neurons and proactively promote the ratios of polysemantic neurons in training neural networks. We validate our conjecture that monosemanticity brings about performance change at different model scales on a variety of neural networks and benchmark datasets in different areas, including language, image, and physics simulation tasks. Further experiments validate our analysis and theory regarding the inhibition of monosemanticity.

papers.title: Get rich quick: exact solutions reveal how unbalanced initializations promote rapid feature learning
papers.research_question: How do layer-specific initialization variances and learning rates determine the transition between lazy and rich learning regimes in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Derives exact solutions for a minimal model showing how unbalanced initializations and learning rates determine the transition between lazy and rich learning via conserved quantities, and shows that upstream initializations accelerate feature learning in nonlinear networks.
papers.conclusion: The theory motivates further exploration of unbalanced initializations to enhance efficient feature learning.
papers.key_findings:
In linear networks, rapid feature learning only occurs from balanced initializations.
In nonlinear networks, unbalanced initializations that promote faster learning in earlier layers (upstream) can accelerate rich learning.
The conserved quantity δ constrains learning trajectories and determines the geometry of parameter dynamics.
Upstream initializations reduce sample complexity for hierarchical data and decrease grokking time in modular arithmetic.
Upstream initializations promote interpretable filters in CNNs.
papers.limitation: Extending the mirror flow analysis to non-trivial piecewise linear networks is very difficult or provably impossible.
future_direction: Further exploration of unbalanced initializations to enhance efficient feature learning.
papers.abstract: While the impressive performance of modern neural networks is often attributed to their capacity to efficiently extract task-relevant features from data, the mechanisms underlying this rich feature learning regime remain elusive, with much of our theoretical understanding stemming from the opposing lazy regime. In this work, we derive exact solutions to a minimal model that transitions between lazy and rich learning, precisely elucidating how unbalanced layer-specific initialization variances and learning rates determine the degree of feature learning. Our analysis reveals that they conspire to influence the learning regime through a set of conserved quantities that constrain and modify the geometry of learning trajectories in parameter and function space. We extend our analysis to more complex linear models with multiple neurons, outputs, and layers and to shallow nonlinear networks with piecewise linear activation functions. In linear networks, rapid feature learning only occurs from balanced initializations, where all layers learn at similar speeds. While in nonlinear networks, unbalanced initializations that promote faster learning in earlier layers can accelerate rich learning. Through a series of experiments, we provide evidence that this unbalanced rich regime drives feature learning in deep finite-width networks, promotes interpretability of early layers in CNNs, reduces the sample complexity of learning hierarchical data, and decreases the time to grokking in modular arithmetic. Our theory motivates further exploration of unbalanced initializations to enhance efficient feature learning.

papers.title: Evaluations and Methods for Explanation through Robustness Analysis
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate feature-based explanations using adversarial robustness, and how can we extract feature sets that optimize this robustness criterion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a new evaluation criterion for feature-based explanations based on adversarial robustness, and introduces a method (Greedy-AS) to generate explanations that optimize this criterion.
papers.conclusion: The paper establishes a link between feature sets and predictions via robustness analysis, and demonstrates that the proposed explanation method effectively captures important features across multiple domains.
papers.key_findings:
Greedy-AS consistently outperforms existing explanation methods on the proposed Robustness-Sr and Robustness-Sr criteria across image and text datasets.
The method captures both pertinent positive and negative features, providing more comprehensive explanations.
Greedy-AS generates interpretable targeted explanations that vary meaningfully with the target class.
The proposed evaluation criteria reduce bias compared to traditional removal-based evaluations.
papers.limitation:
The explanation method has relatively high sensitivity to input perturbations.
The method has higher computational cost compared to some baseline methods.
future_direction: Improving the sensitivity of the Greedy-AS explanation, possibly by using more robust underlying models or smoothing techniques.
Exploring more efficient algorithms for computing the explanations.
papers.abstract: Feature based explanations, that provide importance of each feature towards the model prediction, is arguably one of the most intuitive ways to explain a model. In this paper, we establish a novel set of evaluation criteria for such feature based explanations by robustness analysis. In contrast to existing evaluations which require us to specify some way to "remove" features that could inevitably introduces biases and artifacts, we make use of the subtler notion of smaller adversarial perturbations. By optimizing towards our proposed evaluation criteria, we obtain new explanations that are loosely necessary and sufficient for a prediction. We further extend the explanation to extract the set of features that would move the current prediction to a target class by adopting targeted adversarial attack for the robustness analysis. Through experiments across multiple domains and a user study, we validate the usefulness of our evaluation criteria and our derived explanations.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: The Lazy Neuron Phenomenon: On Emergence of Activation Sparsity in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the prevalence, causes, and benefits of activation sparsity in Transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that activation sparsity is a prevalent phenomenon in Transformers, arising from training dynamics, and that enforcing sparsity via Top-k Transformers improves efficiency, robustness, and calibration.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that activation sparsity is a fundamental property of trained Transformers with benefits for efficiency and reliability, and it may stem from training dynamics.
papers.key_findings:
Activation sparsity is prevalent in Transformers for both NLP and vision tasks, across all layers.
Larger Transformers (deeper and wider) are sparser in terms of percentage of nonzero activations.
Sparsity emerges even with random labels, random images, or infinite data, suggesting it is due to training dynamics rather than dataset properties.
Sparsity reduces FLOPs and can improve computational efficiency during inference.
Enforcing sparser activation via Top-k Transformers improves robustness to noisy training data, input corruptions, and calibration of prediction confidence.
papers.limitation: The benefit of sparse activation is not fully realized due to lack of hardware support for sparse computation.
papers.abstract: This paper studies the curious phenomenon for machine learning models with Transformer architectures that their activation maps are sparse. By activation map we refer to the intermediate output of the multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) after a ReLU activation function, and by sparse we mean that on average very few entries (e.g., 3.0% for T5-Base and 6.3% for ViT-B16) are nonzero for each input to MLP. Moreover, larger Transformers with more layers and wider MLP hidden dimensions are sparser as measured by the percentage of nonzero entries. Through extensive experiments we demonstrate that the emergence of sparsity is a prevalent phenomenon that occurs for both natural language processing and vision tasks, on both training and evaluation data, for Transformers of various configurations, at layers of all depth levels, as well as for other architectures including MLP-mixers and 2-layer MLPs. We show that sparsity also emerges using training datasets with random labels, or with random inputs, or with infinite amount of data, demonstrating that sparsity is not a result of a specific family of datasets. We discuss how sparsity immediately implies a way to significantly reduce the FLOP count and improve efficiency for Transformers. Moreover, we demonstrate perhaps surprisingly that enforcing an even sparser activation via Top-k thresholding with a small value of k brings a collection of desired but missing properties for Transformers, namely less sensitivity to noisy training data, more robustness to input corruptions, and better calibration for their prediction confidence.

papers.title: On the Robustness of Neural Collapse and the Neural Collapse of Robustness
papers.research_question: What is the connection between Neural Collapse and adversarial robustness? Specifically, is Neural Collapse robust to adversarial perturbations and does it appear in robustly trained networks?
papers.core_contribution: This paper empirically studies the connection between Neural Collapse and adversarial robustness, finding that Neural Collapse is fragile to adversarial attacks in standardly trained networks but appears in adversarially trained networks, and that early layers exhibit more robust collapse.
papers.conclusion: Neural Collapse is an elegant phenomenon prevalent in many deep learning settings, but its connection to generalization and robustness remains unclear; it is not necessary for robust optimization.
papers.key_findings:
For standardly trained networks, small adversarial perturbations remove the simplex structure (Neural Collapse) at the representation layer.
Adversarially trained networks exhibit Neural Collapse on both clean and adversarially perturbed data, with the two simplices being aligned.
Early layers of standardly trained networks show some collapse on adversarial data and yield robust nearest-neighbor classifiers.
TRADES training does not lead to Neural Collapse, indicating that Neural Collapse is not necessary for robust classification.
Adversarial perturbations cause 'cluster leaping', where representations jump to the target class-mean with small angular deviation.
future_direction: Theoretical analysis of Neural Collapse beyond the unconstrained feature model.
papers.abstract: Neural Collapse refers to the curious phenomenon in the end of training of a neural network, where feature vectors and classification weights converge to a very simple geometrical arrangement (a simplex). While it has been observed empirically in various cases and has been theoretically motivated, its connection with crucial properties of neural networks, like their generalization and robustness, remains unclear. In this work, we study the stability properties of these simplices. We find that the simplex structure disappears under small adversarial attacks, and that perturbed examples "leap" between simplex vertices. We further analyze the geometry of networks that are optimized to be robust against adversarial perturbations of the input, and find that Neural Collapse is a pervasive phenomenon in these cases as well, with clean and perturbed representations forming aligned simplices, and giving rise to a robust simple nearest-neighbor classifier. By studying the propagation of the amount of collapse inside the network, we identify novel properties of both robust and non-robust machine learning models, and show that earlier, unlike later layers maintain reliable simplices on perturbed data. Our code is available at https://github.com/JingtongSu/robust_neural_collapse .

papers.title: Towards mitigating information leakage when evaluating safety monitors
papers.research_question: Do linear probes for detecting harmful behaviors in language models rely on textual evidence (leakage) in the input, and how does removing such evidence affect their performance?
papers.core_contribution: Linear probes for detecting harmful behaviors in language models often rely on textual evidence (leakage) in the input, such as elicitation prompts or reasoning traces; removing this evidence significantly degrades probe performance.
papers.conclusion: Linear probes for behavior detection often rely on textual evidence (leakage) present in elicitation prompts or reasoning traces, making them brittle when such evidence is absent, as demonstrated across sandbagging, sycophancy, and bias scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Probe performance (AUROC) drops substantially (10-30 points) when textual evidence of the target behavior is removed via content or score filtering.
Probes trained on REPE datasets achieve high baseline AUROC (0.95 for Sandbagging, 0.90 for Sycophancy, 0.74 for Bias) but fail to detect behaviors in fine-tuned Model Organisms that do not produce textual evidence.
Random token filtering has minimal impact compared to targeted removal of leaky tokens, confirming that performance drops are due to leakage removal, not just reduced information.
Probes evaluated on Model Organisms (which internalize behavior without verbalization) show poor performance (e.g., 0.57 vs 0.74 AUROC for Bias), indicating reliance on surface-level cues.
The study highlights a potential brittleness of linear probes in scenarios requiring detection of non-surface-level patterns.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to linear probes across three scenarios on two model families.
Content filtering may put the model out of distribution, potentially confounding results.
Score filtering cannot guarantee complete removal of textual signal due to attention propagation.
future_direction: Future research should investigate whether other monitor architectures (e.g., Sparse Autoencoders, Activation Oracles) are similarly affected by leakage.
More work is needed to develop evaluation protocols that properly control for leakage when assessing white-box monitors.
Exploring methods to train probes that are robust to the absence of textual evidence is an important direction.
papers.abstract: White box monitors that analyze model internals offer promising advantages for detecting potentially harmful behaviors in large language models, including lower computational costs and integration into layered defense systems.However, training and evaluating these monitors requires response exemplars that exhibit the target behaviors, typically elicited through prompting or fine-tuning. This presents a challenge when the information used to elicit behaviors inevitably leaks into the data that monitors ingest, inflating their effectiveness. We present a systematic framework for evaluating a monitor's performance in terms of its ability to detect genuine model behavior rather than superficial elicitation artifacts. Furthermore, we propose three novel strategies to evaluate the monitor: content filtering (removing deception-related text from inputs), score filtering (aggregating only over task-relevant tokens), and prompt distilled fine-tuned model organisms (models trained to exhibit deceptive behavior without explicit prompting). Using deception detection as a representative case study, we identify two forms of leakage that inflate monitor performance: elicitation leakage from prompts that explicitly request harmful behavior, and reasoning leakage from models that verbalize their deceptive actions. Through experiments on multiple deception benchmarks, we apply our proposed mitigation strategies and measure performance retention. Our evaluation of the monitors reveal three crucial findings: (1) Content filtering is a good mitigation strategy that allows for a smooth removal of elicitation signal and can decrease probe AUROC by 30\% (2) Score filtering was found to reduce AUROC by 15\% but is not as straightforward to attribute to (3) A finetuned model organism improves monitor evaluations but reduces their performance by upto 40\%, even when re-trained.

papers.title: Overcoming Simplicity Bias in Deep Networks using a Feature Sieve
papers.research_question: How can we overcome simplicity bias in deep networks by automatically identifying and suppressing spurious features without prior knowledge of them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes SIFER, a feature sieve method that automatically identifies and suppresses spurious features in lower network layers without prior knowledge, enabling higher layers to learn more robust representations and improving performance on debiasing benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: SIFER is an effective method for addressing simplicity bias and spurious correlations in deep networks, and it opens up new research directions in automated adversarial feature extraction and representation learning.
papers.key_findings:
SIFER suppresses simple features and enhances complex feature decodability in higher layers, as shown on controlled datasets.
SIFER allows controllability of feature focus via validation set, enabling targeting of either simple or complex features as needed.
SIFER outperforms baselines on real-world debiasing benchmarks (BAR, CelebA, NICO, ImageNet-A) without using attribute labels or conflicting examples.
SIFER focuses on relevant image regions and suppresses irrelevant background, as visualized by GRAD-CAM.
SIFER does not sacrifice in-distribution accuracy and improves out-of-distribution generalization.
papers.limitation: The paper does not explore ensembling approaches or provide a theoretical understanding of the feature sieve.
future_direction: Exploring ensembling approaches to combine features of varying complexity and predictive power.
Developing a systematic theoretical understanding of feature sieve approaches and their role in supervised learning using DNNs.
papers.abstract: Simplicity bias is the concerning tendency of deep networks to over-depend on simple, weakly predictive features, to the exclusion of stronger, more complex features. This is exacerbated in real-world applications by limited training data and spurious feature-label correlations, leading to biased, incorrect predictions. We propose a direct, interventional method for addressing simplicity bias in DNNs, which we call the feature sieve. We aim to automatically identify and suppress easily-computable spurious features in lower layers of the network, thereby allowing the higher network levels to extract and utilize richer, more meaningful representations. We provide concrete evidence of this differential suppression & enhancement of relevant features on both controlled datasets and real-world images, and report substantial gains on many real-world debiasing benchmarks (11.4% relative gain on Imagenet-A; 3.2% on BAR, etc). Crucially, we do not depend on prior knowledge of spurious attributes or features, and in fact outperform many baselines that explicitly incorporate such information. We believe that our feature sieve work opens up exciting new research directions in automated adversarial feature extraction and representation learning for deep networks.

papers.title: ERNIE-Tiny : A Progressive Distillation Framework for Pretrained Transformer Compression
papers.research_question: How to effectively compress pretrained language models (PLMs) by addressing the pretrain-finetune distillation discrepancy through a smooth transition of teacher, training data, and learning objective?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a four-stage progressive distillation framework (ERNIE-Tiny) that smooths the transition from pretrain to finetune distillation by gradually altering teacher model, training data, and learning objective, introducing a novel general-enhanced distillation stage to improve student generalization.
papers.conclusion: The proposed progressive distillation framework ERNIE-Tiny effectively compresses pretrained language models, maintaining high performance while significantly reducing model size and inference time, and demonstrates improved generalization.
papers.key_findings:
A 4-layer ERNIE-Tiny student maintains over 98% of its 12-layer teacher BERTbase performance on the GLUE benchmark with 9.4x faster inference speed.
The general-enhanced distillation stage, which uses a finetuned teacher on general data, improves the student model's generalization, especially on low-resource tasks.
The task-adaptive distillation stage serves as a crucial bridge, smoothing the transition between general and task-specific data distillation and improving final performance.
ERNIE-Tiny achieves state-of-the-art compression results on both English (GLUE) and Chinese NLP tasks, outperforming the teacher BERTbase on Chinese tasks with 7.5x fewer parameters.
Ablation studies confirm the importance of each distillation stage, with the removal of any stage leading to performance degradation.
papers.limitation: The work did not apply larger unlabeled general data such as C4, leaving more efficient data utilization for future work.
future_direction: Applying larger unlabeled general data (e.g., C4) and exploring more efficient data utilization.
papers.abstract: Pretrained language models (PLMs) such as BERT adopt a training paradigm which first pretrain the model in general data and then finetune the model on task-specific data, and have recently achieved great success. However, PLMs are notorious for their enormous parameters and hard to be deployed on real-life applications. Knowledge distillation has been prevailing to address this problem by transferring knowledge from a large teacher to a much smaller student over a set of data. We argue that the selection of thee three key components, namely teacher, training data, and learning objective, is crucial to the effectiveness of distillation. We, therefore, propose a four-stage progressive distillation framework ERNIE-Tiny to compress PLM, which varies the three components gradually from general level to task-specific level. Specifically, the first stage, General Distillation, performs distillation with guidance from pretrained teacher, gerenal data and latent distillation loss. Then, General-Enhanced Distillation changes teacher model from pretrained teacher to finetuned teacher. After that, Task-Adaptive Distillation shifts training data from general data to task-specific data. In the end, Task-Specific Distillation, adds two additional losses, namely Soft-Label and Hard-Label loss onto the last stage. Empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework and generalization gain brought by ERNIE-Tiny.In particular, experiments show that a 4-layer ERNIE-Tiny maintains over 98.0%performance of its 12-layer teacher BERT base on GLUE benchmark, surpassing state-of-the-art (SOTA) by 1.0% GLUE score with the same amount of parameters. Moreover, ERNIE-Tiny achieves a new compression SOTA on five Chinese NLP tasks, outperforming BERT base by 0.4% accuracy with 7.5x fewer parameters and9.4x faster inference speed.

papers.title: Robust Feature-Level Adversaries are Interpretability Tools
papers.research_question: How can robust, feature-level adversarial perturbations be used as interpretability tools to understand and debug neural networks, specifically to reveal human-describable weaknesses and spurious feature-class associations?
papers.core_contribution: Feature-level adversarial examples are versatile and robust, and can be used as practical interpretability tools to identify spurious feature-class associations and bugs in neural networks.
papers.conclusion: Feature-level adversaries are a promising approach for rigorous interpretability research, supporting the design of tools to better understand what a model has learned and diagnose brittle feature associations.
papers.key_findings:
Feature-level adversarial attacks are more interpretable than pixel-level attacks and provide a useful class of inputs for studying model representations.
These attacks are highly robust and can be designed to be targeted, universal, disguised, physically-realizable, and transferable (black-box) at the ImageNet scale.
The adversaries can guide the design of 'copy/paste' attacks (pasting one natural image into another to cause misclassification), validating their utility for interpretability and understanding model weaknesses.
Adversarial training with feature-level attacks can improve model robustness against such attacks.
The method can reveal both beneficial (e.g., barber pole stripes for barbershop) and harmful (e.g., skin tone for bikini) feature-class associations learned by the model.
papers.limitation:
When optimizing for multiple desiderata simultaneously (e.g., universality, transformation robustness, disguise), attacks are generally less successful, more time-consuming, and require more screening to find good ones.
The evaluation method for copy/paste attacks is a proof-of-concept and should be evaluated more rigorously in future work.
future_direction: Extend the method to Natural Language Processing.
Use adversaries for feature visualization of a network's internal neurons.
Develop a benchmark for interpretability tools based on their ability to aid a human in rediscovering trojans implanted into a model.
Leverage advances in generative modeling to improve attack efficiency and quality.
More rigorously evaluate the design of copy/paste attacks.
papers.abstract: The literature on adversarial attacks in computer vision typically focuses on pixel-level perturbations. These tend to be very difficult to interpret. Recent work that manipulates the latent representations of image generators to create "feature-level" adversarial perturbations gives us an opportunity to explore perceptible, interpretable adversarial attacks. We make three contributions. First, we observe that feature-level attacks provide useful classes of inputs for studying representations in models. Second, we show that these adversaries are uniquely versatile and highly robust. We demonstrate that they can be used to produce targeted, universal, disguised, physically-realizable, and black-box attacks at the ImageNet scale. Third, we show how these adversarial images can be used as a practical interpretability tool for identifying bugs in networks. We use these adversaries to make predictions about spurious associations between features and classes which we then test by designing "copy/paste" attacks in which one natural image is pasted into another to cause a targeted misclassification. Our results suggest that feature-level attacks are a promising approach for rigorous interpretability research. They support the design of tools to better understand what a model has learned and diagnose brittle feature associations. Code is available at https://github.com/thestephencasper/feature_level_adv

papers.title: Linear socio-demographic representations emerge in Large Language Models from indirect cues
papers.research_question: How do LLMs encode sociodemographic attributes of human conversational partners inferred from indirect cues such as names and occupations, and do these representations shape downstream behavior?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs develop linear representations of user sociodemographic attributes within their activation space from indirect cues, and these representations actively shape downstream behavior, revealing an alignment gap where models refuse explicit demographic queries but act on implicit biases.
papers.conclusion: LLMs linearly encode user demographic attributes from indirect cues, and these representations have measurable behavioral consequences, posing significant challenges for fairness in deployed conversational AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs encode user sociodemographics in linear subspaces of activation space that can be decoded with high accuracy using linear probes.
Implicit cues such as names and occupations trigger demographic representations aligned with real-world population statistics (e.g., US Census, Bureau of Labor Statistics).
Inference-time interventions (activation steering) demonstrate that these linear representations causally influence model outputs, such as country-of-origin or name predictions.
Models exhibit an alignment gap: commercial models refuse explicit demographic-based reasoning while implicitly encoding and acting upon demographics inferred from contextual cues.
Stereotypical associations in the model's representations correlate with distributional patterns in the training data, as shown for OLMo and Common Crawl.
papers.limitation:
The study uses synthetic prompts designed for experimental control; generalization to organic user interactions is uncertain.
Binary demographic categories (male/female, Black/White, rich/poor) fail to capture the continuous and multidimensional nature of human identity.
The prompts and data sources (US Census, BLS, Kozlowski et al. survey) reflect Western and primarily American cultural framings.
The findings demonstrate correlational patterns between training data, representations, and behavior but do not establish causation.
future_direction: Deeper cross-cultural analysis to understand how biases manifest across different cultural contexts.
Establishing causal relationships between training data, internal representations, and behavioral outputs.
Developing and evaluating intervention techniques (e.g., activation steering, representation debiasing) to mitigate bias without compromising model capabilities.
papers.abstract: We investigate how LLMs encode sociodemographic attributes of human conversational partners inferred from indirect cues such as names and occupations. We show that LLMs develop linear representations of user demographics within activation space, wherein stereotypically associated attributes are encoded along interpretable geometric directions. We first probe residual streams across layers of four open transformer-based LLMs (Magistral 24B, Qwen3 14B, GPT-OSS 20B, OLMo2-1B) prompted with explicit demographic disclosure. We show that the same probes predict demographics from implicit cues: names activate census-aligned gender and race representations, while occupations trigger representations correlated with real-world workforce statistics. These linear representations allow us to explain demographic inferences implicitly formed by LLMs during conversation. We demonstrate that these implicit demographic representations actively shape downstream behavior, such as career recommendations. Our study further highlights that models that pass bias benchmark tests may still harbor and leverage implicit biases, with implications for fairness when applied at scale.

papers.title: Principles of Lipschitz continuity in neural networks
papers.research_question: The paper investigates three questions: (1) What is the state of knowledge of Lipschitz continuity in neural networks? (2) How does Lipschitz continuity evolve during training? (3) How does Lipschitz continuity modulate frequency signal propagation in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The thesis advances a principled understanding of Lipschitz continuity in neural networks by investigating its training dynamics and its role in modulating frequency signal propagation.
papers.conclusion: The thesis provides a comprehensive study of Lipschitz continuity in neural networks, contributing to the understanding of robustness and generalization, and offers directions for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Lipschitz continuity evolves during training and is driven by optimization dynamics, as captured by a stochastic differential equation framework.
Lipschitz continuity modulates frequency signal propagation in neural networks, affecting robustness and generalization.
A systematic review of Lipschitz continuity in deep learning is provided, covering theoretical foundations, estimation methods, regularization approaches, and certifiable robustness.
A theoretical framework for the dynamics of Lipschitz continuity is developed, identifying principal driving forces such as gradient flow projections and noise.
A spectral method (spectral coalition filtering) is introduced for interpreting global perturbation robustness of image models.
papers.limitation:
The framework assumes continuous-time SGD and uses a low-rank approximation for gradient noise, which may not capture all dynamics.
The spectral coalition filtering method assumes that frequency bands are independent, which may not hold in practice.
future_direction: Spectral-gap regularization
Spectrum-gradient alignment
papers.abstract: Deep learning has achieved remarkable success across a wide range of domains, significantly expanding the frontiers of what is achievable in artificial intelligence. Yet, despite these advances, critical challenges remain --- most notably, ensuring robustness to small input perturbations and generalization to out-of-distribution data. These critical challenges underscore the need to understand the underlying fundamental principles that govern robustness and generalization. This understanding is indispensable for establishing deep learning systems that are: reliable --- performing consistently under expected conditions on in-distribution data; resilient --- capable of recovering from unexpected conditions such as noise or adversarial attacks; and trustworthy --- behaving transparently, ethically, in alignment with intended use, and technically robust, particularly in safety-critical applications. Among the theoretical tools available, Lipschitz continuity plays a pivotal role in governing the fundamental properties of neural networks related to robustness and generalization. It quantifies the worst-case sensitivity of network's outputs to small input perturbations. While its importance is widely acknowledged, prior research has predominantly focused on empirical regularization approaches based on Lipschitz constraints, leaving the underlying principles less explored. This thesis seeks to advance a principled understanding of the principles of Lipschitz continuity in neural networks within the paradigm of machine learning, examined from two complementary perspectives: an internal perspective --- focusing on the temporal evolution of Lipschitz continuity in neural networks during training (i.e., training dynamics); and an external perspective --- investigating how Lipschitz continuity modulates the behavior of neural networks with respect to features in the input data, particularly its role in governing frequency signal propagation (i.e., modulation of frequency signal propagation). Guided by these perspectives, the thesis formulates three primary research questions: (RQ1) State of Knowledge --- what is the state of knowledge of Lipschitz continuity in neural networks? (RQ2) Training Dynamics --- how does Lipschitz continuity in neural networks evolve during the training process? (RQ3) Modulation of Frequency Signal Propagation --- how does Lipschitz continuity modulate frequency signal propagation in neural networks?

papers.title: Mirrored STDP Implements Autoencoder Learning in a Network of Spiking Neurons
papers.research_question: How can autoencoder learning be implemented in a biologically realistic network of spiking neurons using a novel synaptic plasticity rule?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a network of spiking neurons with a novel plasticity rule called Mirrored STDP can implement autoencoder learning, enabling the network to learn sparse distributed representations and receptive fields resembling those in primary visual cortex.
papers.conclusion: Mirrored STDP offers a biologically realistic way for spiking neural networks to perform autoencoder learning, bridging computational neuroscience and machine learning.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Mirrored STDP rule approximates the autoencoder learning rule in a spiking network.
The network learns sparse distributed representations when combined with a synaptic scaling mechanism for sparsity.
When trained on whitened natural image patches, the learned feedforward weights resemble Gabor filters similar to receptive fields in V1 simple cells.
The network can learn from both MNIST digits and natural image datasets, though reconstruction performance is better for MNIST.
The model provides a biologically plausible mechanism for unsupervised feature learning.
papers.limitation:
The network had difficulties with runaway excitation when attempting less sparse solutions in the natural image experiments.
Reconstruction performance for natural image patches was not as good as for the MNIST dataset.
future_direction: Future work is needed to create networks more robust to runaway excitation during training.
Exploring how plasticity in inhibitory neurons might help develop complex receptive fields with inhibitory components.
papers.abstract: The autoencoder algorithm is a simple but powerful unsupervised method for training neural networks. Autoencoder networks can learn sparse distributed codes similar to those seen in cortical sensory areas such as visual area V1, but they can also be stacked to learn increasingly abstract representations. Several computational neuroscience models of sensory areas, including Olshausen & Field's Sparse Coding algorithm, can be seen as autoencoder variants, and autoencoders have seen extensive use in the machine learning community. Despite their power and versatility, autoencoders have been difficult to implement in a biologically realistic fashion. The challenges include their need to calculate differences between two neuronal activities and their requirement for learning rules which lead to identical changes at feedforward and feedback connections. Here, we study a biologically realistic network of integrate-and-fire neurons with anatomical connectivity and synaptic plasticity that closely matches that observed in cortical sensory areas. Our choice of synaptic plasticity rules is inspired by recent experimental and theoretical results suggesting that learning at feedback connections may have a different form from learning at feedforward connections, and our results depend critically on this novel choice of plasticity rules. Specifically, we propose that plasticity rules at feedforward versus feedback connections are temporally opposed versions of spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP), leading to a symmetric combined rule we call Mirrored STDP (mSTDP). We show that with mSTDP, our network follows a learning rule that approximately minimizes an autoencoder loss function. When trained with whitened natural image patches, the learned synaptic weights resemble the receptive fields seen in V1. Our results use realistic synaptic plasticity rules to show that the powerful autoencoder learning algorithm could be within the reach of real biological networks.

papers.title: PIXEL: Adaptive Steering Via Position-wise Injection with eXact Estimated Levels under Subspace Calibration
papers.research_question: How can we perform activation steering in large language models in a principled way that adapts to token-level sensitivity and avoids global hyperparameter tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PIXEL, a position-wise activation steering framework that learns a property-aligned subspace from dual views and selects intervention strength via a constrained geometric objective with a closed-form solution, enabling adaptive control without global hyperparameter tuning.
papers.conclusion: PIXEL provides a practical and principled method for LLM controllable generation, improving attribute alignment while preserving general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
PIXEL outperforms existing activation steering methods across multiple models and tasks (truthfulness, bias, safety, helpfulness).
The dual-view subspace construction (tail-averaged and end-token) is more effective than single-view.
The adaptive intervention strength mechanism (closed-form solution) is crucial for performance.
Orthogonal residual calibration improves alignment by adapting to sample-specific semantics.
PIXEL maintains general capabilities (e.g., on RACE, MMLU) while improving alignment.
papers.abstract: Reliable behavior control is central to deploying large language models (LLMs) on the web. Activation steering offers a tuning-free route to align attributes (e.g., truthfulness) that ensure trustworthy generation. Prevailing approaches rely on coarse heuristics and lack a principled account of where to steer and how strongly to intervene. To this end, we propose Position-wise Injection with eXact Estimated Levels (PIXEL), a position-wise activation steering framework that, in contrast to prior work, learns a property-aligned subspace from dual views (tail-averaged and end-token) and selects intervention strength via a constrained geometric objective with a closed-form solution, thereby adapting to token-level sensitivity without global hyperparameter tuning. PIXEL further performs sample-level orthogonal residual calibration to refine the global attribute direction and employs a lightweight position-scanning routine to identify receptive injection sites. We additionally provide representation-level guarantees for the minimal-intervention rule, supporting reliable alignment. Across diverse models and evaluation paradigms, PIXEL consistently improves attribute alignment while preserving model general capabilities, offering a practical and principled method for LLMs' controllable generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/V1centNevwake/PIXEL-Adaptive-Steering

papers.title: Readout Representation: Redefining Neural Codes by Input Recovery
papers.research_question: How does a system that abstracts away details still preserve the fine-grained information needed for downstream functions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the readout representation framework that defines representation by functional recoverability rather than causal origin, and proposes representation size as a metric to quantify the robustness of representations.
papers.conclusion: The readout representation framework offers a new lens for analyzing how both biological and artificial neural systems learn abstract features while maintaining robust, information-rich representations of the world.
papers.key_findings:
Inputs can be accurately reconstructed from heavily perturbed features in lower to middle layers of various vision and language models.
Representation size is larger for correctly classified images than misclassified ones, and zero for noise images.
Representation size correlates with feature dimensionality in vision models, but this trend weakens in higher layers.
The readout representation framework naturally accounts for phenomena like misrepresentation, illusion, and dreaming.
A single input corresponds to a broad, continuous region in feature space from which it can be recovered, indicating inherent redundancy.
papers.abstract: Sensory representation is typically understood through a hierarchical-causal framework where progressively abstract features are extracted sequentially. However, this causal view fails to explain misrepresentation, a phenomenon better handled by an informational view based on decodable content. This creates a tension: how does a system that abstracts away details still preserve the fine-grained information needed for downstream functions? We propose readout representation to resolve this, defining representation by the information recoverable from features rather than their causal origin. Empirically, we show that inputs can be accurately reconstructed even from heavily perturbed mid-level features, demonstrating that a single input corresponds to a broad, redundant region of feature space, challenging the causal mapping perspective. To quantify this property, we introduce representation size, a metric linked to model robustness and representational redundancy. Our framework offers a new lens for analyzing how both biological and artificial neural systems learn complex features while maintaining robust, information-rich representations of the world.

papers.title: Understanding Neural Networks through Representation Erasure
papers.research_question: How can we interpret neural network decisions by analyzing the effects of erasing various parts of the representation, such as input word-vector dimensions, intermediate hidden units, or input words?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a general methodology for interpreting neural network decisions by erasing parts of the representation and analyzing the effects, which provides explanations for model behavior and enables error analysis.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methodology offers interpretable explanations for neural model decisions and provides a way to conduct error analysis, which can benefit a wide variety of models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The method identifies important word-vector dimensions for linguistic feature classification and shows how importance distributes across dimensions and layers.
In sentiment analysis, LSTM-based models are more sensitive to sentiment-indicative words than standard RNNs.
The method can identify words that confuse the model (negative importance) and reveal common failure patterns, such as sentiment words used in non-standard contexts.
A reinforcement learning approach can find minimal sets of words to erase to change model decisions, providing aspect-specific rationales.
Dropout training leads to more distributed importance across dimensions.
future_direction: Resolving the problems identified in error analysis (e.g., handling concessive sentences, irony, etc.) in sentiment analysis.
papers.abstract: While neural networks have been successfully applied to many natural language processing tasks, they come at the cost of interpretability. In this paper, we propose a general methodology to analyze and interpret decisions from a neural model by observing the effects on the model of erasing various parts of the representation, such as input word-vector dimensions, intermediate hidden units, or input words. We present several approaches to analyzing the effects of such erasure, from computing the relative difference in evaluation metrics, to using reinforcement learning to erase the minimum set of input words in order to flip a neural model's decision. In a comprehensive analysis of multiple NLP tasks, including linguistic feature classification, sentence-level sentiment analysis, and document level sentiment aspect prediction, we show that the proposed methodology not only offers clear explanations about neural model decisions, but also provides a way to conduct error analysis on neural models.

papers.title: Entangled in Representations: Mechanistic Investigation of Cultural Biases in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How are cultural biases, such as Western-dominance bias and cultural flattening, internalized and represented within the parameters of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Culturescope, a mechanistic interpretability method to probe internal representations of cultural knowledge, and finds that LLMs internalize Western-dominance bias and cultural flattening, with low-resource cultures being less susceptible due to limited parametric knowledge.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a foundation for future research on mitigating cultural biases and enhancing LLMs' cultural understanding, suggesting that tailored approaches considering both bias and resource levels are needed.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs internalize Western-dominance bias and cultural flattening in their cultural knowledge space.
Low-resource cultures are less susceptible to cultural biases, likely due to the model's limited parametric knowledge about them.
The Cultural Flattening (CF) score and attention contribution scores reveal asymmetric generalization of culturally distinctive knowledge, often aligned with geographic or cultural proximity.
When models answer cultural questions incorrectly, they show a statistically significant preference for biased options (hard negatives) for mid- and high-resource cultures, but not for low-resource cultures.
Culturescope effectively surfaces relevant cultural knowledge from model representations, as validated by relevance evaluation and irrelevant patching tests.
papers.limitation:
Few existing benchmarks are suitable for the evaluation setup, requiring a consistent QA format across cultures; the methods inherit limitations from the benchmarks such as lack of fine-grained cultures and a 1-to-1 mapping of culture and country.
Due to computational constraints, experiments are limited to 8B parameter models.
future_direction: Future work should develop tailored approaches that consider the impact of bias and resource levels to improve LLMs' cultural understanding.
Future research should aim at mitigating internalized cultural biases and developing culturally aligned LLMs.
papers.abstract: The growing deployment of large language models (LLMs) across diverse cultural contexts necessitates a deeper understanding of LLMs' representations of different cultures. Prior work has focused on evaluating the cultural awareness of LLMs by only examining the text they generate. This approach overlooks the internal sources of cultural misrepresentation within the models themselves. To bridge this gap, we propose Culturescope, the first mechanistic interpretability-based method that probes the internal representations of different cultural knowledge in LLMs. We also introduce a cultural flattening score as a measure of the intrinsic cultural biases of the decoded knowledge from Culturescope. Additionally, we study how LLMs internalize cultural biases, which allows us to trace how cultural biases such as Western-dominance bias and cultural flattening emerge within LLMs. We find that low-resource cultures are less susceptible to cultural biases, likely due to the model's limited parametric knowledge. Our work provides a foundation for future research on mitigating cultural biases and enhancing LLMs' cultural understanding.

papers.title: Implicit assumptions about implicit learning
papers.abstract: A number of ways of taxonomizing human learning have been proposed. We examine the evidence for one such proposal, namely, that there exist independent explicit and implicit learning systems. This combines two further distinctions, (1) between learning that takes place with versus without concurrent awareness, and (2) between learning that involves the encoding of instances (or fragments) versus the induction of abstract rules or hypotheses. Implicit learning is assumed to involve unconscious rule learning. We examine the evidence for implicit learning derived from subliminal learning, conditioning, artificial grammar learning, instrumental learning, and reaction times in sequence learning. We conclude that unconscious learning has not been satisfactorily established in any of these areas. The assumption that learning in some of these tasks (e.g., artificial grammar learning) is predominantly based on rule abstraction is questionable. When subjects cannot report the "implicitly learned" rules that govern stimulus selection, this is often because their knowledge consists of instances or fragments of the training stimuli rather than rules. In contrast to the distinction between conscious and unconscious learning, the distinction between instance and rule learning is a sound and meaningful way of taxonomizing human learning. We discuss various computational models of these two forms of learning.

papers.title: Characteristics of dissociable human learning systems
papers.abstract: Abstract A number of ways of taxonomizing human learning have been proposed. We examine the evidence for one such proposal, namely, that there exist independent explicit and implicit learning systems. This combines two further distinctions, (1) between learning that takes place with versus without concurrent awareness, and (2) between learning that involves the encoding of instances (or fragments) versus the induction of abstract rules or hypotheses. Implicit learning is assumed to involve unconscious rule learning. We examine the evidence for implicit learning derived from subliminal learning, conditioning, artificial grammar learning, instrumental learning, and reaction times in sequence learning. We conclude that unconscious learning has not been satisfactorily established in any of these areas. The assumption that learning in some of these tasks (e.g., artificial grammar learning) is predominantly based on rule abstraction is questionable. When subjects cannot report the “implicitly learned” rules that govern stimulus selection, this is often because their knowledge consists of instances or fragments of the training stimuli rather than rules. In contrast to the distinction between conscious and unconscious learning, the distinction between instance and rule learning is a sound and meaningful way of taxonomizing human learning. We discuss various computational models of these two forms of learning.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Subliminal Learning: When and How Hidden Biases Transfer
papers.abstract: Language models can transfer hidden biases during distillation. For example, a teacher that "likes owls" can make its student "like owls" too, even when the training data consists only of lists of numbers. This surprising phenomenon is called subliminal learning. Subliminal learning can be expected under soft distillation, where the student is trained on the teacher's full next-token distribution. But the fact that this also occurs under hard distillation-where the student only sees sampled tokens-raises a deeper question: when and how does subliminal learning actually occur? We answer this question through controlled experiments and mechanistic analysis. Our results show that subliminal learning does not need (global) token entanglement or logit leakage. Instead, it comes down to a small set of divergence tokens-rare cases where teachers with different biases would predict different tokens. Masking out these tokens mostly removes the hidden bias transfer. Mechanistically, divergence tokens reveal that early layers are critical. Surprisingly, finetuning even a single such early layer is sufficient for subliminal learning. Finally, we find that subliminal learning is fragile. Even small changes, like paraphrasing prompts, are usually sufficient to suppress it.

papers.title: Implicit bias training can remove bias from subliminal stimuli, restoring choice divergence: A proof-of-concept study
papers.abstract: Subliminal information can influence our conscious life. Subliminal stimuli can influence cognitive tasks, while endogenous subliminal neural information can sway decisions before volition. Are decisions inextricably biased towards subliminal information? Or can they diverge away from subliminal biases via training? We report that implicit bias training can remove biases from subliminal sensory primes. We first show that subliminal stimuli biased an imagery-content decision task. Participants (n = 17) had to choose one of two different patterns to subsequently imagine. Subliminal primes significantly biased decisions towards imagining the primed option. Then, we trained participants (n = 7) to choose the non-primed option, via post choice feedback. This training was successful despite participants being unaware of the purpose or structure of the reward schedule. This implicit bias training persisted up to one week later. Our proof-of-concept study indicates that decisions might not always have to be biased towards non-conscious information, but instead can diverge from subliminal primes through training.

papers.title: Unconscious associative learning with conscious cues
papers.abstract: Despite extensive research, the very existence of unconscious learning in humans remains much debated. Skepticism arises chiefly from the difficulty in assessing the level of awareness of the complex associations learned in classical implicit learning paradigms. Here, we show that simple associations between colors and motion directions can be learned unconsciously. In each trial, participants had to report the motion direction of a patch of colored dots but unbeknownst to the participants, two out of the three possible colors were always associated with a given direction/response, while one was uninformative. We confirm the lack of awareness by using several tasks, fulfilling the most stringent criteria. In addition, we show the crucial role of trial-by-trial feedback, and that both the stimulus-response (motor) and stimulus-stimulus (perceptual) associations were learned. In conclusion, we demonstrate that simple associations between supraliminal stimulus features can be learned unconsciously, providing a novel framework to study unconscious learning.

papers.title: Subliminally and Supraliminally Acquired Long-Term Memories Jointly Bias Delayed Decisions
papers.abstract: Common wisdom and scientific evidence suggest that good decisions require conscious deliberation. But growing evidence demonstrates that not only conscious but also unconscious thoughts influence decision-making.
