papers.abstract: Understanding the nature of representation in neural networks is a goal shared by neuroscience and machine learning. It is therefore exciting that both fields converge not only on shared questions but also on similar approaches. A pressing question in these areas is understanding how the structure of the representation used by neural networks affects both their generalization, and robustness to perturbations. In this work, we investigate the latter by juxtaposing experimental results regarding the covariance spectrum of neural representations in the mouse V1 (Stringer et al) with artificial neural networks. We use adversarial robustness to probe Stringer et al's theory regarding the causal role of a 1/n covariance spectrum. We empirically investigate the benefits such a neural code confers in neural networks, and illuminate its role in multi-layer architectures. Our results show that imposing the experimentally observed structure on artificial neural networks makes them more robust to adversarial attacks. Moreover, our findings complement the existing theory relating wide neural networks to kernel methods, by showing the role of intermediate representations.

papers.title: NeuronTune: Towards Self-Guided Spurious Bias Mitigation
papers.research_question: How can spurious bias in deep neural networks be mitigated without requiring external annotations of spurious correlations?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes NeuronTune, a self-guided post hoc method that identifies and suppresses neurons affected by spurious bias in a model's latent space, improving worst-group accuracy without requiring group labels.
papers.conclusion: NeuronTune is a lightweight, self-guided post hoc method that effectively mitigates spurious bias by directly intervening in a model's internal decision process, validated theoretically and empirically across diverse datasets and architectures.
papers.key_findings:
NeuronTune effectively mitigates spurious bias across different model architectures (ResNet, BERT) and data modalities (image, text).
The method outperforms existing sample-level and last-layer retraining methods in worst-group accuracy on multiple benchmarks.
Theoretical analysis shows that neuron activations coupled with prediction outcomes provide self-identifying information for biased dimensions, and NeuronTune brings the model closer to an unbiased solution.
NeuronTune is computationally efficient as it only requires tuning the last layer of the model.
The method operates without external supervision (group labels), making it practical for standard ERM training settings.
papers.limitation: NeuronTune may not fully address spurious bias if the feature extractor is already biased, as it only retrains the last layer.
future_direction: Exploring different choices of identification data and model tuning data to enhance spurious bias mitigation.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks often develop spurious bias, reliance on correlations between non-essential features and classes for predictions. For example, a model may identify objects based on frequently co-occurring backgrounds rather than intrinsic features, resulting in degraded performance on data lacking these correlations. Existing mitigation approaches typically depend on external annotations of spurious correlations, which may be difficult to obtain and are not relevant to the spurious bias in a model. In this paper, we take a step towards self-guided mitigation of spurious bias by proposing NeuronTune, a post hoc method that directly intervenes in a model's internal decision process. Our method probes in a model's latent embedding space to identify and regulate neurons that lead to spurious prediction behaviors. We theoretically justify our approach and show that it brings the model closer to an unbiased one. Unlike previous methods, NeuronTune operates without requiring spurious correlation annotations, making it a practical and effective tool for improving model robustness. Experiments across different architectures and data modalities demonstrate that our method significantly mitigates spurious bias in a self-guided way.

papers.title: Single-weight Model Editing for Post-hoc Spurious Correlation Neutralization
papers.research_question: How can spurious correlations in neural networks be neutralized in a post-hoc manner by editing a single weight, allowing controllable distraction from spurious features?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a post-hoc method that edits a single weight in a neural network to neutralize the impact of spurious correlations, conceptualizing spurious features as fictitious sub-classes that can be removed with controllable extent.
papers.conclusion: The work establishes an effective connection between post-hoc machine unlearning and spurious correlation mitigation, demonstrating that single-weight editing can controllably neutralize spurious features with competitive performance.
papers.key_findings:
Editing a single weight in the last layer can effectively remove a target class, reducing its accuracy to near zero with minimal impact on other classes.
The method can neutralize spurious correlations by treating them as fictitious classes, achieving competitive worst-group accuracy on standard benchmarks.
The proposed Specific Class Association (SCA) score, based on activations, gradients, and entropy, effectively identifies the most significant weight for a given class.
Partial Feature Neutralization (PFN) allows controllable neutralization of spurious features, balancing worst-group and average performance.
The method is architecture-agnostic, working on both convolutional networks and vision transformers.
papers.limitation: If the features of the underlying classes are not exclusive (e.g., digit '3' shares features with '8'), the method may face restrictions in completely removing the subclass.
papers.abstract: Neural network training tends to exploit the simplest features as shortcuts to greedily minimize training loss. However, some of these features might be spuriously correlated with the target labels, leading to incorrect predictions by the model. Several methods have been proposed to address this issue. Focusing on suppressing the spurious correlations with model training, they not only incur additional training cost, but also have limited practical utility as the model misbehavior due to spurious relations is usually discovered after its deployment. It is also often overlooked that spuriousness is a subjective notion. Hence, the precise questions that must be investigated are; to what degree a feature is spurious, and how we can proportionally distract the model's attention from it for reliable prediction. To this end, we propose a method that enables post-hoc neutralization of spurious feature impact, controllable to an arbitrary degree. We conceptualize spurious features as fictitious sub-classes within the original classes, which can be eliminated by a class removal scheme. We then propose a unique precise class removal technique that makes a single-weight modification, which entails negligible performance compromise for the remaining classes. We perform extensive experiments, demonstrating that by editing just a single weight in a post-hoc manner, our method achieves highly competitive, or better performance against the state-of-the-art methods.

papers.title: Shortcut Features as Top Eigenfunctions of NTK: A Linear Neural Network Case and More
papers.research_question: What are the properties of shortcut learning in neural networks when analyzed through the Neural Tangent Kernel framework? Specifically, why do shortcut features correspond to top eigenfunctions of NTK and dominate the network output?
papers.core_contribution: Shortcut features correspond to top eigenfunctions of the Neural Tangent Kernel, with larger eigenvalues, causing faster convergence and greater influence on the network output even after training. The max-margin bias is not the sole cause of shortcut learning.
papers.conclusion: Shortcut features are top eigenfunctions of NTK and dominate learning; debiasing techniques need to consider data variance.
papers.key_findings:
For linear networks, features corresponding to clusters of larger weights have larger eigenvalues and converge faster.
Due to data variance within clusters, features with larger eigenvalues have larger influence on the output after convergence.
Shortcut learning persists even when margin is controlled, indicating max-margin bias is not the only cause.
Shortcut features have lower predictability but higher availability in real-world datasets.
papers.limitation: If the ground-truth is affected by multiple shortcuts, then availability cannot detect the shortcut that is learned later than the other shortcut.
future_direction: More study is left for future works on multiple shortcuts and predictability.
papers.abstract: One of the chronic problems of deep-learning models is shortcut learning. In a case where the majority of training data are dominated by a certain feature, neural networks prefer to learn such a feature even if the feature is not generalizable outside the training set. Based on the framework of Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK), we analyzed the case of linear neural networks to derive some important properties of shortcut learning. We defined a feature of a neural network as an eigenfunction of NTK. Then, we found that shortcut features correspond to features with larger eigenvalues when the shortcuts stem from the imbalanced number of samples in the clustered distribution. We also showed that the features with larger eigenvalues still have a large influence on the neural network output even after training, due to data variances in the clusters. Such a preference for certain features remains even when a margin of a neural network output is controlled, which shows that the max-margin bias is not the only major reason for shortcut learning. These properties of linear neural networks are empirically extended for more complex neural networks as a two-layer fully-connected ReLU network and a ResNet-18.

papers.title: Beyond Distribution Shift: Spurious Features Through the Lens of Training Dynamics
papers.research_question: How do spurious features affect model generalization, and can harmful spurious features be detected early during training by monitoring training dynamics?
papers.core_contribution: Spurious features can be benign or harmful depending on whether they are harder or easier to learn than core features. Harmful spurious features can be detected early by monitoring training dynamics using instance difficulty metrics like Prediction Depth.
papers.conclusion: Monitoring early training dynamics using suitable instance difficulty metrics can help identify harmful spurious features, saving time and computational costs and aiding in developing reliable models.
papers.key_findings:
Not all spurious features are harmful; they are harmful only if they are easier to learn than core features.
Prediction Depth (PD) can quantify feature difficulty and identify harmful spurious features during training.
Harmful spurious features can be detected by observing the learning dynamics of a DNN's early layers.
Monitoring only accuracy during training is insufficient to detect spurious features; instance difficulty metrics are needed.
Theoretical connections exist between Prediction Depth and information-theoretic concepts like V-usable information.
future_direction: Develop intervention schemes to fix spurious feature problems early.
Unlearning spurious features from model representations.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are prone to learning spurious features that correlate with the label during training but are irrelevant to the learning problem. This hurts model generalization and poses problems when deploying them in safety-critical applications. This paper aims to better understand the effects of spurious features through the lens of the learning dynamics of the internal neurons during the training process. We make the following observations: (1) While previous works highlight the harmful effects of spurious features on the generalization ability of DNNs, we emphasize that not all spurious features are harmful. Spurious features can be "benign" or "harmful" depending on whether they are "harder" or "easier" to learn than the core features for a given model. This definition is model and dataset dependent. (2) We build upon this premise and use instance difficulty methods (like Prediction Depth (Baldock et al., 2021)) to quantify "easiness" for a given model and to identify this behavior during the training phase. (3) We empirically show that the harmful spurious features can be detected by observing the learning dynamics of the DNN's early layers. In other words, easy features learned by the initial layers of a DNN early during the training can (potentially) hurt model generalization. We verify our claims on medical and vision datasets, both simulated and real, and justify the empirical success of our hypothesis by showing the theoretical connections between Prediction Depth and information-theoretic concepts like 𝒱-usable information (Ethayarajh et al., 2021). Lastly, our experiments show that monitoring only accuracy during training (as is common in machine learning pipelines) is insufficient to detect spurious features. We, therefore, highlight the need for monitoring early training dynamics using suitable instance difficulty metrics.

papers.title: Regulating Model Reliance on Non-Robust Features by Smoothing Input Marginal Density
papers.research_question: How can we regulate model reliance on non-robust features? The paper investigates using smoothing of the input marginal density to achieve this.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a regularization method that smooths the input marginal density to regulate model reliance on non-robust features, reducing feature leakage and spurious correlations while improving robustness.
papers.conclusion: The proposed regularization effectively regulates model reliance on non-robust features by smoothing the input marginal density, improving model robustness and interpretability across a range of applications.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed regularization reduces feature leakage on BlockMNIST.
It improves adversarial robustness against L2 and L∞ attacks.
It mitigates spurious correlations in CelebA-Hair and Waterbirds datasets, improving worst-group accuracy.
It outperforms input gradient regularization and other baselines in various robustness metrics.
It provides robustness against perturbations in pixel values, input gradients, and density.
papers.limitation:
Increased regularization strength can diminish model sensitivity to features, compromising overall performance.
Adversarial training may be preferable for explicit adversarial defense when computational resources permit.
papers.abstract: Trustworthy machine learning necessitates meticulous regulation of model reliance on non-robust features. We propose a framework to delineate and regulate such features by attributing model predictions to the input. Within our approach, robust feature attributions exhibit a certain consistency, while non-robust feature attributions are susceptible to fluctuations. This behavior allows identification of correlation between model reliance on non-robust features and smoothness of marginal density of the input samples. Hence, we uniquely regularize the gradients of the marginal density w.r.t. the input features for robustness. We also devise an efficient implementation of our regularization to address the potential numerical instability of the underlying optimization process. Moreover, we analytically reveal that, as opposed to our marginal density smoothing, the prevalent input gradient regularization smoothens conditional or joint density of the input, which can cause limited robustness. Our experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, providing clear evidence of its capability to address the feature leakage problem and mitigate spurious correlations. Extensive results further establish that our technique enables the model to exhibit robustness against perturbations in pixel values, input gradients, and density.

papers.title: DORA: Exploring Outlier Representations in Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can we analyze the representational space of deep neural networks to identify outlier representations that may correspond to spurious correlations or undesired concepts in a data-agnostic manner?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DORA, a data-agnostic framework for analyzing neural representations using a novel Extreme-Activation distance metric, which can identify outlier representations that often correspond to spurious or undesired concepts.
papers.conclusion: DORA offers an effective data-agnostic approach to explore and interpret neural representations, enabling the identification of anomalous representations that often encode spurious or undesired concepts, thereby enhancing model transparency and safety.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed Extreme-Activation distance metric aligns well with human judgment of concept similarity and outperforms traditional distance metrics in capturing semantic relationships.
DORA can effectively identify outlier representations that detect spurious correlations, such as watermarks or artifacts, in pre-trained models.
The framework is applicable across various architectures (CNNs, Transformers) and datasets (ImageNet, CIFAR-100).
Outlier representations corresponding to undesired concepts can persist even after fine-tuning on a different dataset.
DORA provides a practical tool for model interpretability and safety by revealing learned concepts that may lead to biased or harmful decisions.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) excel at learning complex abstractions within their internal representations. However, the concepts they learn remain opaque, a problem that becomes particularly acute when models unintentionally learn spurious correlations. In this work, we present DORA (Data-agnOstic Representation Analysis), the first data-agnostic framework for analyzing the representational space of DNNs. Central to our framework is the proposed Extreme-Activation (EA) distance measure, which assesses similarities between representations by analyzing their activation patterns on data points that cause the highest level of activation. As spurious correlations often manifest in features of data that are anomalous to the desired task, such as watermarks or artifacts, we demonstrate that internal representations capable of detecting such artifactual concepts can be found by analyzing relationships within neural representations. We validate the EA metric quantitatively, demonstrating its effectiveness both in controlled scenarios and real-world applications. Finally, we provide practical examples from popular Computer Vision models to illustrate that representations identified as outliers using the EA metric often correspond to undesired and spurious concepts.

papers.title: Exploring biologically inspired mechanisms of adversarial robustness
papers.research_question: What is the interplay between geometry, spectral properties, robustness, and expressivity in neural representations, and how do biologically inspired local learning models compare to backpropagation-trained models in terms of adversarial robustness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that unsupervised local learning models with winner-take-all dynamics learn power law representations, which are associated with smooth manifolds and improved adversarial robustness, providing a mechanistic model for studying optimal representations.
papers.conclusion: The local learning model produces smooth, power law representations that are robust to adversarial attacks, providing a mechanistic model for studying optimal representations in biological and artificial systems.
papers.key_findings:
The hybrid model (KH) is more robust against random perturbations, FGSM, and PGD attacks compared to backpropagation-trained models.
The hybrid model exhibits power law spectra in its latent representations, which are scale-invariant and optimal in the sense of Stringer et al.
Smoothness of hidden representations (as measured by Jacobian norm) correlates with robustness.
Weight regularization (L2, Jacobian) also improves robustness but does not yield power law spectra.
Spectral regularization enforces power law spectra but does not improve robustness, likely due to folded representation surfaces.
papers.limitation: The model's finite nature may limit the applicability of theoretical results derived for infinite-dimensional spaces.
future_direction: Understanding how power law spectra determine optimally smooth encodings
Applying insights to develop more robust artificial systems
Studying robust neural networks in mammalian brains
papers.abstract: Abstract Backpropagation-optimized artificial neural networks, while precise, lack robustness, leading to unforeseen behaviors that affect their safety. Biological neural systems do solve some of these issues already. Unlike artificial models, biological neurons adjust connectivity based on neighboring cell activity. Understanding the biological mechanisms of robustness can pave the way toward building trustworthy and safe systems. Robustness in neural representations is hypothesized to correlate with the smoothness of the encoding manifold. Recent work suggests power law covariance spectra, which were observed studying the primary visual cortex of mice, to be indicative of a balanced trade-off between accuracy and robustness in representations. Here, we show that unsupervised local learning models with winner takes all dynamics learn such power law representations, providing upcoming studies a mechanistic model with that characteristic. Our research aims to understand the interplay between geometry, spectral properties, robustness, and expressivity in neural representations. Hence, we study the link between representation smoothness and spectrum by using weight, Jacobian and spectral regularization while assessing performance and adversarial robustness. Our work serves as a foundation for future research into the mechanisms underlying power law spectra and optimally smooth encodings in both biological and artificial systems. The insights gained may elucidate the mechanisms that realize robust neural networks in mammalian brains and inform the development of more stable and reliable artificial systems.

papers.title: Feature Averaging: An Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent Leading to Non-Robustness in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What implicit bias in gradient descent leads to non-robustness in neural networks? The paper investigates 'Feature Averaging', where networks average multiple discriminative features rather than leveraging them individually.
papers.core_contribution: Gradient descent has an implicit bias called feature averaging, where networks average multiple discriminative features, leading to non-robustness; fine-grained supervision can improve robustness by encouraging feature decoupling.
papers.conclusion: Feature averaging is a key implicit bias of gradient descent that contributes to non-robustness, and providing more granular supervision can mitigate this vulnerability and enhance robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient descent on two-layer ReLU networks converges to feature-averaging solutions where each neuron's weight vector aligns with an average of cluster features.
Feature-averaging solutions are non-robust with robust radius O(sqrt(d/k)), while optimal robust solutions exist with radius O(sqrt(d)).
With fine-grained supervision (feature-level labels), networks can learn feature-decoupling solutions that achieve optimal robustness.
Experiments on synthetic data confirm the feature averaging phenomenon and its impact on adversarial robustness.
Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 show that fine-grained supervision improves robustness compared to binary supervision.
papers.abstract: In this work, we investigate a particular implicit bias in gradient descent training, which we term "Feature Averaging," and argue that it is one of the principal factors contributing to the non-robustness of deep neural networks. We show that, even when multiple discriminative features are present in the input data, neural networks trained by gradient descent tend to rely on an average (or a certain combination) of these features for classification, rather than distinguishing and leveraging each feature individually. Specifically, we provide a detailed theoretical analysis of the training dynamics of two-layer ReLU networks on a binary classification task, where the data distribution consists of multiple clusters with mutually orthogonal centers. We rigorously prove that gradient descent biases the network towards feature averaging, where the weights of each hidden neuron represent an average of the cluster centers (each corresponding to a distinct feature), thereby making the network vulnerable to input perturbations aligned with the negative direction of the averaged features. On the positive side, we demonstrate that this vulnerability can be mitigated through more granular supervision. In particular, we prove that a two-layer ReLU network can achieve optimal robustness when trained to classify individual features rather than merely the original binary classes. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings with experiments on synthetic datasets, MNIST, and CIFAR-10, and confirm the prevalence of feature averaging and its impact on adversarial robustness. We hope these theoretical and empirical insights deepen the understanding of how gradient descent shapes feature learning and adversarial robustness, and how more detailed supervision can enhance robustness.

papers.title: Intriguing properties of neural networks
papers.research_question: Do individual units in neural networks have semantic meaning, and are neural networks robust to small perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that semantic information in neural networks is contained in the space of activations rather than individual units, and that neural networks are vulnerable to adversarial examples that generalize across models and datasets.
papers.conclusion: Deep neural networks have counter-intuitive properties with respect to unit semantics and discontinuities, and adversarial examples are dense and may affect generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Random directions in the activation space are as semantically interpretable as individual units.
Neural networks are susceptible to adversarial examples—imperceptible perturbations that cause misclassification.
Adversarial examples generalize across models with different hyperparameters.
Adversarial examples generalize across models trained on disjoint datasets.
The instability of networks can be analyzed via Lipschitz bounds of layers, which can be large even in early layers.
papers.limitation:
The set of adversarial negatives is of extremely low probability and thus rarely observed in the test set, but we don't have a deep understanding of how often they appear.
The Lipschitz bounds are upper bounds and do not guarantee the existence of adversarial examples.
future_direction: Compare the effects of adversarial examples for different layers
Investigate how often adversarial negatives appear
Regularize networks by penalizing Lipschitz bounds to improve generalization
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks are highly expressive models that have recently achieved state of the art performance on speech and visual recognition tasks. While their expressiveness is the reason they succeed, it also causes them to learn uninterpretable solutions that could have counter-intuitive properties. In this paper we report two such properties. First, we find that there is no distinction between individual high level units and random linear combinations of high level units, according to various methods of unit analysis. It suggests that it is the space, rather than the individual units, that contains of the semantic information in the high layers of neural networks. Second, we find that deep neural networks learn input-output mappings that are fairly discontinuous to a significant extend. We can cause the network to misclassify an image by applying a certain imperceptible perturbation, which is found by maximizing the network's prediction error. In addition, the specific nature of these perturbations is not a random artifact of learning: the same perturbation can cause a different network, that was trained on a different subset of the dataset, to misclassify the same input.

papers.title: Model Guidance via Robust Feature Attribution
papers.research_question: How can we prevent models from relying on shortcut features by using robust feature attribution? Can simultaneously optimizing for explanation robustness and shortcut mitigation be more effective?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces R4, a robust variant of right for the right reasons that simultaneously optimizes for explanation robustness and shortcut mitigation, achieving significant improvements over prior methods.
papers.conclusion: R4 is a novel gradient- and robustness-based method that effectively mitigates shortcut learning and achieves superior results across datasets, especially in non-ideal settings with limited or noisy annotations.
papers.key_findings:
R4 outperforms prior MLX methods across all datasets, reducing test-time misclassifications by 20% compared to state-of-the-art.
R4 is effective even with annotations on just 20% of the training examples.
Annotation quality is more important than quantity for effective shortcut mitigation.
Cert-R4 provides worst-case guarantees but is computationally expensive and less scalable.
R4 is particularly effective in practical scenarios with noisy annotations, complex models, and imbalanced datasets.
papers.limitation:
The method is limited in settings with large models, few or sparse masks, and constrained computational resources.
When multiple shortcuts are present, reducing reliance on only some can lead models to overcompensate by relying more heavily on others.
future_direction: Developing a theoretical framework to understand the role of weight regularization.
Leveraging techniques with statistical guarantees (e.g., randomized smoothing).
Improving bound propagation tightness using methods such as CROWN.
Advancing shortcut learning mitigation in large language models with scalable methods that account for semantic understanding and learned representations.
papers.abstract: Controlling the patterns a model learns is essential to preventing reliance on irrelevant or misleading features. Such reliance on irrelevant features, often called shortcut features, has been observed across domains, including medical imaging and natural language processing, where it may lead to real-world harms. A common mitigation strategy leverages annotations (provided by humans or machines) indicating which features are relevant or irrelevant. These annotations are compared to model explanations, typically in the form of feature salience, and used to guide the loss function during training. Unfortunately, recent works have demonstrated that feature salience methods are unreliable and therefore offer a poor signal to optimize. In this work, we propose a simplified objective that simultaneously optimizes for explanation robustness and mitigation of shortcut learning. Unlike prior objectives with similar aims, we demonstrate theoretically why our approach ought to be more effective. Across a comprehensive series of experiments, we show that our approach consistently reduces test-time misclassifications by 20% compared to state-of-the-art methods. We also extend prior experimental settings to include natural language processing tasks. Additionally, we conduct novel ablations that yield practical insights, including the relative importance of annotation quality over quantity. Code for our method and experiments is available at: https://github.com/Mihneaghitu/ModelGuidanceViaRobustFeatureAttribution.

papers.title: Uncovering Memorization Effect in the Presence of Spurious Correlations
papers.research_question: Does memorization play a role in spurious correlations and imbalanced group performance in neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies that spurious memorization, concentrated in a small subset of neurons, is a key driver of imbalanced group performance in the presence of spurious correlations, and proposes a fine-tuning framework to mitigate this effect.
papers.conclusion: Spurious memorization in a small subset of neurons is a fundamental cause of imbalanced group performance, and strategically disrupting this memorization can lead to more robust models.
papers.key_findings:
A small set of critical neurons is responsible for memorizing minority group examples during training.
Modifying (e.g., pruning, randomizing) these critical neurons significantly affects training accuracy on minority groups but has minimal impact on majority groups.
Both gradient-based and magnitude-based criteria can effectively identify these critical neurons.
Removing spurious memorization through a proposed fine-tuning framework improves worst-group test accuracy across different architectures and datasets.
The memorization of minority examples by a limited neuron subset leads to poor test robustness for those groups.
papers.abstract: Machine learning models often rely on simple spurious features -- patterns in training data that correlate with targets but are not causally related to them, like image backgrounds in foreground classification. This reliance typically leads to imbalanced test performance across minority and majority groups. In this work, we take a closer look at the fundamental cause of such imbalanced performance through the lens of memorization, which refers to the ability to predict accurately on atypical examples (minority groups) in the training set but failing in achieving the same accuracy in the testing set. This paper systematically shows the ubiquitous existence of spurious features in a small set of neurons within the network, providing the first-ever evidence that memorization may contribute to imbalanced group performance. Through three experimental sources of converging empirical evidence, we find the property of a small subset of neurons or channels in memorizing minority group information. Inspired by these findings, we hypothesize that spurious memorization, concentrated within a small subset of neurons, plays a key role in driving imbalanced group performance. To further substantiate this hypothesis, we show that eliminating these unnecessary spurious memorization patterns via a novel framework during training can significantly affect the model performance on minority groups. Our experimental results across various architectures and benchmarks offer new insights on how neural networks encode core and spurious knowledge, laying the groundwork for future research in demystifying robustness to spurious correlation.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: Steering CLIP's vision transformer with sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be used to understand and steer the internal mechanisms of CLIP's vision transformer, and what differences exist between vision and language processing in these models?
papers.core_contribution: Training sparse autoencoders on CLIP's vision transformer to interpret and steer its features, revealing differences between vision and language processing, and demonstrating improved performance on vision disentanglement tasks and typographic attack defense.
papers.conclusion: SAEs on CLIP's vision transformer reveal sparsity differences and provide steerable features that enable improved disentanglement and state-of-the-art defense against typographic attacks.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs on CLIP show distinct sparsity patterns for spatial vs CLS tokens and compared to language models.
10-15% of neurons and features are steerable, with SAEs providing thousands more steerable features than the base model.
Targeted suppression of SAE features improves performance on three vision disentanglement tasks (CelebA, Waterbirds, typographic attacks).
Optimal disentanglement occurs in middle layers.
State-of-the-art performance on defense against typographic attacks.
papers.limitation:
The steerability metric does not capture semantic relationships between promoted concepts.
Some features may not be accurately captured due to limited vocabulary coverage.
future_direction: Improving the steerability metric to capture semantic relationships between concepts.
Exploring larger vocabularies to better capture feature semantics.
papers.abstract: While vision models are highly capable, their internal mechanisms remain poorly understood -- a challenge which sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have helped address in language, but which remains underexplored in vision. We address this gap by training SAEs on CLIP's vision transformer and uncover key differences between vision and language processing, including distinct sparsity patterns for SAEs trained across layers and token types. We then provide the first systematic analysis on the steerability of CLIP's vision transformer by introducing metrics to quantify how precisely SAE features can be steered to affect the model's output. We find that 10-15\% of neurons and features are steerable, with SAEs providing thousands more steerable features than the base model. Through targeted suppression of SAE features, we then demonstrate improved performance on three vision disentanglement tasks (CelebA, Waterbirds, and typographic attacks), finding optimal disentanglement in middle model layers, and achieving state-of-the-art performance on defense against typographic attacks.

papers.title: Identifying and Disentangling Spurious Features in Pretrained Image Representations
papers.research_question: How are spurious features represented in pretrained image representations, and how can we remove or disentangle them to improve worst-group accuracy?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a linear autoencoder method to disentangle core and spurious features in pretrained image representations, leading to improved worst-group accuracy in classification.
papers.conclusion: Spurious features in pretrained representations can be identified and removed, and disentangling them via a linear autoencoder improves worst-group accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Pretrained representations contain spurious features that can be identified and removed to improve worst-group accuracy.
For some representations (ResNet-50 and RegNetY), spurious features are axis-aligned, allowing removal by dropping specific neurons.
For DINOv2, individual neurons are not pure spurious or non-spurious, so simple removal does not work.
The proposed linear autoencoder (GwAE) can disentangle core and spurious features, and training a classifier on the core part improves worst-group accuracy.
Applying PCA on the core features from the autoencoder further improves performance.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is limited to the Waterbirds dataset and three backbones (ResNet-50, RegNetY, DINOv2).
The method requires group information (spurious feature labels) for training the autoencoder.
The use of L-BFGS for linear models may not capture the full potential of SGD with early stopping, which is left for future work.
future_direction: Experiments with more backbones and datasets to see how well the findings generalize.
Analysis of SGD-based optimization with early stopping for linear models.
papers.abstract: Neural networks employ spurious correlations in their predictions, resulting in decreased performance when these correlations do not hold. Recent works suggest fixing pretrained representations and training a classification head that does not use spurious features. We investigate how spurious features are represented in pretrained representations and explore strategies for removing information about spurious features. Considering the Waterbirds dataset and a few pretrained representations, we find that even with full knowledge of spurious features, their removal is not straightforward due to entangled representation. To address this, we propose a linear autoencoder training method to separate the representation into core, spurious, and other features. We propose two effective spurious feature removal approaches that are applied to the encoding and significantly improve classification performance measured by worst group accuracy.

papers.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with\n Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
papers.research_question: How can we interpret neural networks using human-defined concepts and quantify the sensitivity of predictions to these concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) to represent human-friendly concepts in a model's activation space, and a method (TCAV) to quantify the importance of these concepts to model predictions using directional derivatives.
papers.conclusion: TCAV provides a human-friendly linear interpretation of neural networks, allowing analysts to quantify the importance of user-defined concepts to model predictions, and has been shown to be a useful technique in various applications including bias detection and medical image analysis.
papers.key_findings:
CAVs align with intended concepts, validated by sorting images and activation maximization (deep dream).
TCAV can reveal biases in models, such as gender and race biases in image classifiers.
TCAV quantifies the importance of specific concepts to model classes (e.g., stripes for zebras, red for fire engines).
TCAV can help interpret model errors in medical applications, such as diabetic retinopathy grading.
In a controlled experiment, TCAV more accurately communicated concept importance to humans compared to saliency maps.
future_direction: Applying TCAV to other types of data (audio, video, sequences).
Using TCAV to identify adversarial examples.
Automatically identifying concepts.
papers.abstract:
The interpretation of deep learning models is a challenge due to their size,
complexity, and often opaque internal state. In addition, many systems, such as
image classifiers, operate on low-level features rather than high-level
concepts. To address these challenges, we introduce Concept Activation Vectors
(CAVs), which provide an interpretation of a neural net's internal state in
terms of human-friendly concepts. The key idea is to view the high-dimensional
internal state of a neural net as an aid, not an obstacle. We show how to use
CAVs as part of a technique, Testing with CAVs (TCAV), that uses directional
derivatives to quantify the degree to which a user-defined concept is important
to a classification result--for example, how sensitive a prediction of "zebra"
is to the presence of stripes. Using the domain of image classification as a
testing ground, we describe how CAVs may be used to explore hypotheses and
generate insights for a standard image classification network as well as a
medical application.

papers.title: Improving the Adversarial Robustness and Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks by Regularizing their Input Gradients
papers.research_question: Does regularizing input gradients improve adversarial robustness and interpretability of deep neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Training neural networks with input gradient regularization improves their adversarial robustness and makes their input gradients more interpretable, linking interpretability and robustness.
papers.conclusion: Input gradient regularization is a promising defense that improves both adversarial robustness and interpretability, suggesting that progress in one area may lead to progress in the other.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient-regularized models are robust to transferred adversarial examples generated to fool other models.
Adversarial examples generated to fool gradient-regularized models fool all other models equally well and are rated by humans as more interpretable misclassifications.
Regularizing input gradients makes them more naturally interpretable as rationales for model predictions.
Gradient regularization can be combined with adversarial training for even greater robustness.
Defensive distillation does not provide robust defense and can make models more vulnerable to some attacks.
papers.limitation: Gradient regularization is a second-order method that increases training time and may not be supported in all autodifferentiation frameworks.
future_direction: Explore alternative formulations of gradient regularization, such as penalties on logits rather than log probabilities.
Test gradient regularization on larger, more state-of-the-art networks.
Investigate different hyperparameters for networks trained with gradient regularization.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks have proven remarkably effective at solving many classification problems, but have been criticized recently for two major weaknesses: the reasons behind their predictions are uninterpretable, and the predictions themselves can often be fooled by small adversarial perturbations. These problems pose major obstacles for the adoption of neural networks in domains that require security or transparency. In this work, we evaluate the effectiveness of defenses that differentiably penalize the degree to which small changes in inputs can alter model predictions. Across multiple attacks, architectures, defenses, and datasets, we find that neural networks trained with this input gradient regularization exhibit robustness to transferred adversarial examples generated to fool all of the other models. We also find that adversarial examples generated to fool gradient-regularized models fool all other models equally well, and actually lead to more "legitimate," interpretable misclassifications as rated by people (which we confirm in a human subject experiment). Finally, we demonstrate that regularizing input gradients makes them more naturally interpretable as rationales for model predictions. We conclude by discussing this relationship between interpretability and robustness in deep neural networks.

papers.title: Unlearning the Spurious Correlations for Improving Generalization of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate spurious correlations in language models to improve out-of-distribution generalization without retraining the model or constructing external datasets?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes MacU, a machine unlearning method that locates and edits neurons encoding spurious correlations to improve model generalization without retraining or external datasets.
papers.conclusion: MacU effectively mitigates spurious correlations in language models, improving generalization without requiring model retraining or external datasets.
papers.key_findings:
MacU improves generalization on sentiment analysis and natural language inference tasks, outperforming fine-tuning by 3.13% and 2.05% respectively.
MacU effectively corrects spurious correlations, as shown by lower average proximity (η) compared to other methods.
Neurons encoding spurious correlations and causal correlations overlap, which motivates the need for careful neuron editing.
MacU is a plug-and-play method that does not require retraining the model or constructing external datasets.
MacU is effective across multiple model architectures and scales (BERT, GPT-2, LLaMA-2-7B, Qwen-2-1.5B, GLM-4-9B).
papers.limitation:
Golden correlation token set construction is human-centric and may not capture dynamic semantic changes (concept drift) effectively.
The method focuses on spurious correlations in individual semantic units and does not address compound semantic units.
The attention attribution method used for model behavior analysis may lack stable causal correlation with model predictions.
future_direction: Develop human-machine collaboration methods for more efficient and accurate causal correlation token discovery.
Extend MacU to handle spurious correlations in compound semantic units.
Develop more reliable model interpretation methods to improve the reliability of interpretation results.
papers.abstract: Data-driven language models often perform poorly on out-of-distribution data due to the internalization of spurious correlations. Existing mitigation strategies focus on data preprocessing or model regularization, which do not sufficiently correct the spurious correlation and require high costs. We propose a novel plug-and-play method, MacU, a machine unlearning strategy for mitigating the spurious correlation. Firstly, we accurately locate neurons encoding correlation information based on the gradient responses of the proximity. Then, we analyze the model’s neuron storage mechanism of causal or spurious correlation information, and identify overlap between these two types of neurons. Based on the above findings, we develop a neuron editing method based on Particle Swarm Optimization, ensuring that the model forgets spurious correlations while retaining the best memory of causal correlations. Experiments on 5 language models and 11 datasets show that MacU significantly improves generalization, surpassing the fine-tuning baseline by 3.13% and 2.05% in sentiment analysis and natural language inference tasks, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to design a machine unlearning technique to mitigate spurious correlation, which has achieved superior correction capability without requiring retraining the model.

papers.title: On the Brittleness of Robust Features: An Exploratory Analysis of Model Robustness and Illusionary Robust Features
papers.research_question: Whether models trained exclusively on robust features are always robust, and specifically, if they are vulnerable to adversarial attacks that target the robust model itself.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that models trained only on robust features are still vulnerable to adversarial attacks that target the robust model, and introduces the concept of 'illusionary robust features' to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: Robust features are not always robust due to the presence of illusionary robust features, and non-robust features can help improve robustness against certain attacks.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained on robust features only are vulnerable to small perturbations when attacked by a robust attack.
Image perturbation by attacking robust models changes the less robust features, and the more robust features are highly correlated with incorrect labels (illusionary robust features), making robust classifiers vulnerable.
Standard classifiers, which use non-robust features entangled with robust features, are more robust against robust attacks than robust classifiers.
future_direction: Explore the notion of illusionary robust features on other data sets.
Data set robustification by nullifying the effect of illusionary robust features and maximizing the effect of non-robust features entangled with non-illusionary robust features.
papers.abstract: Neural networks have been shown to be vulnerable to visual data perturbations imperceptible to the human eye. Nowadays, the leading hypothesis about the reason for the existence of these adversarial examples is the presence of non-robust features, which are highly predictive but brittle. Also, it has been shown that there exist two types of non-robust features depending on whether or not they are entangled with robust features; perturbing non-robust features entangled with robust features can form adversarial examples. This paper extends earlier work by showing that models trained exclusively on robust features are still vulnerable to one type of adversarial example. Standard-trained networks can classify more accurately than robustly trained networks in this situation. Our experiments show that this phenomenon is due to the high correlation between most of the robust features and both correct and incorrect labels. In this work, we define features highly correlated with correct and incorrect labels as illusionary robust features. We discuss how perturbing an image attacking robust models affects the feature space. Based on our observations on the feature space, we explain why standard models are more successful in correctly classifying these perturbed images than robustly trained models. Our observations also show that, similar to changing non-robust features, changing some of the robust features is still imperceptible to the human eye.

papers.title: Removing Spurious Concepts from Neural Network Representations via Joint Subspace Estimation
papers.research_question: How can we remove spurious concepts from neural network representations without inadvertently removing main-task features?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Joint Subspace Estimation (JSE), an iterative algorithm that jointly estimates orthogonal subspaces for spurious and main-task concepts in neural network embeddings, enabling removal of only spurious features while preserving main-task information.
papers.conclusion: JSE provides an effective post-hoc concept-removal method that improves interpretability and control over spurious concepts in neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
JSE outperforms existing concept-removal methods (INLP, RLACE, LEACE, ADV) in out-of-distribution generalization, especially when spurious correlations are strong.
JSE effectively identifies and removes spurious concept subspaces while retaining main-task subspaces, as validated on vision and NLP benchmarks.
The method includes statistical tests to determine when to stop adding vectors, preventing over-removal of main-task features.
papers.limitation:
The method assumes orthogonality between spurious and main-task subspaces, which may not always hold in practice.
For text data (MultiNLI), the main-task and spurious concepts may become overlapping in the embeddings during finetuning, reducing the effectiveness of the method.
papers.abstract: Out-of-distribution generalization in neural networks is often hampered by spurious correlations. A common strategy is to mitigate this by removing spurious concepts from the neural network representation of the data. Existing concept-removal methods tend to be overzealous by inadvertently eliminating features associated with the main task of the model, thereby harming model performance. We propose an iterative algorithm that separates spurious from main-task concepts by jointly identifying two low-dimensional orthogonal subspaces in the neural network representation. We evaluate the algorithm on benchmark datasets for computer vision (Waterbirds, CelebA) and natural language processing (MultiNLI), and show that it outperforms existing concept removal methods

papers.title: Interpreting vision transformers via residual replacement model
papers.research_question: How do vision transformers (ViTs) represent and process the world?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the residual replacement model, which replaces ViT computations with interpretable SAE features in the residual stream, enabling scalable circuit discovery and application to debiasing spurious correlations.
papers.conclusion: The residual replacement model provides a faithful and interpretable framework for understanding ViT mechanisms, with practical utility in tasks like debiasing.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features in ViTs are interpretable across all layers, evolving from low-level attributes to high-level semantic concepts.
ViTs encode specialized features such as curve detectors and position detectors, analogous to those in CNNs and LMs.
The residual replacement model produces parsimonious circuits that faithfully explain ViT mechanisms, with improvements from edge-based discovery and gradient correction.
The framework enables quantitative analysis of feature similarity across layers, showing convergence for intra-class images.
The model can be applied to debias spurious correlations in ImageNet classifiers through feature ablation.
future_direction: Incorporating higher-order interactions between intermediate features in the gradient-based decomposition.
papers.abstract: How do vision transformers (ViTs) represent and process the world? This paper addresses this long-standing question through the first systematic analysis of 6.6K features across all layers, extracted via sparse autoencoders, and by introducing the residual replacement model, which replaces ViT computations with interpretable features in the residual stream. Our analysis reveals not only a feature evolution from low-level patterns to high-level semantics, but also how ViTs encode curves and spatial positions through specialized feature types. The residual replacement model scalably produces a faithful yet parsimonious circuit for human-scale interpretability by significantly simplifying the original computations. As a result, this framework enables intuitive understanding of ViT mechanisms. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of our framework in debiasing spurious correlations.

papers.title: Identifying and Mitigating Spurious Correlations for Improving Robustness in NLP Models
papers.research_question: How can spurious correlations (shortcuts) in NLP models be automatically identified at scale, and how can mitigating these shortcuts improve model robustness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework to automatically identify spurious correlations (shortcuts) in NLP models at scale and shows that targeted mitigation of these shortcuts improves model robustness across domains and fairness.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that a scalable set of spurious correlations can be automatically identified and that mitigating these correlations improves model robustness, though the reliability of interpretability methods remains a limitation.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed framework (important token extraction, cross-dataset analysis, knowledge-aware perturbation) effectively identifies spurious tokens with high precision, as verified by human annotators.
Masking identified shortcuts during training improves model generalization to out-of-distribution data.
Mitigating shortcuts reduces the performance gap between demographic groups (e.g., male vs. female) in an occupation classification task, leading to fairer models.
The framework is not highly sensitive to the hyperparameter λ used in token importance extraction.
Both attention scores and integrated gradients can be used as effective methods for the initial important token extraction step.
papers.limitation: The interpretability methods used (e.g., attention scores) might not be accurate enough to reflect how a model works and could even deceive human decision makers.
future_direction: Future research should develop better automated methods for improving model robustness with less human intervention or expert knowledge.
papers.abstract: Recently, NLP models have achieved remarkable progress across a variety of tasks; however, they have also been criticized for being not robust. Many robustness problems can be attributed to models exploiting spurious correlations, or shortcuts between the training data and the task labels. Most existing work identifies a limited set of task-specific shortcuts via human priors or error analyses, which requires extensive expertise and efforts. In this paper, we aim to automatically identify such spurious correlations in NLP models at scale. We first leverage existing interpretability methods to extract tokens that significantly affect model's decision process from the input text. We then distinguish "genuine" tokens and "spurious" tokens by analyzing model predictions across multiple corpora and further verify them through knowledge-aware perturbations. We show that our proposed method can effectively and efficiently identify a scalable set of "shortcuts", and mitigating these leads to more robust models in multiple applications.

papers.title: White Noise Analysis of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: What are the inherent biases of deep neural networks and how can we understand and visualize them using methods from computational neuroscience (classification images and spike triggered analysis)?
papers.core_contribution: White noise analysis (using classification images and spike triggered averaging) can reveal inherent biases in neural networks, visualize filters, and be used for adversarial attack and defense.
papers.conclusion: White noise analysis is effective for understanding and interpreting neural networks, demonstrating successful cross-fertilization between neuroscience and machine learning.
papers.key_findings:
Classification images derived from white noise resemble target classes and can be used for classification above chance level.
Classification images can be used to attack black-box classifiers by adding bias maps to inputs.
Classification images can detect adversarial patch attacks by revealing perturbed regions.
Spike triggered averaging can visualize filters in CNNs, showing oriented edges similar to those learned from real data.
Micro-stimulation of neurons in different layers can bias network decisions, producing psychometric curves similar to biological systems.
papers.limitation:
Requires a large number of trials (sample complexity) to compute classification images.
Classification images over natural scene datasets may not resemble sharp object instances.
future_direction: Apply the tools to more complex CNN architectures (e.g., ResNet, InceptionNet) and other models (e.g., CapsuleNets, GANs).
Use classification images to detect and defend against other types of adversarial attacks.
Apply classification images and spike triggered analysis to other computer vision tasks (e.g., object detection, segmentation).
papers.abstract: A white noise analysis of modern deep neural networks is presented to unveil their biases at the whole network level or the single neuron level. Our analysis is based on two popular and related methods in psychophysics and neurophysiology namely classification images and spike triggered analysis. These methods have been widely used to understand the underlying mechanisms of sensory systems in humans and monkeys. We leverage them to investigate the inherent biases of deep neural networks and to obtain a first-order approximation of their functionality. We emphasize on CNNs since they are currently the state of the art methods in computer vision and are a decent model of human visual processing. In addition, we study multi-layer perceptrons, logistic regression, and recurrent neural networks. Experiments over four classic datasets, MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet, show that the computed bias maps resemble the target classes and when used for classification lead to an over twofold performance than the chance level. Further, we show that classification images can be used to attack a black-box classifier and to detect adversarial patch attacks. Finally, we utilize spike triggered averaging to derive the filters of CNNs and explore how the behavior of a network changes when neurons in different layers are modulated. Our effort illustrates a successful example of borrowing from neurosciences to study ANNs and highlights the importance of cross-fertilization and synergy across machine learning, deep learning, and computational neuroscience.

papers.title: Bridging Explainability and Embeddings: BEE Aware of Spuriousness
papers.research_question: How can we identify spurious correlations that models learn during fine-tuning, even when no counterexamples exist in the training or validation data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces BEE, a weight-space framework that identifies and names spurious correlations learned by models during fine-tuning by analyzing how classifier weights drift from their initial concept embeddings, even without counterexamples in the data.
papers.conclusion: BEE is presented as a general and principled tool for diagnosing spurious correlations directly from learned weights, enabling principled dataset auditing and more trustworthy foundation models.
papers.key_findings:
BEE uncovers spurious correlations that persist under full fine-tuning and transfer across diverse state-of-the-art backbones, reducing ImageNet class accuracy by up to 95%.
The method is validated across vision and language tasks and multiple embedding families, proving broad applicability.
SCs identified by BEE can be used to create SC-enhanced zero-shot prompts that improve worst-group accuracy.
The framework reveals previously untapped spurious correlations in general setups like ImageNet-1k and specialized domains like medical notes.
papers.abstract: Current methods for detecting spurious correlations rely on analyzing dataset statistics or error patterns, leaving many harmful shortcuts invisible when counterexamples are absent. We introduce BEE (Bridging Explainability and Embeddings), a framework that shifts the focus from model predictions to the weight space, and to the embedding geometry underlying decisions. By analyzing how fine-tuning perturbs pretrained representations, BEE uncovers spurious correlations that remain hidden from conventional evaluation pipelines. We use linear probing as a transparent diagnostic lens, revealing spurious features that not only persist after full fine-tuning but also transfer across diverse state-of-the-art models. Our experiments cover numerous datasets and domains: vision (Waterbirds, CelebA, ImageNet-1k), language (CivilComments, MIMIC-CXR medical notes), and multiple embedding families (CLIP, CLIP-DataComp.XL, mGTE, BLIP2, SigLIP2). BEE consistently exposes spurious correlations: from concepts that slash the ImageNet accuracy by up to 95%, to clinical shortcuts in MIMIC-CXR notes that induce dangerous false negatives. Together, these results position BEE as a general and principled tool for diagnosing spurious correlations in weight space, enabling principled dataset auditing and more trustworthy foundation models. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/bit-ml/bee.

papers.title: What do neural networks learn in image classification? A frequency shortcut perspective
papers.research_question: What do neural networks learn in image classification from a frequency perspective, and how do frequency shortcuts based on data characteristics affect their learning and generalization?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks in image classification learn frequency shortcuts—specific frequency sets that simplify the objective—which can be texture- or shape-based depending on data characteristics, and these shortcuts impair generalization on out-of-distribution data.
papers.conclusion: Frequency shortcuts are prevalent in neural networks for image classification, driven by data characteristics and simplicity bias, and future research should focus on developing effective training schemes to mitigate this shortcut learning.
papers.key_findings:
NNs tend to learn simple solutions first during training, depending on the most distinctive frequency characteristics in the data, which can be low- or high-frequencies.
Frequency shortcuts are data-dependent and can be texture-based or shape-based, corresponding to specific frequency subsets that NNs exploit for classification.
Frequency shortcuts can be transferred across datasets and models, and their presence in OOD test sets can create an illusion of improved generalization.
Larger model capacity (e.g., ResNet50, ViT-B) and common data augmentation techniques (AutoAugment, AugMix, SIN) cannot fully avoid frequency shortcut learning.
Frequency shortcuts may prevent NNs from learning meaningful semantics, such as shape information, leading to poor generalization on similar-shaped objects with different textures.
future_direction: Focus on effective training schemes mitigating frequency shortcut learning.
Explore novel data augmentation strategies that explicitly target shortcut mitigation, e.g., leveraging dominant frequency maps.
papers.abstract: Frequency analysis is useful for understanding the mechanisms of representation learning in neural networks (NNs). Most research in this area focuses on the learning dynamics of NNs for regression tasks, while little for classification. This study empirically investigates the latter and expands the understanding of frequency shortcuts. First, we perform experiments on synthetic datasets, designed to have a bias in different frequency bands. Our results demonstrate that NNs tend to find simple solutions for classification, and what they learn first during training depends on the most distinctive frequency characteristics, which can be either low- or high-frequencies. Second, we confirm this phenomenon on natural images. We propose a metric to measure class-wise frequency characteristics and a method to identify frequency shortcuts. The results show that frequency shortcuts can be texture-based or shape-based, depending on what best simplifies the objective. Third, we validate the transferability of frequency shortcuts on out-of-distribution (OOD) test sets. Our results suggest that frequency shortcuts can be transferred across datasets and cannot be fully avoided by larger model capacity and data augmentation. We recommend that future research should focus on effective training schemes mitigating frequency shortcut learning.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we discover and use sparse feature circuits, composed of interpretable features, to explain and edit model behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits, which are causally implicated subnetworks of interpretable features, enabling detailed understanding and editing of model behaviors, including a technique (SHIFT) for removing unintended signals without disambiguating data.
papers.conclusion: Sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding and editing of model behaviors, showing promise for interpretability and downstream applications.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse feature circuits are more interpretable and faithful than neuron circuits.
They can be used to understand model mechanisms, such as subject-verb agreement.
SHIFT can remove unintended signals from a classifier without access to disambiguating labeled data.
The method scales to automatically discover thousands of behaviors and their circuits in an unsupervised pipeline.
future_direction: Scaling to larger models
Improving the quality and coverage of SAEs
Applying feature circuits to a wider range of tasks and models
papers.abstract: We introduce methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits. These are causally implicated subnetworks of human-interpretable features for explaining language model behaviors. Circuits identified in prior work consist of polysemantic and difficult-to-interpret units like attention heads or neurons, rendering them unsuitable for many downstream applications. In contrast, sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding of unanticipated mechanisms. Because they are based on fine-grained units, sparse feature circuits are useful for downstream tasks: We introduce SHIFT, where we improve the generalization of a classifier by ablating features that a human judges to be task-irrelevant. Finally, we demonstrate an entirely unsupervised and scalable interpretability pipeline by discovering thousands of sparse feature circuits for automatically discovered model behaviors.

papers.title: Understanding Robust Learning through the Lens of Representation Similarities
papers.research_question: How do the properties of representations learned by robust (adversarially trained) neural networks differ from those obtained from standard, non-robust training?
papers.core_contribution: Robust training leads to representations that lack specialization (disappearance of block structure), exhibit long-range similarities across layers, and deeper layers overfit, which underlies the behavioral differences of robust networks.
papers.conclusion: The lack of specialization and overfitting in deeper layers suggests the need for explicit tools to differentiate between layers during training and layer-wise specialized regularization methods for robust training.
papers.key_findings:
Robust representations are less specialized, with higher similarity across distant layers and a disappearance of the 'block structure' seen in non-robust networks.
Early layers are largely unaffected by adversarial examples, with benign and adversarial representations being similar in robust networks.
Deeper layers overfit during robust training, converging slower and visiting drastically different representations when loss indicates overfitting.
Visually dissimilar adversarial constraints (e.g., ℓp, JPEG, Gabor, Snow) can lead to similar robust representations at lower attack strengths.
Increasing adversarial budget (ϵ) or reducing network width amplifies cross-layer similarity, indicating a drop in relative capacity.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to image classification tasks and specific architectures (Wide ResNets and ResNets).
Representation similarity metrics like CKA have known limitations, such as insensitivity to deletions of principal components that correlate with accuracy.
future_direction: Development of robust learning-specific architectures and training methods.
Adoption of layer-wise specialized regularization methods for robust training.
