We build CB-LLMs for two essential NLP tasks: text classification and text generation. In text classification, CB-LLMs is competitive with, and at times outperforms, traditional black-box models while providing explicit and interpretable reasoning. For the more challenging task of text generation, interpretable neurons in CB-LLMs enable precise concept detection, controlled generation, and safer outputs. The embedded interpretability empowers users to transparently identify harmful content, steer model behavior, and unlearn undesired concepts -- significantly enhancing the safety, reliability, and trustworthiness of LLMs, which are critical capabilities notably absent in existing models. Our code is available at https://github.com/Trustworthy-ML-Lab/CB-LLMs.

papers.title: Towards Unifying Interpretability and Control: Evaluation via Intervention
papers.research_question: How well can interpretability methods control model behavior through interventions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a unifying framework and two evaluation metrics (intervention success rate and coherence-intervention tradeoff) to assess interpretability methods' ability to control model behavior, finding that current methods are inconsistent and often compromise coherence.
papers.conclusion: Current interpretability methods have limitations in achieving control without degrading output quality, and lens-based methods are more effective for simple interventions.
papers.key_findings:
While current interpretability methods allow for intervention, their effectiveness is inconsistent across features and models.
Lens-based methods (Logit Lens and Tuned Lens) outperform SAEs and probes in achieving simple, concrete interventions.
Mechanistic interventions often compromise model coherence, underperforming simpler alternatives like prompting.
Sparse autoencoders have high error rates in feature labeling, leading to lower intervention success.
Probes and steering vectors learn spurious correlations, affecting their intervention performance.
papers.limitation: Interventions often compromise model coherence, leading to repetitive or incoherent outputs.
papers.abstract: With the growing complexity and capability of large language models, a need to understand model reasoning has emerged, often motivated by an underlying goal of controlling and aligning models. While numerous interpretability and steering methods have been proposed as solutions, they are typically designed either for understanding or for control, seldom addressing both. Additionally, the lack of standardized applications, motivations, and evaluation metrics makes it difficult to assess methods' practical utility and efficacy. To address the aforementioned issues, we argue that intervention is a fundamental goal of interpretability and introduce success criteria to evaluate how well methods can control model behavior through interventions. To evaluate existing methods for this ability, we unify and extend four popular interpretability methods-sparse autoencoders, logit lens, tuned lens, and probing-into an abstract encoder-decoder framework, enabling interventions on interpretable features that can be mapped back to latent representations to control model outputs. We introduce two new evaluation metrics: intervention success rate and coherence-intervention tradeoff, designed to measure the accuracy of explanations and their utility in controlling model behavior. Our findings reveal that (1) while current methods allow for intervention, their effectiveness is inconsistent across features and models, (2) lens-based methods outperform SAEs and probes in achieving simple, concrete interventions, and (3) mechanistic interventions often compromise model coherence, underperforming simpler alternatives, such as prompting, and highlighting a critical shortcoming of current interpretability approaches in applications requiring control.

papers.title: Learned feature representations are biased by complexity, learning order, position, and more
papers.research_question: How do extraneous properties like feature complexity, learning order, and distribution affect the learned feature representations in deep neural networks, even when features play equivalent computational roles?
papers.core_contribution: Learned feature representations in deep networks are systematically biased by extraneous properties like feature complexity and learning order, which poses significant challenges for interpretability and comparing representations across systems.
papers.conclusion: The systematic biases in learned feature representations highlight a key challenge for interpretability and for comparing representations between models and brains, as extraneous learning details can be conflated with computationally important aspects.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler features are represented more strongly and densely than complex features, even when both are learned equally well.
Features learned earlier dominate representations, making them path-dependent.
Feature prevalence in the training data and output position also bias representation strength.
These biases are general across architectures (MLPs, ResNets, Transformers) but can interact with hyperparameters like dropout and optimizer.
These representation biases impact downstream analyses like interpretability methods and Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA).
papers.limitation:
Focus on simple, synthetic datasets.
Focus on classification tasks; continuous functions or richer contextual computation (e.g., language modeling) may differ.
Models are of toy scale; biases may differ in larger models.
Main analyses rely on linear regression, which may miss non-linear encodings.
future_direction: Study these biases on more realistic datasets with larger sets of entangled features.
Investigate how biases differ under other objectives (e.g., continuous functions) and in richly contextual computation.
Explore these effects at scale in larger models.
papers.abstract: Representation learning, and interpreting learned representations, are key areas of focus in machine learning and neuroscience. Both fields generally use representations as a means to understand or improve a system's computations. In this work, however, we explore surprising dissociations between representation and computation that may pose challenges for such efforts. We create datasets in which we attempt to match the computational role that different features play, while manipulating other properties of the features or the data. We train various deep learning architectures to compute these multiple abstract features about their inputs. We find that their learned feature representations are systematically biased towards representing some features more strongly than others, depending upon extraneous properties such as feature complexity, the order in which features are learned, and the distribution of features over the inputs. For example, features that are simpler to compute or learned first tend to be represented more strongly and densely than features that are more complex or learned later, even if all features are learned equally well. We also explore how these biases are affected by architectures, optimizers, and training regimes (e.g., in transformers, features decoded earlier in the output sequence also tend to be represented more strongly). Our results help to characterize the inductive biases of gradient-based representation learning. We then illustrate the downstream effects of these biases on various commonly-used methods for analyzing or intervening on representations. These results highlight a key challenge for interpretability $-$ or for comparing the representations of models and brains $-$ disentangling extraneous biases from the computationally important aspects of a system's internal representations.

papers.title: GPT and Prejudice: A Sparse Approach to Understanding Learned Representations in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we trace how different social patterns and biases from pretraining data are encoded in the internal representations of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a pipeline that couples LLMs with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to audit how cultural assumptions and biases from training data are embedded in model representations, demonstrated via a case study on 19th-century novels.
papers.conclusion: The LLM+SAEs pipeline provides a systematic method for exploring cultural and social patterns embedded in corpora, bridging interpretability research and corpus analysis, and is adaptable for applications from literary analysis to fairness auditing.
papers.key_findings:
The model encodes social and moral themes from the corpus, with gender and kinship forming a stable conceptual backbone across layers.
Early layers contain few but relatively pure concept detectors, mid-layers balance clarity and capacity, and deeper layers host more neurons that are increasingly entangled across multiple concepts.
The male category produces the purest, most selective detectors, while female functions as a relational hub, connecting to nearly every other major concept.
The pipeline can be adapted to different domains (e.g., HR, healthcare) by customizing the probing concepts, offering a scalable framework for bias auditing and corpus analysis.
papers.limitation: The results are shaped by the design of the probing dataset and the chosen concepts; other categories might yield different insights.
future_direction: Applying the pipeline to larger, more diverse corpora.
Extending the probing concepts to test different conceptual frames.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are trained on massive, unstructured corpora, making it unclear which social patterns and biases they absorb and later reproduce. Existing evaluations typically examine outputs or activations, but rarely connect them back to the pre-training data. We introduce a pipeline that couples LLMs with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to trace how different themes are encoded during training. As a controlled case study, we trained a GPT-style model on 37 nineteenth-century novels by ten female authors, a corpus centered on themes such as gender, marriage, class, and morality. By applying SAEs across layers and probing with eleven social and moral categories, we mapped sparse features to human-interpretable concepts. The analysis revealed stable thematic backbones (most prominently around gender and kinship) and showed how associations expand and entangle with depth. More broadly, we argue that the LLM+SAEs pipeline offers a scalable framework for auditing how cultural assumptions from the data are embedded in model representations.

papers.title: Which Models have Perceptually-Aligned Gradients? An Explanation via Off-Manifold Robustness
papers.research_question: Why do robust models have perceptually-aligned gradients (PAGs)? The paper provides an explanation via off-manifold robustness.
papers.core_contribution: The paper explains perceptually-aligned gradients (PAGs) via off-manifold robustness, showing that robust models exhibit this property, which causes their gradients to lie on the signal manifold, and identifies three regimes of robustness.
papers.conclusion: Off-manifold robustness explains perceptually-aligned gradients, with bayes-aligned robustness corresponding to the most perceptually aligned gradients, and excessive robustness leading to a drop in accuracy.
papers.key_findings:
Off-manifold robustness leads to on-manifold gradient alignment, explaining PAGs.
Bayes optimal classifiers satisfy off-manifold robustness.
Robust models trained with gradient norm regularization, randomized smoothing, and adversarial training exhibit off-manifold robustness.
Perceptual alignment of gradients (measured by LPIPS similarity with the score of a diffusion model) correlates with off-manifold robustness.
Three regimes of robustness are identified: weak robustness, bayes-aligned robustness, and excessive robustness, which differently affect perceptual alignment and model accuracy.
papers.limitation:
No rigorous theoretical explanation for why off-manifold robustness emerges from robust training.
Only approximate alignment to the Bayes optimal classifier is captured using score-gradients from a diffusion model as a proxy.
future_direction: Formalizing the theoretical argument for off-manifold robustness with simplifying assumptions.
Not exceeding the robustness of the Bayes optimal classifier as a guiding principle.
Exploring more general signal-distractor decompositions beyond masking.
papers.abstract: One of the remarkable properties of robust computer vision models is that their input-gradients are often aligned with human perception, referred to in the literature as perceptually-aligned gradients (PAGs). Despite only being trained for classification, PAGs cause robust models to have rudimentary generative capabilities, including image generation, denoising, and in-painting. However, the underlying mechanisms behind these phenomena remain unknown. In this work, we provide a first explanation of PAGs via \emph{off-manifold robustness}, which states that models must be more robust off- the data manifold than they are on-manifold. We first demonstrate theoretically that off-manifold robustness leads input gradients to lie approximately on the data manifold, explaining their perceptual alignment. We then show that Bayes optimal models satisfy off-manifold robustness, and confirm the same empirically for robust models trained via gradient norm regularization, randomized smoothing, and adversarial training with projected gradient descent. Quantifying the perceptual alignment of model gradients via their similarity with the gradients of generative models, we show that off-manifold robustness correlates well with perceptual alignment. Finally, based on the levels of on- and off-manifold robustness, we identify three different regimes of robustness that affect both perceptual alignment and model accuracy: weak robustness, bayes-aligned robustness, and excessive robustness. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/tml-tuebingen/pags}.

papers.title: Enhancing the Robustness of Spiking Neural Networks with Stochastic Gating Mechanisms
papers.research_question: How can we improve the robustness of spiking neural networks (SNNs) against adversarial attacks and noise perturbations by introducing stochasticity inspired by biological neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a stochastic gating model for SNNs that improves robustness and reduces energy consumption, with theoretical analysis showing it acts as a regularizer and explains the robustness of Poisson coding.
papers.conclusion: The stochastic gating model is an effective method to improve SNN robustness and energy efficiency, providing theoretical insights into the role of stochasticity.
papers.key_findings:
The stochastic gating model (StoG) improves the robustness of SNNs against adversarial attacks.
StoG can be used in conjunction with existing robust enhancement algorithms like adversarial training and weight regularization.
StoG reduces energy consumption during SNN inference by filtering spikes.
Theoretical analysis shows StoG acts as a regularizer and can explain the robustness of Poisson coding.
The model does not cause gradient obfuscation.
papers.limitation:
The method sacrifices a little accuracy in order to enhance robustness.
When opening probabilities are low, almost all signals are filtered out, making it difficult to improve the model's performance.
SNN-specific gradient attacks are not very well studied.
future_direction: Find a method that is more adaptable, allowing for the joint optimization of accuracy, robustness, and performance.
Investigate robustness-enhanced methods evaluated using large EOT steps.
papers.abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) exploit neural spikes to provide solutions for low-power intelligent applications on neuromorphic hardware. Although SNNs have high computational efficiency due to spiking communication, they still lack resistance to adversarial attacks and noise perturbations. In the brain, neuronal responses generally possess stochasticity induced by ion channels and synapses, while the role of stochasticity in computing tasks is poorly understood. Inspired by this, we elaborate a stochastic gating spiking neural model for layer-by-layer spike communication, introducing stochasticity to SNNs. Through theoretical analysis, our gating model can be viewed as a regularizer that prevents error amplification under attacks. Meanwhile, our work can explain the robustness of Poisson coding. Experimental results prove that our method can be used alone or with existing robust enhancement algorithms to improve SNN robustness and reduce SNN energy consumption. We hope our work will shed new light on the role of stochasticity in the computation of SNNs. Our code is available at https://github.com/DingJianhao/StoG-meets-SNN/.

papers.title: Gradient Routing: Masking Gradients to Localize Computation in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: How can gradient routing, a training method that applies data-dependent masks to gradients, be used to localize capabilities to specific subregions of neural networks for interpretability, unlearning, and oversight?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces gradient routing, a training method that uses data-dependent gradient masks to localize capabilities to specific subregions of neural networks, enabling interpretable representations, robust unlearning, and scalable oversight.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that gradient routing is a promising localization technique for real-world applications with scarce quality data, and may address limitations of black-box training in high-stakes machine learning.
papers.key_findings:
Gradient routing can partition learned representations in an interpretable way, as demonstrated by splitting MNIST digit encodings into non-overlapping halves.
Gradient routing enables robust unlearning via ablation of a pre-specified network subregion, outperforming data filtering when labels are limited.
Gradient routing allows scalable oversight in reinforcement learning by localizing modules responsible for different behaviors, even with limited labeled data.
Gradient routing exhibits an absorption effect, where localization applied to narrow data (e.g., specific tokens) generalizes to broader capabilities (e.g., semantic concepts).
Gradient routing can localize concepts to individual dimensions of the residual stream, enabling model steering with a single scalar value.
papers.limitation:
Clean separation of representations in the MNIST autoencoder depends on specific problem setup and heavy L1 regularization.
The learning dynamics of gradient routing, including potential 'internal tug of war' effects, remain an open question.
The reinforcement learning environment used is simple and may not reflect the complexity of real-world problems.
future_direction: Further investigation into the learning dynamics of gradient routing.
Application of gradient routing to more complex environments and larger models.
Empirical and conceptual work needed for scalable oversight in real-world settings.
papers.abstract: Neural networks are trained primarily based on their inputs and outputs, without regard for their internal mechanisms. These neglected mechanisms determine properties that are critical for safety, like (i) transparency; (ii) the absence of sensitive information or harmful capabilities; and (iii) reliable generalization of goals beyond the training distribution. To address this shortcoming, we introduce gradient routing, a training method that isolates capabilities to specific subregions of a neural network. Gradient routing applies data-dependent, weighted masks to gradients during backpropagation. These masks are supplied by the user in order to configure which parameters are updated by which data points. We show that gradient routing can be used to (1) learn representations which are partitioned in an interpretable way; (2) enable robust unlearning via ablation of a pre-specified network subregion; and (3) achieve scalable oversight of a reinforcement learner by localizing modules responsible for different behaviors. Throughout, we find that gradient routing localizes capabilities even when applied to a limited, ad-hoc subset of the data. We conclude that the approach holds promise for challenging, real-world applications where quality data are scarce.

papers.title: Analyzing Finetuning Representation Shift for Multimodal LLMs Steering
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning introduce shifts in learned concepts in Multimodal LLMs, and how can these shifts be analyzed and used for model steering?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a concept-level analysis framework for MLLMs that maps hidden states to interpretable concepts, enabling analysis of fine-tuning-induced concept shifts and training-free steering for debiasing and safety.
papers.conclusion: Proposes a novel, training-free, ready-to-use framework for MLLM behavior interpretability and control.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning can introduce significant alteration in the original concepts, with some concepts refined and others changing completely.
Fine-tuned concepts can be partially recovered from the original model by applying concept shift vectors.
The consistency of individual representation shifts for a concept correlates with the recovery of the fine-tuned concept.
The framework enables steering of MLLM outputs for tasks like changing answer types in VQA, altering caption styles, gender debiasing, and safety alignment.
The features related to different concepts become more linearly separable in deeper layers, supporting the linear representation hypothesis for MLLMs.
papers.abstract: Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) have reached remarkable levels of proficiency in understanding multimodal inputs. However, understanding and interpreting the behavior of such complex models is a challenging task, not to mention the dynamic shifts that may occur during fine-tuning, or due to covariate shift between datasets. In this work, we apply concept-level analysis towards MLLM understanding. More specifically, we propose to map hidden states to interpretable visual and textual concepts. This enables us to more efficiently compare certain semantic dynamics, such as the shift from an original and fine-tuned model, revealing concept alteration and potential biases that may occur during fine-tuning. We also demonstrate the use of shift vectors to capture these concepts changes. These shift vectors allow us to recover fine-tuned concepts by applying simple, computationally inexpensive additive concept shifts in the original model. Finally, our findings also have direct applications for MLLM steering, which can be used for model debiasing as well as enforcing safety in MLLM output. All in all, we propose a novel, training-free, ready-to-use framework for MLLM behavior interpretability and control. Our implementation is publicly available.

papers.title: Biologically inspired protection of deep networks from adversarial attacks
papers.research_question: How can deep neural networks be made robust to adversarial attacks without training on adversarial examples, inspired by biological neurons' nonlinear dendritic computations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a biologically inspired training scheme that pushes neural networks into a saturated, nonlinear regime, achieving state-of-the-art robustness to adversarial attacks on MNIST without using adversarial examples during training.
papers.conclusion: The proposed saturating network training provides a biologically plausible mechanism for adversarial robustness, characterized by flat, low-dimensional internal representations and kurtotic weight distributions.
papers.key_findings:
Saturating networks achieve high robustness to gradient-based and iterative adversarial attacks while maintaining test accuracy.
Saturating networks develop highly kurtotic weight distributions, similar to biological networks.
Internal representations in saturating networks form tight, widely separated clusters for different classes.
The input-output map of saturating networks is highly flat and sensitive to few input directions, making adversarial perturbations difficult.
High kurtosis in weight distributions can protect even linear classifiers from adversarial examples.
papers.abstract: Inspired by biophysical principles underlying nonlinear dendritic computation in neural circuits, we develop a scheme to train deep neural networks to make them robust to adversarial attacks. Our scheme generates highly nonlinear, saturated neural networks that achieve state of the art performance on gradient based adversarial examples on MNIST, despite never being exposed to adversarially chosen examples during training. Moreover, these networks exhibit unprecedented robustness to targeted, iterative schemes for generating adversarial examples, including second-order methods. We further identify principles governing how these networks achieve their robustness, drawing on methods from information geometry. We find these networks progressively create highly flat and compressed internal representations that are sensitive to very few input dimensions, while still solving the task. Moreover, they employ highly kurtotic weight distributions, also found in the brain, and we demonstrate how such kurtosis can protect even linear classifiers from adversarial attack.

papers.title: Rethinking Sparse Autoencoders: Select-and-Project for Fairness and Control from Encoder Features Alone
papers.research_question: Can encoder-centric approaches provide a more efficient and effective foundation for model steering than traditional decoder-based reconstructions?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces S&P Top-K, an encoder-centric selection and projection framework for model steering that outperforms traditional decoder-based SAE methods in fairness and behavioral control tasks.
papers.conclusion: The encoder-centric selection and projection architecture (S&P Top-K) effectively suppresses VLM gender biases and LLM unwanted behaviors, outperforming traditional masked reconstruction.
papers.key_findings:
S&P Top-K improves fairness metrics on CelebA and FairFace by up to 3.2 times over conventional SAE usage.
S&P Top-K reduces aggressiveness and sycophancy in Llama-3 8B Instruct, achieving up to 3.6 times gains over masked reconstruction.
The encoder-centric approach provides a more effective mechanism for shaping model behavior than traditional decoder-centric SAE usage.
papers.limitation:
No mechanism for introducing characteristics into neutral inputs.
Interpolation methodology is constrained to binary attributes.
Does not address the whac-a-mole phenomenon in debiasing.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are widely employed for mechanistic interpretability and model steering. Within this context, steering is by design performed by means of decoding altered SAE intermediate representations. This procedure essentially rewrites the original activations as a weighted sum of decoder features. In contrast to existing literature, we forward an encoder-centric alternative to model steering which demonstrates a stronger cross-modal performance. We introduce S&P Top-K, a retraining-free and computationally lightweight Selection and Projection framework that identifies Top-K encoder features aligned with a sensitive attribute or behavior, optionally aggregates them into a single control axis, and computes an orthogonal projection to be subsequently applied directly in the model's native embedding space. In vision-language models, it improves fairness metrics on CelebA and FairFace by up to 3.2 times over conventional SAE usage, and in large language models, it substantially reduces aggressiveness and sycophancy in Llama-3 8B Instruct, achieving up to 3.6 times gains over masked reconstruction. These findings suggest that encoder-centric interventions provide a general, efficient, and more effective mechanism for shaping model behavior at inference time than the traditional decoder-centric use of SAEs.

papers.title: Knowledge Circuits in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative circuits of components such as attention heads and MLPs, and how can these circuits be used to analyze model behaviors and knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces knowledge circuits as a method to uncover how transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative components, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing knowledge editing and model behaviors like hallucinations and in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge circuits provide a valuable framework for understanding how transformers store and express knowledge, and can inform the design of better knowledge editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge circuits effectively capture knowledge representations, maintaining over 70% of original performance with less than 10% of the graph.
Knowledge is aggregated in early-to-middle layers and enhanced in later layers.
Special components like mover heads and relation heads are critical for information transfer and relational capture.
ROME editing incorporates information at the edited layer, while fine-tuning directly writes knowledge and dominates predictions.
Hallucinations occur when the circuit lacks effective mover heads or they select incorrect information.
papers.limitation:
Coarse granularity of circuits, not capturing fine-grained neuron-level behavior.
Logit lens method may have discrepancies between middle layers and output unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Finer-grained circuit analysis at the neuron level.
Developing more robust techniques to map intermediate representations to outputs (e.g., Attention Lens).
Investigating activation mechanisms of reused heads and polysemanticity.
papers.abstract: The remarkable capabilities of modern large language models are rooted in their vast repositories of knowledge encoded within their parameters, enabling them to perceive the world and engage in reasoning. The inner workings of how these models store knowledge have long been a subject of intense interest and investigation among researchers. To date, most studies have concentrated on isolated components within these models, such as the Multilayer Perceptrons and attention head. In this paper, we delve into the computation graph of the language model to uncover the knowledge circuits that are instrumental in articulating specific knowledge. The experiments, conducted with GPT2 and TinyLLAMA, have allowed us to observe how certain information heads, relation heads, and Multilayer Perceptrons collaboratively encode knowledge within the model. Moreover, we evaluate the impact of current knowledge editing techniques on these knowledge circuits, providing deeper insights into the functioning and constraints of these editing methodologies. Finally, we utilize knowledge circuits to analyze and interpret language model behaviors such as hallucinations and in-context learning. We believe the knowledge circuits hold potential for advancing our understanding of Transformers and guiding the improved design of knowledge editing. Code and data are available in https://github.com/zjunlp/KnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Feature learning is decoupled from generalization in high capacity neural networks
papers.research_question: Do current theories of feature learning measure the quality of learned features (which impacts generalization) or just the strength of representation changes?
papers.core_contribution: Current feature learning theories measure the strength of representation changes (FL strength) but not the quality of features, and these are decoupled. The paper introduces the FL gap to measure feature quality and shows that FL strength does not predict generalization.
papers.conclusion: Current theories of feature learning do not predict generalization because they measure strength rather than quality, indicating the need for a more comprehensive FL theory.
papers.key_findings:
The feature learning gap (∆NT) quantifies the performance improvement of neural networks over kernel methods.
Current FL definitions (NTK-based, CK-based, superposition-based) measure FL strength, not feature quality.
FL strength metrics (e.g., SNT, SCK) fail to distinguish between networks trained on true vs. shuffled labels, indicating decoupling from generalization.
The NTK-based FL strength can be manipulated by output scaling without affecting generalization.
CK-based cumulative utility does not differentiate between shuffled and non-shuffled data.
future_direction: Developing a more comprehensive feature learning theory that links feature learning to generalization.
papers.abstract: Neural networks outperform kernel methods, sometimes by orders of magnitude, e.g. on staircase functions. This advantage stems from the ability of neural networks to learn features, adapting their hidden representations to better capture the data. We introduce a concept we call feature quality to measure this performance improvement. We examine existing theories of feature learning and demonstrate empirically that they primarily assess the strength of feature learning, rather than the quality of the learned features themselves. Consequently, current theories of feature learning do not provide a sufficient foundation for developing theories of neural network generalization.

papers.title: Demonstrating and Reducing Shortcuts in Vision-Language Representation Learning
papers.research_question: In the context of VL representation learning with multiple captions per image, to what extent does the presence of a shortcut hinder learning task-optimal representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a framework to study shortcut learning in contrastive vision-language representation learning and shows that contrastive losses are not sufficient for learning task-optimal representations; also demonstrates that two existing methods partially reduce shortcut learning.
papers.conclusion: Contrastive losses mainly rely on minimal, easy-to-detect features shared among image-caption pairs while suppressing remaining task-relevant information, highlighting the need for more robust methods to mitigate shortcut learning in vision-language representation learning.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive vision-language models mainly learn shortcut features when shortcuts are present, rather than task-optimal representations.
Contrastive losses are not sufficient to learn task-optimal representations, as they mainly capture easy-to-detect shared features and suppress other task-relevant information.
Latent target decoding (LTD) and implicit feature modification (IFM) improve performance on the evaluation task but only partially reduce shortcut learning.
The proposed synthetic shortcuts framework poses challenges that existing shortcut reduction techniques can only partially address.
Both models trained from scratch (VSE++) and fine-tuned (CLIP) rely heavily on shortcut features when shortcuts are present.
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) mainly rely on contrastive training to learn general-purpose representations of images and captions. We focus on the situation when one image is associated with several captions, each caption containing both information shared among all captions and unique information per caption about the scene depicted in the image. In such cases, it is unclear whether contrastive losses are sufficient for learning task-optimal representations that contain all the information provided by the captions or whether the contrastive learning setup encourages the learning of a simple shortcut that minimizes contrastive loss. We introduce synthetic shortcuts for vision-language: a training and evaluation framework where we inject synthetic shortcuts into image-text data. We show that contrastive VLMs trained from scratch or fine-tuned with data containing these synthetic shortcuts mainly learn features that represent the shortcut. Hence, contrastive losses are not sufficient to learn task-optimal representations, i.e., representations that contain all task-relevant information shared between the image and associated captions. We examine two methods to reduce shortcut learning in our training and evaluation framework: (i) latent target decoding and (ii) implicit feature modification. We show empirically that both methods improve performance on the evaluation task, but only partly reduce shortcut learning when training and evaluating with our shortcut learning framework. Hence, we show the difficulty and challenge of our shortcut learning framework for contrastive vision-language representation learning.

papers.title: SAE-SSV: Supervised Steering in Sparse Representation Spaces for Reliable Control of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we reliably control large language model behavior in open-ended generation settings by using supervised steering in sparse, interpretable representation spaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a supervised steering framework (SAE-SSV) that constrains interventions to a sparse, task-relevant latent subspace identified via labeled data and sparse autoencoders, enabling more targeted control and better preservation of generation quality.
papers.conclusion: SAE-SSV enables effective LLM steering by operating in sparse, task-specific subspaces, outperforming existing methods and providing a more targeted and interpretable approach to behavior control.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-SSV consistently outperforms baseline steering methods (CAA, RePe, Top PC, ITI) in steering success rate across sentiment, truthfulness, and political polarity tasks.
A notably small subspace of SAE latent dimensions is sufficient for effective steering, enabling targeted and interpretable interventions.
Steering in the structured SAE subspace preserves or improves generation quality (lexical diversity, entropy) compared to baselines, which often degrade it.
The method generalizes to unseen datasets within the same task domain, capturing both semantic directions and stylistic patterns.
The top SAE features used for steering are interpretable and correspond to semantically meaningful concepts related to the target attribute.
papers.limitation:
Requires access to pretrained sparse autoencoders (SAEs), which may not be available for all models or domains.
Only evaluated on LLMs with up to 9B parameters; scaling to larger models is future work.
Evaluation focused on open-ended generation tasks with limited human evaluation; generalizability to more specialized domains remains to be explored.
future_direction: Achieve universal and style-invariant SSVs that generalize across datasets, tasks, and model families by curating diverse training corpora and developing objectives that encourage semantic steering while minimizing stylistic sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in natural language understanding and generation, but controlling their behavior reliably remains challenging, especially in open-ended generation settings. This paper introduces a novel supervised steering approach that operates in sparse, interpretable representation spaces. We employ sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to obtain sparse latent representations that aim to disentangle semantic attributes from model activations. Then we train linear classifiers to identify a small subspace of task-relevant dimensions in latent representations. Finally, we learn supervised steering vectors constrained to this subspace, optimized to align with target behaviors. Experiments across sentiment, truthfulness, and political polarity steering tasks with multiple LLMs demonstrate that our supervised steering vectors achieve higher success rates with minimal degradation in generation quality compared to existing methods. Further analysis reveals that a notably small subspace is sufficient for effective steering, enabling more targeted and interpretable interventions. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/Ineedanamehere/SAE-SSV.

papers.title: How Can We Be So Dense? The Benefits of Using Highly Sparse Representations
papers.research_question: How can high-dimensional sparse representations in neural networks provide benefits such as robustness to noise and interference, and how can efficient sparse networks be constructed to exploit these properties?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that high-dimensional sparse representations are inherently more robust to noise and interference, and introduces an efficient sparse network construction (with sparse weights and k-winner activations) that achieves competitive accuracy while significantly improving robustness.
papers.conclusion: Sparse representations offer significant benefits in robustness and computational efficiency, and moving beyond pure test accuracy is important for evaluating model performance under realistic, noisy conditions.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse networks with sparse weights and activations show significantly improved robustness to noisy inputs compared to dense networks, while maintaining competitive accuracy on standard benchmarks.
The robustness of sparse representations increases with the dimensionality of the representation space, as the probability of false matches with random vectors decreases exponentially.
The computational complexity of sparse networks is lower due to fewer non-zero products, though current deep learning frameworks lack efficient sparse matrix support to realize these gains.
Introducing sparsity at any level (e.g., sparse weights, sparse activations, or both) can improve noise robustness compared to fully dense networks.
Test set accuracy alone is not a reliable indicator of a network's robustness to adverse conditions like noise.
papers.limitation:
Current deep learning frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow) lack adequate support for sparse matrices, so the computational efficiency benefits of sparse networks are not realized in practice.
The theoretical benefits of sparse representations assume a near-uniform distribution of input vectors; non-uniform distributions can lead to higher error rates.
future_direction: Extending the sparse network techniques to other architectures such as RNNs.
Exploring the introduction of sparsity into convolutional filter weights themselves.
Combining the proposed sparse construction methods with existing pruning techniques.
papers.abstract: Most artificial networks today rely on dense representations, whereas biological networks rely on sparse representations. In this paper we show how sparse representations can be more robust to noise and interference, as long as the underlying dimensionality is sufficiently high. A key intuition that we develop is that the ratio of the operable volume around a sparse vector divided by the volume of the representational space decreases exponentially with dimensionality. We then analyze computationally efficient sparse networks containing both sparse weights and activations. Simulations on MNIST and the Google Speech Command Dataset show that such networks demonstrate significantly improved robustness and stability compared to dense networks, while maintaining competitive accuracy. We discuss the potential benefits of sparsity on accuracy, noise robustness, hyperparameter tuning, learning speed, computational efficiency, and power requirements.

papers.title: Low-dimensional intrinsic dimension reveals a phase transition in gradient-based learning of deep neural networks
papers.research_question: How does the intrinsic dimension of hidden representations in deep neural networks evolve during training, and how is it affected by training hyperparameters such as learning rate and batch size?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that the intrinsic dimension of hidden representations in deep neural networks can either increase or decrease during training, exhibiting a phase transition from expansion to compression depending on the ratio of learning rate to batch size. This variation is consistent with hypothesis complexity and is due to changing neuronal correlation.
papers.conclusion: Deep neural networks exhibit distinct learning curves under different training regimes, with the intrinsic dimension revealing a phase transition from expansion to compression. This helps understand how DNNs learn robust representations by adaptively eliminating or retaining redundancies.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimension of hidden representations can increase (expansion) or decrease (compression) during training, determined by the learning rate and batch size.
The variation in intrinsic dimension is consistent with hypothesis complexity, which can be measured by the critical sample ratio.
The proposed FASS method for estimating critical sample ratio outperforms the existing LASS method.
The variation in intrinsic dimension is due to the changing correlation between neurons, with expansion corresponding to decreasing correlation and compression to increasing correlation.
The power-law exponent of representations predicts adversarial robustness only at the end of training, not during training.
papers.limitation:
It remains theoretically unclear how the learning rate and batch size jointly determine the Fisher information matrix F.
The approach of studying gradient-based algorithms from the perspective of stochastic differential equation may fail when the squared gradient norm is larger than its variance at equilibrium.
future_direction: Theoretical understanding of how learning rate and batch size jointly determine the Fisher information matrix F.
Further investigation into the different regimes (noise dominated and curvature dominated) in the hyperparameter space.
papers.abstract: Abstract Deep neural networks complete a feature extraction task by propagating the inputs through multiple modules. However, how the representations evolve with the gradient-based optimization remains unknown. Here we leveraged the intrinsic dimension of the representations to study the learning dynamics and found that the training process underwent a phase transition from expansion to compression under disparate training regimes---a phenomenon that is ubiquitous across a wide variety of model architectures, optimizers, and data sets. We showed that the variation in the intrinsic dimension is consistent with the complexity of the learned hypothesis, which can be quantitatively assessed by the critical sample ratio that was rooted in adversarial robustness. Meanwhile, we mathematically demonstrated that this phenomenon can be analyzed in terms of the mutable correlation between neurons. Although the evoked activities obey a power-law decaying rule in biological circuits, we identified that the power-law exponent of the representations in deep neural networks predicted adversarial robustness well only at the end of the training but not during the training process. These results together suggest that deep neural networks are prone to producing robust representations by adaptively eliminating or retaining redundancies. The code is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/cltan023/learning2022}.

papers.title: From Low-Rank Features to Encoding Mismatch: Rethinking Feature Distillation in Vision Transformers
papers.research_question: Why does feature-map knowledge distillation (KD), which works so well for CNNs, usually fail for Vision Transformers (ViTs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies an encoding mismatch between wide teachers and narrow students in Vision Transformers as the reason for the failure of feature-map knowledge distillation, and proposes two minimal strategies (post-hoc feature lifting and native width alignment) to resolve this mismatch, reactivating simple feature distillation.
papers.conclusion: The encoding mismatch is the key reason for the failure of feature distillation in ViTs, and the proposed strategies effectively resolve this mismatch, providing a simple and interpretable design cue for compact ViT architectures.
papers.key_findings:
ViT representations are globally low-rank, with a small number of singular components capturing most of the feature energy.
Despite global low-rank structure, individual tokens use a high fraction of channel capacity, leading to an encoding mismatch between wide teachers and narrow students.
This encoding mismatch explains why naive feature-map distillation fails in ViTs.
Two proposed strategies (post-hoc feature lifting and native width alignment) reactivate feature distillation, improving DeiT-Tiny accuracy by up to 3.37% when distilling from CaiT-S24.
The architectural modifications also improve standalone student performance without distillation, indicating a genuine bottleneck in compact ViTs.
papers.abstract: Feature-map knowledge distillation (KD) is highly effective for convolutional networks but often fails for Vision Transformers (ViTs). To understand this failure and guide method design, we conduct a two-view representation analysis of ViTs. First, a layer-wise Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of full feature matrices shows that final-layer representations are globally low-rank: for CaiT-S24, only $121/61/34/14$ dimensions suffice to capture $99\%/95\%/90\%/80\%$ of the energy. In principle, this suggests that a compact student plus a simple linear projector should be enough for feature alignment, contradicting the weak empirical performance of standard feature KD. To resolve this paradox, we introduce a token-level Spectral Energy Pattern (SEP) analysis that measures how each token uses channel capacity. SEP reveals that, despite the global low-rank structure, individual tokens distribute energy over most channels, forming a high-bandwidth encoding pattern. This results in an encoding mismatch between wide teachers and narrow students. Motivated by this insight, we propose two minimal, mismatch-driven strategies: (1) post-hoc feature lifting with a lightweight projector retained during inference, or (2) native width alignment that widens only the student's last block to the teacher's width. On ImageNet-1K, these strategies reactivate simple feature-map distillation in ViTs, raising DeiT-Tiny accuracy from $74.86\%$ to $77.53\%$ and $78.23\%$ when distilling from CaiT-S24, while also improving standalone students trained without any teacher. Our analysis thus explains why ViT feature distillation fails and shows how exploiting low-rank structure yields effective, interpretable remedies and concrete design guidance for compact ViTs.

papers.title: VAST: The Valence-Assessing Semantics Test for Contextualizing Language\n Models
papers.research_question: How can we measure the semantic quality of contextualized word embeddings and understand the effects of contextualization, tokenization, and model-specific geometry on word-level semantics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces V AST, an intrinsic evaluation task for contextualized word embeddings that uses valence to measure word-level semantics and reveals how contextualization, tokenization, and high-magnitude neurons affect semantic representations.
papers.conclusion: V AST is a novel intrinsic evaluation task that allows researchers to measure and isolate word-level semantics in CWEs, revealing how context changes CWE semantics, how tokenization leads to a different encoding process for uncommon words, and how high-magnitude neurons mask word-level semantics and social biases.
papers.key_findings:
V AST shows that context alters CWE semantics in the top layers of GPT-2, with scores diverging between contextual settings after layer 8.
Multiply tokenized words are not semantically encoded until layer 8 in GPT-2, indicating a different encoding process for singly vs. multiply tokenized words.
High-magnitude neurons in the top layer mask word-level semantics, and nullifying non-semantic principal components recovers semantics (Pearson's ρ improves from .32 to .76 in the top layer).
After isolating semantics, V AST improves over prior work on word similarity tasks (e.g., .50 on SimLex-999 vs. previous best .45 for GPT-2).
Isolating semantics reveals more stereotype-congruent biases in 8 of 10 WEA T tests, indicating that non-semantic structures also mask social biases.
papers.limitation:
Sentence structure may affect CWEs in ways that distort semantic analysis beyond what V AST detects.
The effect size for some biases, especially for names, varies with the number of PCs nullified.
V AST does not deal with the senses of polysemous words.
V AST's tokenization experiment does not control for word frequency.
future_direction: Address the effect of sentence structure on CWEs.
Study the variation in bias effect sizes with the number of PCs nullified.
Extend V AST to handle polysemous words.
papers.abstract:
VAST, the Valence-Assessing Semantics Test, is a novel intrinsic evaluation
task for contextualized word embeddings (CWEs). VAST uses valence, the
association of a word with pleasantness, to measure the correspondence of
word-level LM semantics with widely used human judgments, and examines the
effects of contextualization, tokenization, and LM-specific geometry. Because
prior research has found that CWEs from GPT-2 perform poorly on other intrinsic
evaluations, we select GPT-2 as our primary subject, and include results
showing that VAST is useful for 7 other LMs, and can be used in 7 languages.
GPT-2 results show that the semantics of a word incorporate the semantics of
context in layers closer to model output, such that VAST scores diverge between
our contextual settings, ranging from Pearson's rho of .55 to .77 in layer 11.
We also show that multiply tokenized words are not semantically encoded until
layer 8, where they achieve Pearson's rho of .46, indicating the presence of an
encoding process for multiply tokenized words which differs from that of singly
tokenized words, for which rho is highest in layer 0. We find that a few
neurons with values having greater magnitude than the rest mask word-level
semantics in GPT-2's top layer, but that word-level semantics can be recovered
by nullifying non-semantic principal components: Pearson's rho in the top layer
improves from .32 to .76. After isolating semantics, we show the utility of
VAST for understanding LM semantics via improvements over related work on four
word similarity tasks, with a score of .50 on SimLex-999, better than the
previous best of .45 for GPT-2. Finally, we show that 8 of 10 WEAT bias tests,
which compare differences in word embedding associations between groups of
words, exhibit more stereotype-congruent biases after isolating semantics,
indicating that non-semantic structures in LMs also mask biases.

papers.title: Dictionary Learning Improves Patch-Free Circuit Discovery in Mechanistic Interpretability: A Case Study on Othello-GPT
papers.research_question: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features extracted via sparse dictionary learning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a patch-free circuit discovery framework that uses dictionary learning to decompose model activations into monosemantic features and then traces contributions between these features to identify interpretable circuits, avoiding out-of-distribution issues and improving asymptotic complexity compared to patching-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dictionary learning enables patch-free circuit discovery, providing a macroscopic view of the model's internal information flow and turning microscopic understanding into a more comprehensive one.
papers.key_findings:
The framework successfully identifies interpretable dictionary features in Othello-GPT, such as current move position, board state, empty cells, and legal move features.
It discovers a local OV circuit that computes board state by combining information from previous moves via specific attention heads.
The QK circuit's attention patterns (e.g., attending to opponent's moves) are implemented through resonance between low-level dictionary feature pairs representing move colors.
Early MLP layers identify flipped pieces by performing an 'and' operation on features representing consecutive moves on a line, with attention heads introducing color information.
papers.limitation:
The dictionary training may have used too small sparsity coefficients, leading to near-perfect reconstruction and about 75% dead neurons in each dictionary.
The QK decomposition only interprets individual attention scores and fails to account for the relative strength introduced by the Softmax normalization across the sequence.
Approximate Direct Contribution (ADC) for MLPs is an approximation that treats part of the activation function input as constant.
Circuit analysis is based on specific inputs and does not claim universal understanding of the model; discovering general motifs is left for future work.
future_direction: Discovering general motifs in Transformers is a central problem left for future work.
Alleviating the dictionary training problem of dead neurons to achieve deeper understanding.
Extending the method to language models, which have sparser features and a more complex world compared to the Othello task.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning has been a rapidly growing technique in mechanistic interpretability to attack superposition and extract more human-understandable features from model activations. We ask a further question based on the extracted more monosemantic features: How do we recognize circuits connecting the enormous amount of dictionary features? We propose a circuit discovery framework alternative to activation patching. Our framework suffers less from out-of-distribution and proves to be more efficient in terms of asymptotic complexity. The basic unit in our framework is dictionary features decomposed from all modules writing to the residual stream, including embedding, attention output and MLP output. Starting from any logit, dictionary feature or attention score, we manage to trace down to lower-level dictionary features of all tokens and compute their contribution to these more interpretable and local model behaviors. We dig in a small transformer trained on a synthetic task named Othello and find a number of human-understandable fine-grained circuits inside of it.

papers.title: Transferring Linear Features Across Language Models With Model Stitching
papers.research_question: Can linear features (e.g., from Sparse Autoencoders, probes, and steering vectors) be transferred between language models of different sizes using affine mappings (model stitching), and what are the implications for efficiency and feature universality?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that affine mappings (stitches) between residual streams can effectively transfer linear features across language models, enabling compute-efficient training of Sparse Autoencoders and transfer of probes and steering vectors, while revealing differences in how semantic and structural features transfer.
papers.conclusion: Linear features can be transferred between language models via affine mappings, supporting weak universality and providing a method to improve the training efficiency of interpretability tools like Sparse Autoencoders.
papers.key_findings:
Using transferred SAEs as initialization can reduce FLOPs by ~50% when training SAEs on larger models.
Probes and steering vectors can be transferred between models with no additional training in specific cases (e.g., language steering).
Structural features (syntactic) transfer more consistently than semantic features, which are more polarized in transferability.
Specific functional features (e.g., entropy and attention deactivation features) preserve their roles after transfer.
Linear stitches support a weak universality hypothesis, showing that small and large models learn similar representation spaces.
papers.limitation:
Stitches are only trained on general internet text between models in the same family with the same tokenizer.
The scaling law analysis is theoretically incomplete due to lack of high-compute regime data to fit the irreducible loss.
The semantic/structural classification is imperfect and noisy due to reliance on another LLM for augmentations.
Probing and steering experiments are limited to particular tasks and settings.
future_direction: Verify findings in cross-family model settings and finetune stitches on special tokens or chat-templated data.
Explore other applications of stitches, such as transferring linear weight updates like LoRAs.
Expand probing and steering experiments to examine robustness and broader task settings.
papers.abstract: In this work, we demonstrate that affine mappings between residual streams of language models is a cheap way to effectively transfer represented features between models. We apply this technique to transfer the weights of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) between models of different sizes to compare their representations. We find that small and large models learn similar representation spaces, which motivates training expensive components like SAEs on a smaller model and transferring to a larger model at a FLOPs savings. In particular, using a small-to-large transferred SAE as initialization can lead to 50% cheaper training runs when training SAEs on larger models. Next, we show that transferred probes and steering vectors can effectively recover ground truth performance. Finally, we dive deeper into feature-level transferability, finding that semantic and structural features transfer noticeably differently while specific classes of functional features have their roles faithfully mapped. Overall, our findings illustrate similarities and differences in the linear representation spaces of small and large models and demonstrate a method for improving the training efficiency of SAEs.

papers.title: Improved Feature Distillation via Projector Ensemble
papers.research_question: What is the effect of the feature projector in knowledge distillation, and can an ensemble of projectors improve feature distillation performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the role of the projector in feature distillation, hypothesizing it prevents overfitting to teacher features, and proposes a simple yet effective method using an ensemble of projectors to improve student network performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates the positive effect of a projector in feature distillation and shows that an ensemble of projectors can further improve student network performance on image classification tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Adding a projector improves distillation performance even when student and teacher feature dimensions are identical, by disentangling the tasks of feature extraction for classification and feature matching for distillation.
Training a student without a projector leads to overfitting to the teacher's feature distribution, resulting in less discriminative features for classification.
An ensemble of projectors further improves student performance by providing diverse transformed features and improving generalization.
The proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art feature distillation methods on CIFAR-100 and ImageNet across various teacher-student pairs.
Simply increasing the depth or width of a single projector does not improve performance and can degrade it, whereas a horizontal ensemble of shallow projectors is effective.
papers.limitation: The proposed method is only evaluated on image classification tasks; its application to other downstream tasks (e.g., object detection and semantic segmentation) remains for future work.
future_direction: Applying the proposed method to other downstream tasks such as object detection and semantic segmentation.
Exploring how to effectively and efficiently integrate logits and similarity information into the proposed projector ensemble framework.
papers.abstract: In knowledge distillation, previous feature distillation methods mainly focus on the design of loss functions and the selection of the distilled layers, while the effect of the feature projector between the student and the teacher remains under-explored. In this paper, we first discuss a plausible mechanism of the projector with empirical evidence and then propose a new feature distillation method based on a projector ensemble for further performance improvement. We observe that the student network benefits from a projector even if the feature dimensions of the student and the teacher are the same. Training a student backbone without a projector can be considered as a multi-task learning process, namely achieving discriminative feature extraction for classification and feature matching between the student and the teacher for distillation at the same time. We hypothesize and empirically verify that without a projector, the student network tends to overfit the teacher's feature distributions despite having different architecture and weights initialization. This leads to degradation on the quality of the student's deep features that are eventually used in classification. Adding a projector, on the other hand, disentangles the two learning tasks and helps the student network to focus better on the main feature extraction task while still being able to utilize teacher features as a guidance through the projector. Motivated by the positive effect of the projector in feature distillation, we propose an ensemble of projectors to further improve the quality of student features. Experimental results on different datasets with a series of teacher-student pairs illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers.title: Reactive Model Correction: Mitigating Harm to Task-Relevant Features via Conditional Bias Suppression
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate the unintended overcorrection of model behavior (collateral damage to task-relevant features) when suppressing spurious correlations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a reactive model correction framework that conditionally suppresses artifacts based on model-derived knowledge and XAI insights, minimizing collateral damage to clean samples while reducing reliance on spurious features.
papers.conclusion: Reactive model correction minimizes collateral damage to task-relevant features and demonstrates superior performance over traditional non-reactive post-hoc correction methods.
papers.key_findings:
Artifact concept representations (CAVs) are entangled with non-artifact concepts in the latent space, leading to unintended suppression of valid features when applying global corrections.
Reactive model correction (R-ClArC) preserves model performance on clean samples significantly better than the non-reactive baseline (P-ClArC) while still effectively reducing artifact relevance.
The reactive approach allows for more targeted suppression, such as correcting only for specific predicted classes or when an artifact is detected, reducing harmful overcorrection.
papers.limitation:
The choice of reactive heuristics is not always straightforward, and condition-generating functions may not always be accurate, resulting in the correction not being activated when required.
The method does not fully address all flaws of the underlying correction method (e.g., P-ClArC), such as the entanglement of artifact directions with valid concepts, which can still lead to altered representations even when applied reactively.
future_direction: Application of the reactive principle to other post-hoc correction methods, such as classifier editing, LEACE, and INLP.
Exploration of more granular reactive conditions, such as those based on prediction strategy or artifact relevance.
papers.abstract: Deep Neural Networks are prone to learning and relying on spurious correlations in the training data, which, for high-risk applications, can have fatal consequences. Various approaches to suppress model reliance on harmful features have been proposed that can be applied post-hoc without additional training. Whereas those methods can be applied with efficiency, they also tend to harm model performance by globally shifting the distribution of latent features. To mitigate unintended overcorrection of model behavior, we propose a reactive approach conditioned on model-derived knowledge and eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) insights. While the reactive approach can be applied to many post-hoc methods, we demonstrate the incorporation of reactivity in particular for P-ClArC (Projective Class Artifact Compensation), introducing a new method called R-ClArC (Reactive Class Artifact Compensation). Through rigorous experiments in controlled settings (FunnyBirds) and with a real-world dataset (ISIC2019), we show that introducing reactivity can minimize the detrimental effect of the applied correction while simultaneously ensuring low reliance on spurious features.

papers.title: On the Encoding of Gender in Transformer-based ASR Representations
papers.research_question: How much gender-related information can we linearly erase from an ASR model and what are the implications of linear erasure?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that gender information can be linearly erased from transformer-based ASR models with minimal impact on performance, and reveals that gender is concentrated in the first and last frames in the final layers.
papers.conclusion: This work sheds light on how ASR models encode gender and paves the way to creating usable but speaker-blind embeddings.
papers.key_findings:
Gender can be linearly erased from all layers of Wav2Vec2 and HuBERT without model training.
Linear erasure has minimal impact on ASR performance, as shown by small changes in Word Error Rate (WER).
Gender information is concentrated in the first and last frames in the final layers of the models.
Fine-tuning affects gender encoding, localizing it to specific frames in the later layers.
The ease of gender removal in later layers is due to its localization in shared subspaces within the first and last frame positions.
papers.limitation: lack of non-binary gender labels in the datasets used
papers.abstract: While existing literature relies on performance differences to uncover gender biases in ASR models, a deeper analysis is essential to understand how gender is encoded and utilized during transcript generation. This work investigates the encoding and utilization of gender in the latent representations of two transformer-based ASR models, Wav2Vec2 and HuBERT. Using linear erasure, we demonstrate the feasibility of removing gender information from each layer of an ASR model and show that such an intervention has minimal impacts on the ASR performance. Additionally, our analysis reveals a concentration of gender information within the first and last frames in the final layers, explaining the ease of erasing gender in these layers. Our findings suggest the prospect of creating gender-neutral embeddings that can be integrated into ASR frameworks without compromising their efficacy.

papers.title: Matching the Neuronal Representations of V1 is Necessary to Improve Robustness in CNNs with V1-like Front-ends
papers.research_question: Does precisely matching the distribution of receptive field (RF) properties found in primate V1 (neuronal representations) improve robustness to image corruptions in CNNs with V1-like front-ends, compared to uniform sampling?
papers.core_contribution: Precisely matching the neuronal representations (RF property distributions) of primate V1 in a CNN front-end is necessary to achieve improved robustness to common image corruptions, compared to a front-end with uniformly sampled RF properties.
papers.conclusion: Precisely mimicking the neuronal representations found in primate V1 is necessary to improve robustness in CNNs with V1-like front-ends, suggesting these biological representations are optimized for processing a wide variety of image distributions.
papers.key_findings:
The VOneResNet18 model with biological sampling of GFB parameters shows higher robustness to image corruptions (average relative improvement of 7.85%) compared to the standard ResNet18, and a relative improvement of 8.72% compared to the uniform sampling variant.
Neuronal sub-populations with similar RF properties across the biological and uniform model variants exhibit similar response properties (mean activation, sparseness) and learn similar downstream weights.
The neuronal sub-populations that have the greatest impact on downstream layers differ between the biological and uniform variants, shifting from neurons with high spatial frequency and small RF size (uniform) to neurons with larger RF size and somewhat smaller spatial frequency (biological).
The improvement in robustness from biological sampling is not due to a simple low-pass filtering effect, as both variants contain similar numbers of high spatial frequency neurons and the biological model performs marginally better on clean images.
The non-uniform sampling of the biological distribution is critical for shifting the impactful neuronal sub-populations, explaining the observed difference in model robustness.
papers.abstract: While some convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have achieved great success in object recognition, they struggle to identify objects in images corrupted with different types of common noise patterns. Recently, it was shown that simulating computations in early visual areas at the front of CNNs leads to improvements in robustness to image corruptions. Here, we further explore this result and show that the neuronal representations that emerge from precisely matching the distribution of RF properties found in primate V1 is key for this improvement in robustness. We built two variants of a model with a front-end modeling the primate primary visual cortex (V1): one sampling RF properties uniformly and the other sampling from empirical biological distributions. The model with the biological sampling has a considerably higher robustness to image corruptions that the uniform variant (relative difference of 8.72%). While similar neuronal sub-populations across the two variants have similar response properties and learn similar downstream weights, the impact on downstream processing is strikingly different. This result sheds light on the origin of the improvements in robustness observed in some biologically-inspired models, pointing to the need of precisely mimicking the neuronal representations found in the primate brain.

papers.title: Disentangling the Causes of Plasticity Loss in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: To what extent do known mechanisms of plasticity loss overlap, and how can mitigation strategies be combined to best maintain the trainability of a network?
papers.core_contribution: Plasticity loss can be decomposed into multiple independent mechanisms, and a combination of layer normalization and weight decay is highly effective at maintaining plasticity in nonstationary learning tasks.
papers.conclusion: By addressing multiple independent mechanisms of plasticity loss, we can develop robust learning algorithms for nonstationary problems.
papers.key_findings:
Plasticity loss is driven by multiple independent mechanisms, including preactivation distribution shift, regression target magnitude, and parameter norm growth.
Intervening on any single mechanism is insufficient to avoid plasticity loss in all cases.
A combination of layer normalization and weight decay is highly effective at maintaining plasticity in synthetic nonstationary tasks and naturally arising nonstationarities like reinforcement learning.
The proposed mitigation strategy reduces the combinatorial complexity of searching over mitigation strategies.
papers.abstract: Underpinning the past decades of work on the design, initialization, and optimization of neural networks is a seemingly innocuous assumption: that the network is trained on a \textit{stationary} data distribution. In settings where this assumption is violated, e.g.\ deep reinforcement learning, learning algorithms become unstable and brittle with respect to hyperparameters and even random seeds. One factor driving this instability is the loss of plasticity, meaning that updating the network's predictions in response to new information becomes more difficult as training progresses. While many recent works provide analyses and partial solutions to this phenomenon, a fundamental question remains unanswered: to what extent do known mechanisms of plasticity loss overlap, and how can mitigation strategies be combined to best maintain the trainability of a network? This paper addresses these questions, showing that loss of plasticity can be decomposed into multiple independent mechanisms and that, while intervening on any single mechanism is insufficient to avoid the loss of plasticity in all cases, intervening on multiple mechanisms in conjunction results in highly robust learning algorithms. We show that a combination of layer normalization and weight decay is highly effective at maintaining plasticity in a variety of synthetic nonstationary learning tasks, and further demonstrate its effectiveness on naturally arising nonstationarities, including reinforcement learning in the Arcade Learning Environment.

papers.title: Grad-CAM: Visual Explanations from Deep Networks via Gradient-Based Localization
papers.research_question: How can we produce visual explanations for decisions from a large class of CNN-based models to make them more transparent and explainable?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Grad-CAM, a technique that uses gradients flowing into the final convolutional layer to produce coarse localization maps highlighting important image regions for a prediction, applicable to a wide variety of CNN model families without architectural changes or re-training.
papers.conclusion: Grad-CAM is an effective visualization technique for understanding CNN decisions, providing insights into model behavior, failure modes, and biases, and has been successfully applied to image classification, captioning, and VQA tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Grad-CAM produces class-discriminative localization maps that generalize the earlier CAM approach to a broader range of CNN architectures.
Grad-CAM visualizations help diagnose model failure modes, showing that seemingly unreasonable predictions have reasonable explanations.
Grad-CAM is robust to adversarial perturbations and can identify dataset biases, aiding in model generalization and fairness.
Human studies show that Grad-CAM explanations help users establish appropriate trust in predictions and discern a stronger network from a weaker one.
Grad-CAM can be combined with fine-grained visualizations (Guided Backpropagation) to create Guided Grad-CAM, which is both high-resolution and class-discriminative.
papers.limitation:
Grad-CAM produces coarse, low-resolution heatmaps (e.g., 14x14 for VGG/AlexNet).
The discriminative ability of Grad-CAM reduces when applied to earlier convolutional layers or at downsampling layers in architectures like ResNet.

papers.title: FairSteer: Inference Time Debiasing for LLMs with Dynamic Activation Steering
papers.research_question: Can fairness-related concepts be encoded as separable geometric structures in the hidden activation spaces of LLMs, enabling bias mitigation through activation steering?
